Management becomes palliative, and median survival is significantly reduced.

sections.overview: A Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) is a congenital heart defect characterized by an abnormal opening in the interventricular septum, the wall that separates the left and right ventricles. This opening allows blood to shunt between the ventricles. VSD is the most common congenital heart anomaly. The clinical significance depends on the size of the defect and the degree of shunting. As it typically involves a left-to-right shunt, it is classified as an **acyanotic** congenital heart disease.
sections.epidemiology: - The most common congenital heart defect, accounting for ~30% of all cases. - Incidence is approximately 2-6 per 1,000 live births. - **Classification by Location**: - **Perimembranous (80%)**: Most common type. Located in the upper septum, near the tricuspid and aortic valves. - **Muscular (15%)**: Located in the muscular portion of the septum. Often multiple ("Swiss cheese" septum). High rate of spontaneous closure. - **Supracristal / Outlet (5%)**: Located in the RV outflow tract, just below the pulmonary valve. High association with aortic valve prolapse and aortic regurgitation. More common in Asian populations. - **Inlet (5%)**: Located posterior and inferior, near the tricuspid and mitral valves. Often associated with atrioventricular canal defects (common in Trisomy 21).
riskFactors: Exposure to teratogens (e.g., phenytoin, valproic acid)
**Family History**: Increased risk if a first-degree relative has a congenital heart defect.
sections.clinicalPresentation: - **Small VSD**: Often discovered incidentally due to a loud murmur on routine examination in an otherwise asymptomatic, thriving infant. - **Moderate to Large VSD**: Symptoms of CHF typically appear at **4-6 weeks of age** as the pulmonary vascular resistance naturally falls, increasing the left-to-right shunt. The presentation includes failure to thrive, feeding difficulties, and respiratory distress.

diagnostics.notes: - **Echocardiogram (with Doppler)**: **Gold standard.** - Confirms the diagnosis. - Identifies the location, size, and number of defects. - Quantifies the shunt magnitude (Qp:Qs ratio). - Estimates RV and pulmonary artery pressures. - Assesses for chamber enlargement and associated anomalies. - **Chest X-ray (CXR)**: - **Small VSD**: Normal. - **Large VSD**: **Cardiomegaly** (due to LA and LV enlargement), **increased pulmonary vascular markings** (pulmonary plethora). - **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**: - **Small VSD**: Normal. - **Large VSD**: **Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH)** is classic due to volume overload. May show **Biventricular Hypertrophy (BVH)** if RV pressures are elevated. Left Atrial Enlargement (LAE) may also be present. - **Cardiac Catheterization**: Rarely needed for diagnosis. Used to precisely measure pulmonary vascular resistance in older patients before surgical consideration or for transcatheter device closure.

treatment: **Small, Asymptomatic VSDs**:
**Observation**: Many (especially muscular VSDs) close spontaneously, typically within the first 2 years of life.
Regular follow-up with cardiology.
Endocarditis prophylaxis is generally **not** recommended unless there is a prior history of endocarditis.
**Moderate to Large, Symptomatic VSDs**:
Goal: Control CHF symptoms and promote growth.
**Diuretics**: Furosemide (to reduce preload/pulmonary congestion).
**Afterload Reduction**: ACE inhibitors (e.g., Captopril, Enalapril) to decrease SVR and promote forward flow, thereby reducing the L->R shunt.
**Inotropic Support**: Digoxin (improves contractility, less commonly used now).
**Nutritional Support**: High-calorie formula/fortified breast milk to combat FTT. Nasogastric (NG) tube feeding may be necessary.
**Indications**:
Medically refractory CHF or failure to thrive.
Large VSD with evidence of developing pulmonary hypertension (Qp:Qs > 2:1).
VSD with associated aortic regurgitation.
**Timing**: Typically performed at **3-6 months of age**.
**Procedure**: Open-heart surgery with a patch closure (Dacron or pericardium).
management: **Follow-up**: Lifelong cardiology follow-up is recommended, even after repair, to monitor for residual shunts, arrhythmias, or valve issues.

**Endocarditis Prophylaxis**: Recommended for the first **6 months after surgical/device repair** with prosthetic material. Also recommended for life if there is a residual defect near the prosthetic patch.
**Activity**: No restrictions for small VSDs or after successful repair. Restrictions may apply if significant pulmonary hypertension persists.
complications: **Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)**: Most common complication in infancy with large defects.
**Eisenmenger Syndrome**: Irreversible pulmonary hypertension leading to shunt reversal (R->L), cyanosis, and severe exercise intolerance. This is a late and devastating complication.
**Infective Endocarditis**: Increased risk due to turbulent blood flow across the defect.
**Aortic Regurgitation**: Prolapse of an aortic valve cusp into the defect, most common with supracristal VSDs.
**Arrhythmias**: Can occur pre- or post-operatively (e.g., right bundle branch block is common after surgical repair).
**Failure to Thrive (FTT)**: Due to increased caloric expenditure from the work of breathing.
sections.prognosis: - **Excellent** for small VSDs, with most closing spontaneously. - **Excellent** for hemodynamically significant VSDs that are surgically repaired in infancy before the onset of irreversible pulmonary hypertension. Post-repair, patients typically have a normal life expectancy. - **Poor** for patients who develop Eisenmenger syndrome. Life expectancy is significantly reduced, and management is palliative (heart-lung transplant may be an option).

sections.overview: A Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) is a persistent connection between the descending thoracic aorta and the pulmonary artery that results from the failure of the fetal ductus arteriosus to close after birth. In fetal circulation, the ductus is a normal and essential structure that shunts blood away from the non-functional lungs. After birth, this connection's failure to close leads to a left-to-right shunt, causing abnormal blood flow between the two major vessels.
sections.epidemiology: * Occurs in approximately 1 in 2,000 live term births. * Significantly more common in **premature infants**, affecting up to 60% of infants born before 28 weeks gestation. * More common in females (2:1 ratio).
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation depends entirely on the size of the PDA and the degree of left-to-right shunting. * **Small PDA:** Often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally due to a characteristic murmur on routine examination. * **Moderate to Large PDA:** Presents in infancy with signs of heart failure and poor growth as pulmonary vascular resistance falls in the first few weeks of life.

diagnostics.notes: * **Echocardiogram (with Doppler):** * **Gold standard / test of choice.** * Directly visualizes the patent ductus. * Doppler flow shows the direction and velocity of the shunt. * Assesses secondary effects: LA and LV size, pulmonary artery pressure. * **Chest X-Ray (CXR):** * **Normal** in a small PDA. * **Large PDA:** Shows cardiomegaly (specifically LA and LV enlargement) and increased pulmonary vascular markings (**pulmonary plethora**). * **Electrocardiogram (ECG):** * **Normal** in a small PDA. * **Large PDA:** May show Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH) and Left Atrial Enlargement (LAE). Biventricular hypertrophy can be seen if pulmonary hypertension develops. * **Cardiac Catheterization:** * Primarily used for **therapeutic intervention** (device closure), not for diagnosis.

sections.prognosis: * **Excellent** with timely diagnosis and closure. Patients live a normal life with no restrictions post-closure. * If a large PDA is left untreated, mortality from heart failure or pulmonary hypertension is high in infancy or early adulthood.

sections.overview: An aortic aneurysm is a localized or diffuse dilation of the aorta to a diameter of at least 1.5 times its normal size. The normal aortic diameter is ~2 cm, with an aneurysm generally defined as **> 3.0 cm**. Aneurysms are classified by location (abdominal vs. thoracic) and morphology (fusiform vs. saccular). The primary clinical concern is the risk of rupture, a catastrophic event with extremely high mortality. * **Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA):** Most common type (~75%). Typically located **infrarenally** (below the renal arteries). * **Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA):** Less common. Can involve the aortic root, ascending aorta, aortic arch, or descending aorta. * **True Aneurysm:** Involves all three layers of the vessel wall (intima, media, adventitia). * **Pseudoaneurysm (False Aneurysm):** A contained rupture; the vessel wall is breached, and blood is contained by the adventitia or surrounding tissues.
sections.epidemiology: * **AAA:** * Prevalence: ~5% in men over 65. * Strong male predominance (M:F ratio 4:1). * Incidence increases significantly with age. * **TAA:** * Less common than AAA but incidence is rising due to increased imaging. * Affects men and women more equally than AAA. * Often diagnosed at a slightly younger age, especially when associated with genetic syndromes.
sections.clinicalPresentation: **The vast majority of aortic aneurysms are asymptomatic** and are discovered incidentally on imaging performed for other reasons. * **Asymptomatic:** Most common presentation. * **Symptomatic (unruptured):** * **AAA:** Vague, deep, gnawing pain in the abdomen, flank, or back. A new-onset of pain in a patient with a known aneurysm is a sign of impending rupture. * **TAA:** Chest, back (interscapular), or shoulder pain. Symptoms can arise from compression of adjacent structures: * **Hoarseness:** Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (Ortner's syndrome). * **Dysphagia:** Compression of the esophagus. * **Dyspnea, cough, stridor:** Compression of the trachea or bronchi. * **Rupture / Acute Dissection:** A surgical emergency. * **AAA Rupture:** Sudden onset of severe, tearing abdominal or back pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile abdominal mass. * **TAA Rupture/Dissection:** Sudden onset of severe, tearing/ripping chest or interscapular back pain, syncope, shock, unequal BPs in arms.

diagnostics.notes: | Test | Use | Notes | | | - | | | **Abdominal Ultrasound** | **Best initial test** for screening, diagnosis, and surveillance of AAA. | Non-invasive, no radiation, cost-effective. Limited by bowel gas and obesity. | | **CT Angiography (CTA)** | **Gold standard** for definitive diagnosis and pre-operative planning. | Provides precise size, location, extent, and involvement of branch vessels (renal, mesenteric). Requires IV contrast. | | **MRA** | Alternative to CTA for pre-operative planning. | Used in patients with contrast allergy or renal insufficiency. | | **Chest X-ray** | May show a **widened mediastinum** or enlarged aortic knob (TAA). Often an incidental finding. | Not sensitive or specific. | | **Bedside US (FAST)** | **Used in hemodynamically unstable patients** with suspected AAA rupture to rapidly confirm diagnosis before going to the OR. | The goal is rapid confirmation, not detailed measurement. If positive, patient goes directly to surgery. |

sections.prognosis: * **Elective Repair:** Low mortality rate (~2-5%). * **Ruptured AAA:** Extremely high mortality. **>50% die before reaching the hospital**. Of those who undergo surgery, perioperative mortality is still 30-50%. Overall mortality approaches 80-90%. * **Aneurysm Growth:** The annual risk of rupture increases exponentially with diameter. * < 4.0 cm: < 0.5% / year * 5.0 - 5.9 cm: 3-15% / year * > 7.0 cm: > 20% / year

sections.overview: Coarctation of the Aorta (CoA) is a congenital narrowing of the aortic lumen, most commonly located just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery at the site of the ductus arteriosus insertion (juxtaductal). This discrete stenosis creates an obstruction to blood flow, leading to hypertension in the upper extremities (proximal to the coarctation) and relative hypotension in the lower extremities (distal to the coarctation). The clinical presentation varies significantly with the severity of the narrowing, ranging from cardiogenic shock in newborns to asymptomatic hypertension discovered in adulthood.
sections.epidemiology: * Accounts for 5-8% of all congenital heart defects (CHD). * Male-to-female predominance of approximately 2:1. * Strong association with **Turner Syndrome (XO)**; CoA is found in ~15-20% of patients with Turner Syndrome.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation is highly dependent on the severity of the coarctation and the patient's age. * **Neonates (Severe Coarctation):** * Present within the first few days to weeks of life as the ductus arteriosus closes. * Develop sudden signs of cardiogenic shock and severe heart failure: poor feeding, lethargy, tachypnea, respiratory distress, and acidosis. This is a life-threatening emergency. * **Infants & Children (Moderate Coarctation):** * May present with failure to thrive, respiratory distress with feeding, or a heart murmur detected on routine exam. * **Older Children & Adults (Milder Coarctation):** * Often asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally due to hypertension or a murmur. * May present with symptoms related to hypertension (headaches, epistaxis) or lower extremity hypoperfusion (claudication, cold feet).

diagnostics.notes: * **Initial Evaluation:** * **Four-Limb Blood Pressure Measurement:** Essential for diagnosis. Confirms the upper-to-lower extremity systolic gradient. * **ECG:** May be normal. In significant cases, shows **Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH)** (high voltage in precordial leads, left axis deviation). * **Chest X-ray (CXR):** * **"Figure 3" Sign:** The indentation of the aorta at the coarctation site with pre- and post-stenotic dilation gives the aortic knob a "3" shape. * **Rib Notching:** **Pathognomonic finding** in older children/adults. Bilateral erosion of the inferior surfaces of the 3rd to 8th ribs by enlarged, pulsatile intercostal arteries. * **Confirmatory & Definitive Diagnosis:** * **Echocardiogram (Transthoracic):** **Primary diagnostic tool.** Directly visualizes the coarctation site, assesses severity with Doppler (measures pressure gradient), evaluates LV function and hypertrophy, and identifies associated anomalies like a bicuspid aortic valve. * **Advanced Imaging (for surgical/interventional planning):** * **CT Angiography (CTA) or MR Angiography (MRA):** Provide excellent, detailed 3D anatomical images of the entire aorta, the coarctation segment, and the collateral circulation.

sections.prognosis: * **With timely repair:** Excellent. Most individuals can expect a normal life expectancy and quality of life. * **Without repair:** Poor. The mean age of death is around 35 years due to complications like heart failure, aortic rupture, or intracranial hemorrhage. * The most common long-term morbidity is systemic hypertension.

sections.overview: Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA) is a cyanotic congenital heart defect characterized by **ventriculoarterial discordance**. In this condition, the aorta arises from the right ventricle (RV) and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle (LV). This creates two separate, parallel circulatory systems instead of a single series circuit. Deoxygenated systemic venous blood is pumped back to the body by the RV via the aorta, while oxygenated pulmonary venous blood is pumped back to the lungs by the LV via the pulmonary artery. This arrangement is incompatible with life unless there is mixing of blood between the two circuits through an associated defect such as an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD), Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD), or Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA).
sections.epidemiology: * Accounts for 5-7% of all congenital heart defects. * It is the **most common cyanotic heart lesion presenting in the neonatal period** (first 30 days of life). * Incidence is approximately 20-30 per 100,000 live births. * There is a male predominance (approx. 3:1).
sections.clinicalPresentation: * The classic presentation is a **full-term male infant** who develops profound central cyanosis within the **first few hours of life**. * The cyanosis is notable for being **unresponsive to supplemental oxygen**. * The infant often appears otherwise well-developed and comfortable at rest ("happy blue baby") initially, but respiratory distress (tachypnea) develops as metabolic acidosis worsens.

diagnostics.notes: * **Pulse Oximetry:** Low oxygen saturation, typically in the 70s-80s. * **Hyperoxia Test:** * The infant is placed on 100% inspired oxygen for 10 minutes. * A post-ductal (e.g., foot) PaO2 is measured. * In TGA, the PaO2 will show **minimal or no improvement** (typically remains <100 mmHg), distinguishing it from pulmonary causes of cyanosis. * **Chest X-ray (CXR):** * Classic finding is the "**egg on a string**" appearance. * The "egg" is the cardiomegaly from RV enlargement. * The "string" is the narrow superior mediastinum due to the abnormal anteroposterior alignment of the great vessels and involution of the thymus. * Pulmonary vascular markings are often increased. * **Electrocardiogram (ECG):** * Often normal in the newborn period. * May show right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) as the RV is the systemic ventricle. * **Echocardiogram:** * **Gold standard** for diagnosis. * Directly visualizes the aorta arising from the RV and the pulmonary artery from the LV. * Identifies the presence and size of associated defects (ASD, VSD, PDA) and assesses coronary artery anatomy, which is crucial for surgical planning. * **Cardiac Catheterization:** * Primarily therapeutic (**Balloon Atrial Septostomy**) rather than diagnostic.

sections.prognosis: * **Untreated:** Uniformly fatal. 90% mortality by 1 year of age. * **Treated:** With successful arterial switch surgery, the long-term prognosis is excellent. Survival rates are >95% at 20 years. Most individuals lead normal, active lives but require lifelong surveillance.

sections.overview: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the most common cyanotic congenital heart defect. It is defined by a constellation of four specific anatomical abnormalities that result from a single embryologic defect: the anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular (conal) septum. This displacement leads to a right-to-left shunting of deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation, causing central cyanosis. The severity of the clinical presentation is primarily determined by the degree of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (RVOTO).
sections.epidemiology: * Most common **cyanotic** congenital heart disease, accounting for ~10% of all congenital heart defects. * Incidence is approximately 1 in 2,500 live births. * Occurs equally in males and females.
sections.clinicalPresentation: Presentation depends entirely on the degree of RVOTO. * **"Pink Tet":** Infants with mild RVOTO may have minimal shunting and be acyanotic or have only intermittent cyanosis. They may present later in infancy with a heart murmur and signs of heart failure (due to a left-to-right shunt through the VSD). * **"Blue Tet":** Infants with severe RVOTO are cyanotic at birth or within the first few months of life. * **"Tet Spells" (Hypercyanotic Spells):** * Paroxysmal episodes of profound cyanosis and hypoxia. * Often precipitated by events that decrease SVR (crying, feeding, defecation, waking up) or increase RVOTO (infundibular spasm). * Pathophysiology: Decreased SVR or increased RVOTO worsens the right-to-left shunt, leading to a sudden drop in arterial oxygen saturation. This creates a vicious cycle of hypoxia, acidosis, and further infundibular spasm.

diagnostics.notes: * **Echocardiogram:** **Diagnostic test of choice.** Directly visualizes all four anatomic abnormalities, assesses the severity of RVOTO, and shows the direction of the shunt with color Doppler. * **Chest X-ray (CXR):** * **"Boot-shaped heart" (Coeur en sabot):** Caused by RVH (which uplifts the cardiac apex) and a concave main pulmonary artery segment. * Decreased pulmonary vascular markings (oligemia) if RVOTO is severe. * **Electrocardiogram (EKG):** * **Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH):** Tall R waves in V1, deep S waves in V6. * **Right Axis Deviation (RAD).** * **Pulse Oximetry:** Shows low oxygen saturation (<95%) that does not improve significantly with supplemental oxygen. * **Complete Blood Count (CBC):** Polycythemia (elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit) due to chronic hypoxia.

sections.prognosis: * **Untreated:** Poor. 25% mortality by age 1, 50% by age 5, and rare survival past age 40. * **Treated:** Excellent. With timely surgical repair, the 30-year survival rate is >90%. Most patients have a good quality of life, though they require lifelong monitoring and may require further intervention (e.g., pulmonary valve replacement).

sections.overview: Asthma is a chronic, heterogeneous inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by **airway hyperresponsiveness** and **reversible airflow obstruction**. The underlying inflammation leads to recurrent, episodic symptoms such as wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness, and cough, particularly at night or in the early morning. It is a common condition managed with a stepwise approach involving rescue and controller medications.
sections.epidemiology: * Affects ~8-10% of the U.S. population. * One of the most common chronic diseases of childhood. * **Childhood:** More common in boys. * **Adulthood:** More common in women. * Prevalence, morbidity, and mortality are higher in urban, low-income, and minority populations (particularly African American and Puerto Rican).
sections.clinicalPresentation: Patients typically present with a history of episodic respiratory symptoms. The presentation can range from mild, intermittent complaints to a life-threatening acute exacerbation (status asthmaticus). * **Triggers:** Symptoms are often precipitated by specific triggers such as exercise, upper respiratory infections, cold air, allergens, or smoke. * **Diurnal Variation:** Symptoms are classically worse **at night** or in the **early morning hours**. * **Cough-Variant Asthma:** Some patients may present with a chronic, non-productive cough as their sole symptom.

diagnostics.notes: * **Spirometry (Pulmonary Function Tests - PFTs):** * **Gold standard** for diagnosis. * Shows an **obstructive pattern**: * Decreased Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second (FEV1). * Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio (typically < 0.70 or below the lower limit of normal). * **Demonstration of Reversibility:** A significant increase in FEV1 (**>12% AND >200 mL**) after administration of a short-acting bronchodilator (SABA) confirms the diagnosis. * **Bronchial Provocation Test:** * Used when spirometry is non-diagnostic but clinical suspicion remains high. * Patient inhales a bronchoconstricting agent (e.g., **methacholine** or histamine). * A positive test is a **20% fall in FEV1** at a low concentration. High negative predictive value. * **Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) Meter:** * Excellent for **home monitoring** and assessing response to treatment, not for initial diagnosis. * A >20% diurnal variation is suggestive of asthma. * **Chest X-ray (CXR):** * Often normal. * Primarily used to rule out other conditions (e.g., pneumonia, pneumothorax, foreign body). * During a severe exacerbation, may show signs of **hyperinflation** (flattened diaphragms). * **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG):** * Reserved for severe exacerbations. * **Initially:** Hypoxemia (low PaO2) with respiratory alkalosis (low PaCO2) due to hyperventilation. * **Impending Respiratory Failure:** A "normalizing" or elevated PaCO2 is an ominous sign indicating patient fatigue and imminent failure. * **Other:** CBC may show eosinophilia; allergy testing can identify specific triggers.

sections.prognosis: * Excellent with proper diagnosis, education, and adherence to a management plan. * Mortality is rare but often preventable. * Many children experience remission during adolescence, although symptoms may return in adulthood. * Poorly controlled asthma can lead to a progressive decline in lung function.

sections.overview: Chronic Bronchitis is a clinical diagnosis defined by a **chronic productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years**, in a patient in whom other causes of chronic cough have been excluded. It is a subtype of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) characterized by inflammation and mucus hypersecretion in the bronchial airways. The classic phenotype is the **"Blue Bloater,"** referring to the cyanosis (from hypoxemia) and peripheral edema (from right heart failure) often seen in advanced disease.
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** Affects millions of Americans; a major component of COPD, which is the 4th leading cause of death in the US. * **Age:** Onset typically after age 40. * **Gender:** Historically more common in men, but the incidence in women is rising and now nearly equal due to changes in smoking patterns.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The classic patient is an overweight, cyanotic smoker in their 50s or 60s who presents with a chief complaint of a chronic, daily "smoker's cough" that produces phlegm, especially in the mornings. They often report frequent "chest colds" (acute exacerbations) each winter. Dyspnea on exertion is common, but they may be comfortable at rest ("quiet tachypnea" is less common than in emphysema).

diagnostics.notes: * **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs) / Spirometry:** **Gold standard for diagnosis of COPD.** * **Required finding:** Post-bronchodilator **FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.70**. This confirms persistent airflow obstruction. * **FEV1 is decreased**, and the degree of reduction is used for staging severity (GOLD Criteria). * Increased Residual Volume (RV) and Total Lung Capacity (TLC) due to air trapping. * **Chest X-Ray (CXR):** * Often nonspecific. May show increased bronchovascular markings ("dirty lungs") and bronchial wall thickening. * Primarily used to rule out other conditions like pneumonia, lung cancer, or heart failure. * Diaphragms are typically normal or rounded (not flattened like in emphysema). * **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG):** * Reveals **chronic respiratory acidosis**: low PaO2 (hypoxemia), high PaCO2 (hypercapnia), and compensatory high HCO3-. * **Complete Blood Count (CBC):** * May show **polycythemia** (elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit) as a result of chronic hypoxemia stimulating erythropoietin production. * **Sputum Culture:** Useful during acute exacerbations to identify bacterial pathogens if there is a poor response to initial therapy.

sections.prognosis: * Chronic bronchitis is a progressive, irreversible disease. * Prognosis is poor without smoking cessation. * The **BODE Index** (Body mass index, Obstruction [FEV1], Dyspnea [mMRC scale], Exercise capacity [6-minute walk test]) is a validated tool for predicting mortality. * FEV1 is a strong predictor of survival.

sections.overview: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a common, preventable, and treatable disease characterized by **persistent respiratory symptoms** and **airflow limitation** that is due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities, usually caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases. The airflow limitation is **not fully reversible**. COPD includes two primary phenotypes that often coexist: * **Emphysema:** Pathologic diagnosis defined by the permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by the destruction of their walls and without obvious fibrosis. * **Chronic Bronchitis:** Clinical diagnosis defined by a chronic productive cough for **three months in each of two successive years** in a patient in whom other causes of chronic cough have been excluded.
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** 3rd leading cause of death worldwide. * **Age:** Disease prevalence increases with age; rarely diagnosed in patients <40 years old. * **Gender:** Historically more common in men, but rates are now nearly equal due to changes in smoking patterns.
sections.clinicalPresentation: Presentation is typically insidious, with a gradual progression of symptoms over years. Patients are often former or current smokers over the age of 40. The classic phenotypes are useful for understanding pathophysiology but patients often present with a mix of features. * **Emphysema-Dominant ("Pink Puffer"):** * **Primary Symptom:** Severe dyspnea, often with minimal cough. * **Appearance:** Thin, cachectic, barrel-chested. * **Breathing:** Uses accessory muscles, breathes through pursed lips to maintain airway pressure ("auto-PEEP"). * **ABG:** Often maintain normal oxygenation (PaO2) and CO2 levels (PaCO2) until late-stage disease by increasing minute ventilation (hence "puffer"). * **Chronic Bronchitis-Dominant ("Blue Bloater"):** * **Primary Symptom:** Chronic, productive cough. * **Appearance:** Often overweight and cyanotic. * **Signs:** Peripheral edema (due to cor pulmonale), noisy lungs with rhonchi and wheezes. * **ABG:** Chronic hypoxemia and hypercapnia are common due to severe V/Q mismatch. This drives pulmonary vasoconstriction and polycythemia (hence "blue").

diagnostics.notes: * **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs) / Spirometry:** * **THE GOLD STANDARD for diagnosis.** * A post-bronchodilator **FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.70** confirms the presence of persistent airflow limitation and thus COPD. * **FEV1 (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second):** Decreased. The severity of obstruction is classified based on the post-bronchodilator FEV1 % predicted (GOLD stages 1-4). * **Lung Volumes:** Increased Total Lung Capacity (TLC) and Residual Volume (RV) indicate air trapping/hyperinflation. Decreased Diffusing Capacity for Carbon Monoxide (DLCO) is characteristic of emphysema due to alveolar destruction. * **Chest X-Ray (CXR):** * Not diagnostic but used to rule out other pathology. * **Classic Findings:** * **Flattened diaphragms** * Increased AP diameter on lateral view * Hyperlucency of lung fields * Bullae (lucent, air-filled spaces) * **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG):** * Not routine for stable patients. * Assesses for hypoxemia and hypercapnia in severe disease or acute exacerbations. * **Findings:** Chronic respiratory acidosis (elevated PaCO2) with metabolic compensation (elevated HCO3-). * **CBC:** May show **polycythemia** (increased hematocrit/hemoglobin) as a response to chronic hypoxemia. * **Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) Level:** Screen in patients diagnosed at a young age (<45), non-smokers, or with a strong family history.

sections.prognosis: * Prognosis is generally poor and the disease is progressive. * The **BODE Index** is a validated tool for predicting mortality: * **B**MI (lower is worse) * **O**bstruction (FEV1) * **D**yspnea (mMRC scale) * **E**xercise capacity (6-minute walk test) * Frequent exacerbations are associated with a faster decline in lung function and higher mortality.

sections.overview: Emphysema is a major pathologic type of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). It is anatomically defined by the permanent, abnormal enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by the destruction of their walls and without obvious fibrosis. This destruction leads to a loss of alveolar surface area for gas exchange and a loss of elastic recoil, resulting in expiratory airflow limitation and air trapping. Clinically, it is characterized by progressive dyspnea. The classic patient phenotype is the "pink puffer."
sections.epidemiology: * Emphysema is a component of COPD, which is the 4th leading cause of death in the United States. * Prevalence increases with age, most commonly diagnosed in individuals > 40 years old. * Strongly associated with a cumulative history of cigarette smoking (measured in pack-years). * AAT deficiency affects approximately 1 in 2,500-5,000 individuals and accounts for 1-2% of all COPD cases.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The "Pink Puffer" is the classic archetype for a patient with predominant emphysema. * **History:** Long history of slowly progressive dyspnea on exertion, often present for years before seeking care. They may have a minimal, non-productive cough. * **General Appearance:** Often thin with evidence of weight loss (cachexia) due to the high work of breathing. They appear uncomfortable, often sitting in a **tripod position** (leaning forward, hands on knees) to maximize use of accessory respiratory muscles. * **Breathing Pattern:** They use **pursed-lip breathing** to increase intra-airway pressure and prevent premature airway collapse during expiration. There is a prolonged expiratory phase.

diagnostics.notes: * **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs) / Spirometry:** **Gold standard for diagnosis.** * **Obstructive Pattern:** Decreased **FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.70** (post-bronchodilator) is required for diagnosis. * **Decreased FEV1:** Correlates with disease severity (GOLD staging). * **Increased Lung Volumes:** Increased Total Lung Capacity (TLC), Functional Residual Capacity (FRC), and Residual Volume (RV) due to air trapping. * **Decreased Diffusing Capacity (DLCO):** A key finding that distinguishes emphysema from pure chronic bronchitis or asthma. Caused by the destruction of the alveolar-capillary membrane. * **Chest X-Ray (CXR):** * **Hyperinflation:** Over-aeration of the lungs. * **Flattened Diaphragms**. * Increased AP diameter (seen on lateral view). * Bullae (lucent, air-filled spaces >1 cm). * Small, vertical-appearing heart ("hanging heart"). * **High-Resolution CT (HRCT) Chest:** * Most sensitive and specific imaging modality. * Directly visualizes parenchymal destruction and bullae. * Can differentiate between centriacinar and panacinar patterns. * **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG):** * Early/Mild: May be normal or show mild hypoxemia. * Advanced: Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation ( PaCO2, HCO3-, near-normal pH). * **Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) Level:** * Screen all patients diagnosed with COPD, especially those < 45 years old, non-smokers, or with a basilar-predominant pattern of emphysema.

sections.prognosis: * Prognosis is generally poor and the disease is progressive. * FEV1 is a strong predictor of mortality. * **BODE Index** is a multidimensional scoring system that is a better predictor of mortality than FEV1 alone: * **B**ody Mass Index (BMI) * **O**bstruction (FEV1) * **D**yspnea (mMRC scale) * **E**xercise capacity (6-minute walk test)

sections.overview: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (*CFTR*) gene. This defect leads to impaired transport of chloride, bicarbonate, and water across epithelial surfaces, resulting in thick, viscous secretions in multiple organ systems. It is a progressive, multi-system disease primarily affecting the respiratory, gastrointestinal (pancreas, liver, intestines), and reproductive tracts.
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence**: The most common life-shortening inherited disease among Caucasians of Northern European descent. * **Incidence**: Approximately 1 in 3,000 live births in the Caucasian population. * **Carrier Frequency**: ~1 in 25 Caucasians. * **Screening**: Included in standard newborn screening panels in all 50 U.S. states.
sections.clinicalPresentation: Presentation varies significantly with age and genotype. * **Newborns/Infants**: * **Meconium ileus**: Bowel obstruction in a newborn who fails to pass stool. * **Failure to thrive**: Poor weight gain despite adequate appetite. * **Steatorrhea**: Frequent, greasy, foul-smelling stools. * Recurrent respiratory infections, persistent cough. * Salty-tasting skin. * **Children/Adolescents**: * Chronic sinopulmonary disease: persistent productive cough, recurrent pneumonia, chronic sinusitis, **nasal polyps**. * GI symptoms: Poor growth, constipation, **rectal prolapse** (from straining and malnutrition), DIOS. * Physical signs: **Digital clubbing**. * **Adults**: * Often present with milder or "atypical" CF. * May be diagnosed due to chronic pancreatitis, bronchiectasis of unknown cause, or infertility (especially males with CBAVD).

diagnostics.notes: | Test | Purpose | Findings in CF | | : | : | : | | **Newborn Screen (NBS)** | Initial screening | Elevated **Immunoreactive Trypsinogen (IRT)**. | | **Sweat Chloride Test** | **Gold standard** for diagnosis | ** 60 mmol/L** on two separate occasions is diagnostic. 30-59 mmol/L is intermediate. | | **CFTR Genetic Analysis** | Confirmatory testing, identifies mutations | Identifies two disease-causing *CFTR* mutations. Essential for guiding CFTR modulator therapy. | | **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs)** | Assess lung function & disease progression | **Obstructive pattern** ( FEV1, FEV1/FVC ratio). Air trapping ( RV/TLC ratio). | | **Chest Imaging (CXR/CT)** | Assess structural lung damage | Hyperinflation, mucus plugging, bronchial wall thickening (**bronchial cuffing**), **bronchiectasis** ("tram tracks"). | | **Sputum Culture** | Identify pathogens for targeted therapy | Common pathogens: ***S. aureus***, ***H. influenzae*** (early); ***P. aeruginosa*** (later); ***B. cepacia*** (ominous). | | **Fecal Elastase-1** | Screen for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency | **Low** (<200 mcg/g) indicates insufficiency. |

sections.prognosis: * The prognosis has improved dramatically. The median predicted survival age in the U.S. is now in the **early 50s** and continues to increase, especially with the widespread use of CFTR modulators. * The primary cause of mortality remains progressive respiratory failure.

sections.overview: Bronchiectasis is a chronic pulmonary disease characterized by **permanent, irreversible dilation and destruction of the bronchial airways**. This structural damage impairs mucociliary clearance, leading to a "vicious cycle" of chronic bacterial infection, airway inflammation, and further structural damage. It is an obstructive lung disease.
sections.epidemiology: * Prevalence is increasing, particularly in older adults. * More common in women than men. * Non-CF bronchiectasis is more common than CF-related bronchiectasis overall.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient typically presents with a long history of a persistent productive cough and recurrent respiratory infections ("chest colds") that are slow to resolve, often requiring multiple or prolonged courses of antibiotics. They may report daily sputum production, sometimes tinged with blood.

diagnostics.notes: * **High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) of the chest:** * **This is the diagnostic test of choice.** * **Key Findings:** * **Bronchial wall thickening and dilation**: Airways appear larger than the adjacent pulmonary artery (**"signet ring" sign**). * **Lack of airway tapering**: Bronchi remain wide in the lung periphery. * Parallel bronchial walls that look like linear opacities (**"tram tracks"**). * Visible cysts or saccules, sometimes with air-fluid levels. * **Chest X-ray (CXR):** * Often the first imaging test performed but is insensitive and non-specific. * May show "tram tracks," cystic changes, or increased interstitial markings, but a normal CXR does not rule out bronchiectasis. * **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs):** * Show an **obstructive pattern**: decreased FEV1, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio (<0.70). * Unlike asthma, there is often little to no reversibility with bronchodilators. * **Sputum Analysis:** * **Crucial for management**, especially during exacerbations. * Gram stain and culture to identify bacterial pathogens (e.g., *H. influenzae*, *P. aeruginosa*, *S. aureus*, *M. catarrhalis*). * AFB smear and culture to test for TB and NTM (especially MAC). * **Etiology Workup (once diagnosed):** * **Sweat chloride test / CFTR genetic testing** (to rule out CF). * Quantitative immunoglobulin levels (to rule out CVID). * *Aspergillus* skin testing, precipitins, and total IgE (for ABPA). * Alpha-1 antitrypsin level.

sections.prognosis: * A chronic, progressive disease with no cure. * Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the underlying etiology, severity of lung damage, and frequency of exacerbations. * Negative prognostic factors include older age, low FEV1, and chronic colonization with ***Pseudomonas aeruginosa***.

sections.overview: Pulmonary Hypertension (PH) is a pathophysiological state defined by an elevated mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) of **> 20 mmHg at rest**, as determined by right heart catheterization. It is not a single disease but a hemodynamic condition that can result from numerous underlying causes. The condition leads to increased pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), progressive right ventricular (RV) overload, and eventual right heart failure (cor pulmonale), which is the primary cause of death. The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies PH into 5 distinct groups based on etiology, which is critical for guiding diagnosis and treatment.
sections.epidemiology: * Overall prevalence is significant, but Group 1 PAH is rare (approx. 15-50 cases per million). * Group 2 PH (due to LHD) is the most prevalent form. * Group 1 PAH shows a female predominance (~2:1) and typically presents in young to middle-aged adults (30-60 years).
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation is often insidious, with non-specific symptoms leading to a significant delay in diagnosis (average >2 years). The classic patient is a young-to-middle-aged female presenting with progressive, unexplained dyspnea on exertion. As the disease progresses, signs of right heart failure become more prominent.

diagnostics.notes: The diagnostic workup is aimed at confirming the presence of PH, identifying the WHO group, and assessing severity. 1. **Best Initial Test (Screening):** **Transthoracic Echocardiogram (TTE)** * Estimates the right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) and pulmonary artery pressure. * Assesses RV size, thickness, and function. * Evaluates for left heart disease (Group 2) or congenital defects. 2. **Gold Standard (Confirmatory):** **Right Heart Catheterization (RHC)** * **Required for definitive diagnosis** and to guide therapy. * Directly measures: * Mean Pulmonary Arterial Pressure (mPAP) * Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) - an estimate of left atrial pressure. * Pulmonary Vascular Resistance (PVR) * Cardiac Output (CO) * **Hemodynamic Definitions:** * **PH:** mPAP > 20 mmHg * **Pre-capillary PH (Groups 1, 3, 4, 5):** mPAP > 20, **PCWP 15 mmHg**, PVR 3 Wood units. * **Post-capillary PH (Group 2):** mPAP > 20, **PCWP > 15 mmHg**. 3. **Tests to Determine Etiology (WHO Group):** * **Chest X-Ray (CXR):** May show enlarged central pulmonary arteries ("pruning" of peripheral vessels) and RV enlargement (cardiomegaly). * **ECG:** May be normal or show signs of RV hypertrophy (right axis deviation, R wave in V1 > S wave) and RV strain (T wave inversions in V1-V3, inferior leads). * **V/Q Scan:** **Screening test of choice for CTEPH (Group 4).** Preferred over CTPA for chronic clots. * **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs):** To diagnose underlying lung disease (Group 3). Often shows a reduced DLCO. * **Labs:** CBC, CMP, LFTs, HIV test, ANA panel (for CTD), BNP/NT-proBNP (prognostic marker).

sections.prognosis: * Without treatment, idiopathic PAH has a very poor prognosis with a median survival of <3 years. * With modern therapies, the prognosis has significantly improved, but it remains a life-limiting chronic illness. * Prognosis for other groups is largely determined by the severity and management of the underlying condition.

sections.overview: Cor pulmonale is defined as **right ventricular (RV) hypertrophy and/or dilation and dysfunction** that is caused by **pulmonary hypertension (PH)**, which in turn results from a primary disease of the **lung parenchyma, vasculature, or chest wall**. Crucially, it is **NOT** caused by left-sided heart failure or congenital heart disease. It is purely right-sided heart failure secondary to a pulmonary process. * **Acute Cor Pulmonale:** RV dilation and failure following a sudden increase in pulmonary artery pressure (e.g., massive pulmonary embolism). * **Chronic Cor Pulmonale:** Gradual RV hypertrophy and subsequent dilation due to a slowly progressing underlying lung condition (e.g., COPD).
sections.epidemiology: * Difficult to determine precise incidence as it is a complication of other diseases. * The prevalence directly mirrors that of its underlying causes, especially **COPD**. * Estimated to account for 5-10% of all hospital admissions for heart failure. * Predominantly affects older adults, consistent with the demographics of chronic lung disease.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation is often insidious, with symptoms of right heart failure superimposed on the symptoms of the underlying chronic lung disease. Patients typically present with a gradual worsening of their baseline respiratory status, now with new or worsening signs of fluid overload.

diagnostics.notes: * **ECG:** * **P pulmonale:** Peaked P waves (>2.5 mm) in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) indicating right atrial enlargement. * **Right Axis Deviation**. * **RV Hypertrophy:** R wave > S wave in lead V1; deep S wave in V6. * S1Q3T3 pattern (seen in acute cor pulmonale/PE). * **Chest X-ray (CXR):** * Enlargement of the right atrium, right ventricle, and central pulmonary arteries. * "Pruning" of the peripheral pulmonary vessels. * Evidence of the underlying lung disease (e.g., hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms in COPD). * **Echocardiogram (Transthoracic):** * **Best initial imaging test** to assess cardiac structure. * Shows **RV hypertrophy, RV dilation**, and paradoxical septal motion. * Allows for estimation of the **pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP)**. * Crucially helps **rule out left-sided heart disease** as the cause of the RHF. * **BNP / NT-proBNP:** * Elevated due to ventricular stretch but is **not specific** for cor pulmonale; can be elevated in any cause of heart failure. * **Right Heart Catheterization:** * **Gold standard** for diagnosing pulmonary hypertension and confirming cor pulmonale. * Directly measures pulmonary artery pressure (mean PAP 25 mmHg at rest). * Measures pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP). A **normal PCWP (15 mmHg)** confirms the PH is **pre-capillary** (i.e., from the lungs) and rules out left heart failure as the cause. * **Other:** * **PFTs:** To diagnose and quantify the severity of the underlying lung disease. * **CT Angiography / V/Q Scan:** To evaluate for chronic thromboembolic disease (CTEPH). * **Sleep Study (Polysomnography):** If OSA is suspected.

sections.prognosis: * The prognosis is generally **poor** as cor pulmonale represents an advanced stage of chronic pulmonary disease. * The prognosis is tied directly to the severity and progression of the underlying lung condition. * The presence of cor pulmonale is a significant negative prognostic indicator in patients with COPD. Median survival after diagnosis can be as low as 2-5 years, but this is highly variable.

sections.overview: Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) is an acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma in a patient who has acquired the infection in the community, as distinguished from hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP). Diagnosis is established by the presence of a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest imaging combined with clinical signs and symptoms of a lower respiratory tract infection. The decision to treat as an outpatient or inpatient is a critical management step, often guided by clinical scoring systems like CURB-65.
sections.epidemiology: * One of the most common infectious diseases. * A leading cause of hospitalization and death, especially in the elderly. * Incidence is highest during winter months, correlating with viral respiratory season. * Mortality rate is <1-5% for outpatients but can be as high as 25% for patients requiring ICU admission.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation can be divided into "typical" and "atypical" syndromes, although significant overlap exists. * **Typical Pneumonia:** Characterized by the sudden onset of: * High fever, shaking chills (rigors) * Productive cough with purulent or rust-colored sputum * Pleuritic chest pain * Significant dyspnea * Patient appears acutely ill. * **Atypical Pneumonia ("Walking Pneumonia"):** Characterized by a more indolent, subacute course: * Low-grade fever * Dry, non-productive cough * Prominent constitutional and extrapulmonary symptoms: headache, malaise, myalgias, sore throat, GI symptoms. * Patient often appears less ill than CXR findings might suggest.

diagnostics.notes: * **Chest X-Ray (CXR):** * **The cornerstone of diagnosis.** A new infiltrate is required. * **Findings:** * **Lobar consolidation:** Classic for *S. pneumoniae*. * **Patchy/Interstitial infiltrates:** Often seen in atypical or viral pneumonia. * **Cavitary lesions:** Suggestive of *S. aureus*, *Klebsiella*, or anaerobes (abscess). * **Pleural effusion:** Fluid in the pleural space. * **Laboratory Studies:** * **CBC with differential:** Leukocytosis (>12,000) with a left shift (increased neutrophils/bands) is common in bacterial pneumonia. * **CMP:** To assess for dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities (e.g., **hyponatremia with *Legionella***), and renal/hepatic function (important for CURB-65 and antibiotic choice). * **Procalcitonin (PCT):** Can help differentiate bacterial vs. viral etiologies. High levels (>0.5 ng/mL) suggest bacterial infection. * **C-Reactive Protein (CRP):** Non-specific inflammatory marker, usually elevated. * **Microbiologic Testing (Mainly for Hospitalized Patients):** * **Sputum Gram Stain and Culture:** Obtain before antibiotics if possible. A good quality sample has >25 PMNs and <10 squamous epithelial cells per low-power field. * **Blood Cultures x2:** Indicated for all severe CAP patients (ICU) and recommended for most hospitalized patients prior to antibiotic administration. * **Urinary Antigen Tests:** Rapid tests for *S. pneumoniae* and *Legionella pneumophila* serogroup 1. High specificity. * **Nasopharyngeal Swab (PCR):** For influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and other respiratory viruses.

sections.prognosis: * Excellent for young, healthy outpatients. * Mortality increases significantly with age, comorbidities, and severity of illness. * CURB-65 score correlates with mortality: * Score 0-1: ~1.5% mortality * Score 2: ~9% mortality * Score 3-5: ~15-40% mortality

sections.overview: Viral pneumonia is an infection of the lung parenchyma caused by a viral pathogen. It is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), particularly in children and older adults. The clinical presentation is often characterized as an "atypical pneumonia," with a more gradual onset and prominent constitutional symptoms compared to classic bacterial pneumonia. The inflammatory response primarily affects the interstitial space rather than causing lobar consolidation.
sections.epidemiology: * Accounts for approximately 15-30% of all CAP cases. * **Seasonality:** Follows predictable patterns. * **Influenza:** Peaks in fall and winter. * **RSV & hMPV:** Peak in winter and early spring. * **Outbreaks:** Often occur in closed communities like nursing homes, military barracks, and schools. * **Pandemics:** Viruses like Influenza and Coronaviruses have pandemic potential.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation is often insidious, beginning with a prodrome of upper respiratory infection (URI) symptoms that progresses over several days. Constitutional symptoms are typically more prominent than in bacterial pneumonia.

diagnostics.notes: * **Imaging:** * **Chest X-Ray (CXR):** * **Classic Finding:** **Bilateral, diffuse interstitial infiltrates.** * Other patterns: Patchy infiltrates, peribronchial cuffing. Lobar consolidation is uncommon. * **Chest CT (High Resolution):** * More sensitive than CXR. * **Hallmark Finding:** **Ground-glass opacities (GGOs)**, often bilateral and peripheral. * **Laboratory Studies:** * **CBC with Differential:** * WBC count can be normal, low, or mildly elevated. * Often shows a **lymphocytic predominance** rather than the neutrophilia seen in bacterial infections. * **Inflammatory Markers:** * C-reactive protein (CRP) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) are elevated but non-specific. * **Procalcitonin (PCT):** * **High-yield:** Typically **normal or only minimally elevated (<0.25 ng/mL)**. A high PCT (>0.5 ng/mL) should raise suspicion for a secondary bacterial infection. * **Pathogen Identification (Gold Standard):** * **PCR (NAAT - Nucleic Acid Amplification Test):** Test of choice for identifying specific viral pathogens. * **Sample Source:** Nasopharyngeal swab, sputum, or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid. * **Rapid Antigen Tests:** Available for Influenza, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. They are faster but less sensitive than PCR.

sections.prognosis: * **Good** in most young, healthy individuals who often recover fully. * **Guarded to Poor** in elderly patients, those with significant comorbidities, or the immunocompromised. * Mortality is significantly increased in patients who develop ARDS or secondary bacterial infections.

sections.overview: Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP) is a pneumonia that is not incubating at the time of hospital admission and occurs ** 48 hours after admission**. It is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in hospitalized patients. * **Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP)**: A subtype of HAP that develops **> 48 hours after endotracheal intubation**. It is associated with the highest mortality rates among nosocomial infections. * **Key Distinction from CAP**: Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) develops outside of the hospital setting. HAP is distinguished by a different, more resistant spectrum of causative pathogens, most notably *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* and MRSA. * **Deprecated Term**: Healthcare-Associated Pneumonia (HCAP) is an outdated term. The current guidelines focus on assessing individual patient risk factors for multidrug-resistant (MDR) organisms rather than the site of care.
sections.epidemiology: * HAP is the second most common nosocomial infection (after UTI). * It is the **leading cause of death** among all hospital-acquired infections. * VAP occurs in 9-27% of all mechanically ventilated patients. * The risk of developing VAP increases by approximately 1-3% for each day of mechanical ventilation.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The diagnosis requires a **new or progressive pulmonary infiltrate on imaging** plus at least two of the following clinical criteria in a patient hospitalized for 48 hours: 1. **Fever** (>38.0C / 100.4F) 2. **Leukocytosis** (>12,000/L) or **Leukopenia** (<4,000/L) 3. **Purulent sputum** (new onset or change in character) 4. Worsening gas exchange (hypoxia, increased O2 requirement)

diagnostics.notes: * **Imaging**: * **Chest X-Ray (CXR)**: **Essential for diagnosis.** Will show a new or progressive opacity, consolidation, cavitation, or pleural effusion. Can be difficult to interpret in patients with pre-existing ARDS or CHF. * **Chest CT**: More sensitive than CXR for identifying infiltrates, abscesses, and empyema. * **Laboratory**: * **CBC with differential**: Leukocytosis with a left shift or leukopenia. * **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG)**: To quantify hypoxemia and assess acid-base status. * **Inflammatory Markers**: Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin. Procalcitonin is more specific for bacterial infections and can be trended to guide de-escalation of antibiotics. * **Microbiology (Crucial for targeted therapy)**: * **Blood Cultures (x2)**: Obtain prior to starting antibiotics. * **Lower Respiratory Tract Sampling**: * **Non-invasive**: Spontaneous or induced sputum sample for Gram stain and culture. Often contaminated by upper airway flora. A good quality sample has >25 neutrophils and <10 squamous epithelial cells per low-power field. * **Invasive (for intubated patients)**: **Endotracheal aspirate** is easily obtained. **Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL)** or a **protected specimen brush (PSB)** via bronchoscopy provides a higher-quality sample with less contamination and allows for quantitative cultures.

sections.prognosis: * Mortality is high, ranging from **20-50%**. * Prognosis is worse for VAP compared to HAP. * Negative prognostic factors include infection with MDR organisms (*Pseudomonas*, MRSA, *Acinetobacter*), bacteremia, delayed or inappropriate empiric antibiotics, and severe underlying comorbidities.

sections.overview: Atypical pneumonia is a type of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) caused by organisms that are not detectable on a standard Gram stain and are not susceptible to beta-lactam antibiotics. The term "atypical" originally referred to the insidious onset and extrapulmonary manifestations that differ from the "typical" abrupt presentation of *Streptococcus pneumoniae*. It is often referred to as "walking pneumonia" because the symptoms are frequently mild enough that patients do not require bed rest or hospitalization.
sections.epidemiology: * ***Mycoplasma pneumoniae***: Peak incidence in school-aged children, military recruits, and college students. Epidemics occur in 3-7 year cycles, often in late summer and fall. Accounts for up to 20% of all CAP. * ***Chlamydophila pneumoniae***: Common worldwide, responsible for 5-15% of CAP cases. Outbreaks can occur in closed populations. * ***Legionella pneumophila***: Sporadic outbreaks are common. More prevalent in the summer and fall. Tends to affect older adults, smokers, and immunocompromised individuals. Not transmitted person-to-person.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation is typically subacute and insidious over several days to weeks. Patients often appear non-toxic and are able to continue daily activities, hence the term "walking pneumonia."

diagnostics.notes: * **Chest X-ray (CXR)**: * The classic finding is **diffuse, patchy, reticulonodular or interstitial infiltrates**, most commonly in the lower lobes. * Pleural effusions can be seen but are uncommon. * Lobar consolidation is rare, in contrast to typical pneumonia. * **Laboratory Studies**: * **CBC**: WBC count is often normal or only mildly elevated. * **Sputum Gram Stain**: Reveals few or no bacteria and few neutrophils. * **Pathogen-Specific Testing**: * ***Mycoplasma pneumoniae***: * **PCR** of throat swab or sputum is the test of choice (sensitive and specific). * **Serology** (IgM, IgG): A four-fold rise in IgG titers between acute and convalescent samples is diagnostic. * **Cold agglutinins**: A bedside test showing clumping of RBCs when cooled. It is classic for board exams but has low sensitivity and specificity. * ***Legionella pneumophila***: * **Urine antigen test**: Rapid and highly specific for serogroup 1 (the most common cause of disease), but less sensitive. The test of choice for rapid diagnosis. * **Sputum culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar**: The gold standard, but slow. * **Labs**: May show **hyponatremia**, elevated liver function tests (LFTs), and elevated creatine kinase (CK). * ***Chlamydophila pneumoniae***: * **PCR** is the preferred method. * **Serology**: Difficult to interpret due to high baseline seroprevalence.

sections.prognosis: * The prognosis for *Mycoplasma* and *Chlamydophila* pneumonia in healthy individuals is excellent with appropriate treatment. The cough may linger for several weeks. * The prognosis for *Legionella* is more guarded, with mortality rates of 10-15% in hospitalized patients, and higher in those who are immunocompromised or have delayed treatment.

sections.overview: A pleural effusion is an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pleural space, the potential space between the visceral pleura (lining the lung) and the parietal pleura (lining the chest wall). Normally, this space contains a small amount (~5-15 mL) of serous fluid that acts as a lubricant. Pathologic accumulation occurs when the rate of fluid formation exceeds the rate of fluid removal by the pleural lymphatics.
sections.epidemiology: - Affects approximately 1.5 million people in the United States annually. - The most common causes are CHF, pneumonia, and malignancy. - Malignant pleural effusions are a common complication of metastatic cancer and carry a poor prognosis.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation depends on the size of the effusion, the rate of fluid accumulation, and the underlying disease process. A patient may be asymptomatic with a small effusion discovered incidentally, or present in severe respiratory distress with a large, rapidly accumulating effusion.

imaging: **Initial test of choice.**
**PA/AP View:** **Blunting of the costophrenic angle** is the earliest sign (requires ~250 mL of fluid). A "meniscus sign" may be visible as fluid tracks up the chest wall.
**Lateral Decubitus View:** Most sensitive CXR view. Can detect as little as 50 mL of fluid. Fluid layers out on the dependent side.
Highly sensitive for detecting small effusions.
Excellent for identifying loculations (septations) and guiding thoracentesis.

Not required for simple effusions but is the best test for evaluating underlying lung parenchyma, pleural thickening, loculations, and identifying potential causes like malignancy or empyema ("split pleura sign").

management: **Transudate:** Focus on systemic disease management (diuresis, etc.).

**Exudate:** Further investigation to find the local cause (CT chest, cytology, etc.) and treat specifically. For complicated infections, ensure prompt and complete drainage. For recurrent malignant effusions, plan for definitive management with an IPC or pleurodesis.
complications: **Empyema:** Infection of the pleural space.
**Trapped Lung (or Encased Lung):** A fibrous peel forms on the visceral pleura, preventing the lung from re-expanding after fluid removal.
**Respiratory Failure:** Large effusions can compromise lung function.
**Iatrogenic Complications from Thoracentesis:**
Pneumothorax
Hemothorax
Re-expansion pulmonary edema (if >1.5 L is removed too quickly)
Infection
sections.prognosis: - The prognosis is entirely dependent on the underlying etiology. - Effusions related to benign, treatable conditions (e.g., uncomplicated pneumonia) have an excellent prognosis. - Effusions from CHF are associated with advanced heart disease. - **A malignant pleural effusion is a sign of advanced cancer and has a poor prognosis, with a median survival of 4-12 months.**

sections.overview: Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic, granulomatous infectious disease caused by the bacterium *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It primarily affects the lungs (pulmonary TB) but can also affect other parts of the body (extrapulmonary TB). The clinical spectrum ranges from a dormant, asymptomatic state known as Latent TB Infection (LTBI) to a symptomatic, contagious state known as Active TB Disease.
sections.epidemiology: * Globally, approximately one-quarter of the world's population is estimated to have LTBI. * In the United States, TB is less common but disproportionately affects foreign-born individuals from high-prevalence countries, residents of congregate settings (prisons, homeless shelters), and immunocompromised populations.
sections.clinicalPresentation: * **Latent TB (LTBI)**: Asymptomatic by definition. The only positive finding is a TST or IGRA test. * **Active Pulmonary TB (most common)**: Insidious onset over weeks to months with both constitutional and pulmonary symptoms. * **Extrapulmonary TB**: Can affect any organ system. * **Lymph nodes (Scrofula)**: Most common site. Painless, matted cervical lymphadenopathy. * **Pleura**: Pleural effusion, pleuritic chest pain. * **Vertebral spine (Pott's Disease)**: Back pain, gibbus deformity. * **Miliary TB**: Disseminated, hematogenous spread of bacilli. Presents with sepsis-like picture, organ failure. "Millet-seed" pattern on chest x-ray.
sections.prognosis: * Excellent (>95% cure rate) for drug-susceptible TB that is diagnosed and treated appropriately. * Prognosis is significantly worse for patients with MDR/XDR-TB, advanced immunosuppression (e.g., low CD4 count in HIV), or who are non-adherent to therapy.

sections.overview: An empyema (or pyothorax) is a collection of purulent fluid (pus) within the pleural space, the potential space between the visceral and parietal pleura. It is most commonly a complication of pneumonia but can also arise from other sources of infection. Empyema represents the final, organized stage of a parapneumonic effusion. Its management is distinct from simple effusions because it requires both systemic antibiotics and drainage of the infected pleural fluid.
sections.epidemiology: * Most commonly develops as a complication of bacterial pneumonia. * Occurs in approximately 2-5% of patients hospitalized with pneumonia. * Incidence is higher in older adults, children, and immunocompromised individuals.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The classic presentation is a **patient with pneumonia who fails to improve despite 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy**. They may have persistent or recurrent fever, worsening dyspnea, or pleuritic chest pain.
sections.prognosis: * Mortality rate is approximately 10-20%. * Prognosis is worse in elderly patients, those with significant comorbidities, and when diagnosis or drainage is delayed. * Full recovery of pulmonary function can take several months.

sections.overview: A pneumothorax is the presence of air or gas in the pleural space (the potential space between the visceral and parietal pleura), which causes the lung to collapse due to a loss of negative intrapleural pressure. This condition can range from a small, asymptomatic finding to a life-threatening medical emergency. It is broadly classified into spontaneous (primary or secondary), traumatic, and tension pneumothorax.
sections.epidemiology: * **PSP:** Incidence is highest in tall, thin males aged 20-40. Male-to-female ratio is ~6:1. * **SSP:** Incidence increases with age, typically occurring in patients >55 years old with underlying lung pathology. * A bimodal age distribution is often seen: a peak in the early 20s (PSP) and another peak after age 60 (SSP).
sections.clinicalPresentation: The classic presentation is the sudden onset of unilateral, pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea in a patient with known risk factors (e.g., a young male smoker or an elderly patient with COPD). The severity of symptoms depends on the size of the pneumothorax and the patient's underlying pulmonary reserve.

diagnostics.notes: * **Chest X-ray (CXR):** * **Initial test of choice.** An upright expiratory film may accentuate the finding, but an inspiratory film is usually sufficient. * **Key Finding:** **Visceral pleural line**-a thin white line that defines the edge of the collapsed lung, separated from the parietal pleura by a lucent, air-filled space with no lung markings. * **Supine CXR (common in trauma):** Look for the **"deep sulcus sign,"** where the costophrenic angle appears abnormally deep and lucent. * Mediastinal shift toward the contralateral side suggests a tension pneumothorax. * **Chest CT:** * **Most sensitive and specific imaging modality.** * Used when CXR is equivocal, to differentiate a large bulla from a pneumothorax, or to better quantify the size. * **Ultrasound (POCUS - Point-of-Care Ultrasound):** * Highly sensitive and rapid, especially in the ED or trauma setting. * **Key Findings:** * **Absence of lung sliding** ("ants marching" sign is absent). * **"Barcode" or "Stratosphere" sign** on M-mode (normal is "seashore" sign). * **Lung point:** The specific point on the chest wall where the collapsed lung intermittently touches the chest wall; its presence is **pathognomonic** for pneumothorax. * **Arterial Blood Gas (ABG):** * Not diagnostic but assesses physiological status. * Typically shows hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis (due to hyperventilation).

sections.prognosis: * **PSP:** Excellent prognosis with treatment, but recurrence is common. Smoking cessation significantly reduces recurrence risk. * **SSP:** Prognosis is more guarded and depends heavily on the severity of the underlying lung disease. Mortality is significantly higher than in PSP.

sections.overview: A hemothorax is the accumulation of blood within the pleural space, the potential space between the visceral and parietal pleura. This condition is a medical emergency that can lead to both respiratory and hemodynamic collapse. The accumulation of blood compresses the ipsilateral lung, causing atelectasis and ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch, leading to hypoxia. Simultaneously, significant blood loss into the thorax can result in hypovolemic shock.
sections.epidemiology: * Hemothorax is primarily associated with trauma. * It occurs in approximately 25% of patients with major chest trauma. * Penetrating trauma is more likely to cause significant hemothorax than blunt trauma.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation is highly dependent on the volume and rate of bleeding. * Often occurs in the setting of multi-system trauma. * Patient may be anxious, pale, and diaphoretic. * Signs of respiratory distress (e.g., tachypnea, use of accessory muscles). * Signs of hypovolemic shock (e.g., tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status).
sections.prognosis: * Prognosis is highly dependent on the underlying cause, the rate of blood loss, and the presence of associated injuries. * Small, isolated hemothoraces have an excellent prognosis. * Massive hemothorax associated with major trauma (e.g., great vessel injury) carries a high mortality rate. Prompt diagnosis and surgical intervention are key to survival.

sections.overview: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive, and ultimately fatal fibrosing interstitial lung disease (ILD) of unknown cause. It is characterized by the progressive scarring of lung tissue, leading to irreversible loss of lung function. The diagnosis of IPF requires the exclusion of other known causes of ILD and is associated with the histopathologic and/or radiologic pattern of **Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP)**.
sections.epidemiology: * **Incidence:** ~15 per 100,000 persons per year. * **Prevalence:** Increases significantly with age. * **Age of Onset:** Typically affects individuals **> 60 years old**. Rare before age 50. * **Sex:** More common in **males** than females (~2:1 ratio).
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation is typically **insidious and gradually progressive** over months to years. A classic vignette is an older male smoker presenting with shortness of breath that he initially attributed to aging or being out of shape.

diagnostics.notes: The diagnostic process is aimed at confirming the UIP pattern and excluding all other potential causes of interstitial lung disease. * **Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs):** * **Pattern:** Classic **restrictive** pattern. * **Spirometry:** * Decreased Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) * Decreased Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second (FEV1) * **Normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio (> 0.7)** * **Lung Volumes:** Decreased Total Lung Capacity (TLC). * **Diffusing Capacity (DLCO):** **Markedly reduced**, often disproportionately to the reduction in lung volumes. Reflects impaired gas exchange across the thickened interstitium. * **Imaging:** * **Chest X-Ray (CXR):** Often the initial test. * Findings: Increased reticular markings (net-like lines), particularly at the **lung bases and periphery**. * Late findings include low lung volumes and visible honeycombing. * **High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) of the Chest:** **The key imaging modality for diagnosis.** * **Classic UIP Pattern Findings:** * **Basilar and subpleural (peripheral) predominance.** * **Reticular abnormalities.** * **Honeycombing** (clustered cystic air spaces, often in multiple layers). * Traction bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis. * **Crucially, there is an *absence* of features suggestive of other diagnoses** (e.g., extensive ground-glass opacities, micronodules, consolidation, pleural plaques). * **Labs:** Primarily used to rule out other causes. * ANA, RF, anti-CCP, anti-Scl-70, anti-Jo-1 to screen for connective tissue disease-associated ILD. * **Surgical Lung Biopsy:** * **When:** Performed when HRCT findings are not classic for a UIP pattern, but clinical suspicion remains high. * **Method:** Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) is preferred. * **Histology:** Considered the **gold standard**. Reveals the **histopathologic UIP pattern**: patchy fibrosis, architectural distortion with honeycombing, and scattered collections of myofibroblasts known as **fibroblastic foci**.

sections.prognosis: * Poor. The disease is universally progressive. * Median survival from the time of diagnosis is approximately **3-5 years** without treatment. * Antifibrotic therapy can slow the rate of functional decline but does not halt progression or reverse fibrosis.

sections.overview: Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC) is a high-grade, aggressive neuroendocrine carcinoma of the lung. It is characterized by rapid tumor growth, a high propensity for early metastasis, and a strong association with cigarette smoking. SCLC accounts for approximately 15% of all lung cancers. Unlike Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC), SCLC is typically widespread at diagnosis and is considered a systemic disease, making chemotherapy the cornerstone of treatment rather than surgery. It is notorious for its association with various paraneoplastic syndromes.
sections.epidemiology: - **Incidence**: Represents ~15% of all lung cancers. Incidence is decreasing in the U.S. due to lower smoking rates. - **Demographics**: Typically a disease of older adults, with a peak incidence between ages 60 and 80. - **Gender**: Historically more common in men, but the gender gap has narrowed significantly with changing smoking patterns.
riskFactors: **Cigarette Smoking**: The single most important risk factor. Risk is proportional to the number of pack-years smoked.
**Occupational Exposures**: Radon gas (especially in uranium miners), asbestos, and other carcinogens.
**Genetics**: A family history of lung cancer may slightly increase risk.
sections.clinicalPresentation: SCLC presents aggressively and rapidly. Patients often have a short duration of symptoms (weeks to months) before seeking medical attention. The presentation is dictated by the location of the primary tumor (typically central), the extent of regional spread, the sites of distant metastases, and the presence of paraneoplastic syndromes. Most patients (~70%) present with metastatic (Extensive-Stage) disease.

diagnostics.notes: - **Imaging**: - **Chest X-ray**: Often the first test. Typically shows a **large hilar or perihilar mass** with bulky mediastinal lymphadenopathy. - **CT Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis with IV Contrast**: Essential for evaluating the primary tumor, lymph nodes, and common metastatic sites (liver, adrenals). - **Biopsy (Definitive Diagnosis)**: - **Bronchoscopy with biopsy** and/or endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (EBUS-FNA) is the preferred method for central lesions. - CT-guided biopsy for peripheral lesions or metastatic sites. - **Pathology & Immunohistochemistry (IHC)**: - Histology shows small, blue, round cells. - IHC stains will be positive for neuroendocrine markers: **Chromogranin A**, **Synaptophysin**, and **CD56**. - **Staging**: SCLC is staged differently from NSCLC. - **Goal**: To determine if the disease is "Limited" or "Extensive." - **Staging Workup**: **PET/CT** (to identify distant mets) and **MRI of the brain** (high incidence of brain mets at diagnosis) are mandatory. - **Limited-Stage Disease (LD-SCLC)**: Tumor is confined to one hemithorax and can be encompassed within a single, tolerable radiation field. Includes ipsilateral mediastinal and supraclavicular nodes. (~30% of patients). - **Extensive-Stage Disease (ED-SCLC)**: Tumor has spread beyond one hemithorax, including distant metastases or malignant pleural/pericardial effusion. (~70% of patients).

treatment: **Limited-Stage SCLC (LD-SCLC)**:
**Goal**: Curative intent.
**Standard of Care**: **Concurrent Chemoradiation**.
**Chemotherapy**: 4-6 cycles of **Cisplatin + Etoposide**.
**Radiation**: Concurrent thoracic radiation therapy, typically started with the 1st or 2nd cycle of chemo.

**Prophylactic Cranial Irradiation (PCI)**: Offered to patients who achieve a complete or very good partial response after chemoradiation. Significantly reduces the incidence of brain metastases and improves overall survival.
**Extensive-Stage SCLC (ED-SCLC)**:
**Goal**: Palliative; to improve survival and quality of life.
**Standard of Care**: **Combination Chemotherapy + Immunotherapy**.
**Chemo**: 4 cycles of **Carboplatin + Etoposide**.
**Immunotherapy**: Concurrent and maintenance **Atezolizumab** or **Durvalumab** (PD-L1 inhibitors).

**Radiation**: Used for palliation of symptoms (e.g., painful bone mets, brain mets, bronchial obstruction, SVC compression). PCI is more controversial in ED-SCLC but may be considered in select patients with good response.
management: **Symptom Control**: Aggressive management of pain, dyspnea, nausea, and fatigue. Early involvement of palliative care is crucial.
**Oncologic Emergencies**: Be prepared to manage SVC syndrome (radiation, steroids, stenting), spinal cord compression (steroids, radiation), and brain metastases (steroids, radiation).
**Paraneoplastic Syndromes**: Treat the underlying malignancy. For SIADH, this includes fluid restriction and potentially demeclocycline or vaptans.
**Surveillance**: After initial treatment, patients are monitored closely with physical exams and serial imaging (CT scans) every 3-6 months to detect recurrence.
complications: **Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Syndrome**
**Brain Metastases**
**Spinal Cord Compression**
**Paraneoplastic Syndromes** (SIADH, LEMS, Cushing's)
**Treatment-related Toxicity**: Myelosuppression, neuropathy (cisplatin), radiation pneumonitis, radiation esophagitis.
sections.prognosis: - **Overall poor**, though treatment can significantly extend survival. - **Limited-Stage**: Median survival is approximately 20-25 months with treatment. 5-year survival is ~25%. - **Extensive-Stage**: Median survival is approximately 12 months with modern chemo-immunotherapy. 5-year survival is <5%. - **Negative Prognostic Factors**: Extensive-stage disease, poor performance status (ECOG >2), significant weight loss, elevated LDH.

sections.overview: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem inflammatory disease of unknown etiology, characterized by the hallmark finding of **non-caseating granulomas** in affected organs. While it can affect any organ, the **lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes** are involved in over 90% of cases. The clinical course is highly variable, ranging from asymptomatic incidental findings to chronic, debilitating disease.
sections.epidemiology: - **Prevalence:** Varies by geography and race. - **Race:** Highest incidence in **African Americans** (3-4 times higher than Caucasians) and **Northern Europeans** (e.g., Scandinavians). African Americans tend to have more severe and chronic disease. - **Age:** Bimodal age distribution. The major peak is in young adults aged **20-40 years**. A smaller, second peak occurs in women over 50. - **Sex:** Slightly higher incidence in females.
riskFactors: **Genetic predisposition:** Family history of sarcoidosis, specific HLA alleles.
Inorganic dusts/particles (e.g., occupational exposure for firefighters).
