sections.prognosis: - **Excellent.** The vast majority of patients experience complete resolution of symptoms with conservative treatment. - Recurrence is possible, especially if the underlying biomechanical issues (e.g., abductor weakness, poor flexibility) are not adequately addressed through physical therapy.

sections.overview: Iliotibial (IT) Band Syndrome is a common overuse injury and a leading cause of lateral knee pain, particularly in runners and cyclists. It is characterized by inflammation and irritation of the distal portion of the iliotibial band where it crosses the lateral femoral epicondyle. It is primarily considered an overuse, non-traumatic inflammatory condition.
sections.epidemiology: * Most common cause of lateral knee pain in runners. * Accounts for up to 12% of all running-related overuse injuries. * Also prevalent in cyclists, hikers, and military personnel. * Incidence is highest in individuals aged 15-50 who participate in repetitive flexion/extension activities of the knee.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient, typically a runner or cyclist, presents with an insidious onset of lateral knee pain. The history is crucial and often follows a classic pattern: * Pain develops at a predictable and consistent time/distance during an activity (e.g., "always starts at mile 2 of my run"). * Pain is absent at the beginning of the activity but progressively worsens. * Pain resolves shortly after cessation of the activity. * The patient can often point with one finger to the exact location of the pain.

diagnostics.notes: ITBS is a **clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam. * **Imaging is generally not required** unless the diagnosis is uncertain or the patient fails to improve with conservative therapy. * **X-rays:** Typically normal. Useful to rule out bony pathology such as stress fracture or lateral compartment osteoarthritis. * **MRI:** The modality of choice if imaging is needed. * **Findings:** May show thickening of the distal IT band, T2 signal hyperintensity (edema) in the space between the IT band and lateral femoral epicondyle, or a fluid collection (bursitis). * Useful for ruling out intra-articular pathology like a lateral meniscal tear. * **Ultrasound:** Can also be used to visualize IT band thickening and inflammation/fluid in the underlying bursa.

sections.prognosis: * **Excellent** with a dedicated conservative treatment plan. * The vast majority (>90%) of patients recover fully with non-operative management. * Recovery typically takes 4-8 weeks. * Recurrence is common if the underlying biomechanical deficits and training errors are not fully addressed.

sections.overview: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) is the most common entrapment neuropathy, resulting from the compression of the **median nerve** as it passes through the carpal tunnel at the wrist. This compression leads to ischemia and demyelination of the nerve, causing a characteristic pattern of pain, numbness, and paresthesias in the median nerve distribution, and can progress to motor weakness and muscle atrophy if left untreated.
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** Affects 3-6% of the general adult population. * **Gender:** **Women > Men** (approx. 3:1 ratio). * **Age:** Peak incidence between **40-60 years of age**. * **Bilateral Involvement:** Common (~60% of cases), though the dominant hand is usually affected first and more severely.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation is typically one of insidious onset of sensory symptoms in the median nerve distribution, often worse at night. Patients frequently report waking from sleep with numbness and pain, which is relieved by shaking their hand (the **"Flick Sign"**). Symptoms are often exacerbated by activities that involve sustained wrist flexion or extension, such as driving, talking on the phone, or typing.

diagnostics.notes: * **Clinical Diagnosis:** CTS is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on a characteristic history and physical exam findings. * **Confirmatory Testing (Gold Standard):** * **Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS) and Electromyography (EMG):** * **Purpose:** To confirm the diagnosis, localize the compression to the wrist, assess severity (demyelinating vs. axonal damage), and rule out other neuropathies. * **Findings:** NCS will show **slowed sensory and motor conduction velocity** across the carpal tunnel. EMG can show signs of denervation in thenar muscles in severe cases. * **Indication:** Often required before surgical intervention or when the diagnosis is uncertain. * **Imaging:** * **Ultrasound:** Can be used to visualize the median nerve, showing swelling proximal to the tunnel and flattening within the tunnel. Can also identify structural causes like cysts. It is becoming a first-line imaging modality. * **X-ray:** Not useful for diagnosing CTS itself, but can identify underlying bony abnormalities like fractures or severe arthritis. * **MRI:** Rarely indicated. Reserved for cases where a tumor or mass is suspected.

sections.prognosis: * The prognosis is generally **excellent** with timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment. * Mild cases often respond well to conservative therapy, especially splinting. * Surgical release has a high success rate (>90%) for relieving pain and paresthesias. * Recovery of motor function and sensation is less predictable if significant atrophy or axonal damage was present pre-operatively.

sections.overview: Trigger finger, medically known as stenosing tenosynovitis, is a common hand condition characterized by inflammation and thickening of the flexor tendon sheath, most notably at the A1 pulley. This thickening creates a size mismatch between the flexor tendon and its sheath, causing the tendon to catch or "trigger" as it attempts to glide through the narrowed pulley during finger flexion and extension. The affected finger may become painfully locked in a flexed position.
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** Lifetime risk is approximately 2-3%, but increases to 10% in individuals with diabetes. * **Age:** Most common in the 5th and 6th decades of life (age 40-60). * **Gender:** More common in females (Female:Male ratio of 2:1 to 6:1). * **Affected Digits:** Most commonly affects the **ring finger** and **thumb**, followed by the middle, index, and small fingers.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient, typically a middle-aged female, presents with a gradual onset of pain at the base of a finger on the palmar side. They report a sensation of catching or locking, which is often more pronounced in the morning. They may need to use their other hand to passively extend the affected digit. The history may or may not include a preceding history of overuse or repetitive hand activities.

diagnostics.notes: * Trigger finger is a **clinical diagnosis**. History and physical exam are sufficient. * **Imaging is not routinely necessary.** * **X-rays:** May be ordered to rule out bony pathology like fracture or severe arthritis but will be normal in trigger finger. * **Ultrasound:** Can be used to visualize thickening of the A1 pulley and inflammation of the flexor tendon (tenosynovitis), but is typically reserved for atypical cases. * **Labs:** Not indicated unless there is suspicion of an underlying systemic inflammatory condition (e.g., RA factor, uric acid).

sections.prognosis: The prognosis is **excellent**. The vast majority of patients achieve complete resolution of symptoms with treatment, whether through corticosteroid injection or surgical release. Recurrence is uncommon after surgical release but can occur after injections, particularly in patients with underlying risk factors like diabetes.

sections.overview: Mechanical Low Back Pain (LBP), often called lumbosacral strain or sprain, is pain originating from the spinal structures, including vertebrae, intervertebral discs, facet joints, ligaments, or muscles of the lumbar spine. It is the most common cause of low back pain, accounting for over 90% of cases. It is characterized by the absence of specific underlying pathology (e.g., infection, fracture, malignancy, or nerve root compression). It is a diagnosis of exclusion after "red flag" conditions have been ruled out.
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** Extremely common, with a lifetime prevalence of up to 85%. * **Incidence:** Peak incidence occurs between ages 30-50. * **Disability:** The leading cause of activity limitation and work absence worldwide. It is the most common cause of disability in patients under 45 years of age. * **Course:** Most episodes (approx. 90%) are acute and self-limiting, resolving within 4-6 weeks regardless of treatment.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A typical patient presents with acute onset of low back pain, often following a specific precipitating event like lifting a heavy object. The pain is localized to the lumbosacral region and may radiate to the buttocks or posterior thighs but **not** in a dermatomal pattern below the knee. The patient's general health is otherwise good, with no systemic symptoms.

diagnostics.notes: * **Imaging:** For acute (<4-6 weeks) mechanical LBP **without red flags**, imaging is **NOT indicated**. It does not improve outcomes and can lead to unnecessary procedures. * **Indications for Imaging:** 1. **Presence of Red Flags:** * Major trauma -> **X-ray** first. * Suspected cancer, infection, or epidural abscess -> **MRI with and without contrast** is the study of choice. * Cauda Equina Syndrome -> **Emergent MRI.** 2. **Failure of Conservative Therapy:** No improvement after 4-6 weeks of treatment. 3. **New or Progressive Neurologic Deficit.** * **Laboratory Studies:** Not indicated unless red flags for infection (CBC, ESR, CRP) or malignancy are present.

sections.prognosis: * **Excellent** for acute episodes. Over 90% of patients experience significant improvement or complete resolution within 4-6 weeks. * **Recurrence is common,** with up to 50% of patients having another episode within one year. * A small percentage (~5-10%) will develop chronic low back pain. The presence of "yellow flags" is the strongest predictor of chronicity.

sections.overview: A ganglion cyst is a benign, non-cancerous, fluid-filled sac (pseudocyst) that arises from a joint capsule or tendon sheath. It is the most common soft-tissue mass of the hand and wrist. These cysts are filled with a thick, clear, mucinous (gelatinous) fluid. They lack a true epithelial lining, which differentiates them from true cysts.
sections.epidemiology: - **Most Common:** The most common soft-tissue tumor of the hand. - **Age:** Peak incidence is between 20-40 years old. - **Gender:** More common in women (Female:Male ratio 3:1).
riskFactors: **Repetitive Use:** Activities involving repetitive wrist/hand motion (e.g., gymnastics, typing, musicians).
**Prior Trauma:** History of joint injury or sprain.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient, typically a young adult female, presents with a chief complaint of a "lump" on their hand or wrist that has appeared gradually over weeks or months. The lump may fluctuate in size and is often asymptomatic, but the patient may be concerned about its appearance or have mild associated aching. **Common Locations:** 1. **Dorsal Wrist (60-70%):** Most common site, typically arising from the scapholunate (SL) ligament. 2. **Volar Wrist (15-20%):** Second most common, often near the radial artery and arising from the radioscaphoid or scaphotrapezial joint. 3. **Dorsal Foot/Ankle:** Can arise from extensor tendons or joints. 4. **Digital Flexor Tendon Sheath:** Presents as a small, firm, pea-sized nodule at the base of a finger (volar aspect), often near the A1 pulley.

diagnostics.notes: - **Clinical Diagnosis:** Diagnosis is usually made based on history and physical exam findings, especially positive transillumination. - **Ultrasound (US):** - **First-line imaging** if the diagnosis is uncertain. - Confirms the anechoic (cystic) nature of the mass. - Can differentiate from a solid mass and identify the stalk's origin. - Useful for guiding aspiration, especially for volar wrist ganglia near the radial artery. - **MRI:** - Rarely needed. - Used for atypical presentations, suspected intra-articular pathology, or for pre-operative planning to define the cyst's anatomy and its relationship to surrounding neurovascular structures. - **X-ray:** - Not useful for visualizing the cyst itself. - May be ordered to rule out underlying bony pathology, arthritis, or fractures.

treatment: For asymptomatic cysts.
Inform the patient of the benign nature. Up to 50% may resolve spontaneously over time.
Avoid "Bible therapy" (smashing with a heavy object) due to risk of injury.
A large-bore needle (e.g., 18-gauge) is used to drain the thick, gelatinous fluid.
Often combined with a corticosteroid injection (though evidence for its added benefit is mixed).
**High recurrence rate (~50%).**
Aspiration of volar wrist ganglia should be done with extreme caution (or under US guidance) due to proximity to the radial artery.
**Most effective treatment** with the lowest recurrence rate (~5-10%).
Indicated for symptomatic cysts that fail conservative management or for cysts causing neurovascular compromise.
**Key to success:** Complete excision of the cyst, its stalk, and a small portion of the underlying joint capsule or tendon sheath.
management: **Asymptomatic cysts:** Reassure and observe. Follow up as needed if symptoms develop.

**Mildly symptomatic cysts:** Consider temporary wrist splinting and activity modification. If persistent, offer aspiration as the next step, ensuring the patient understands the high recurrence rate.
**Symptomatic cysts failing conservative care:** Refer to Hand Surgery or Orthopedics for consideration of surgical excision.
complications: **From the Cyst:** Nerve compression (e.g., carpal or Guyon's canal syndrome), vascular compression, pain, weakness, cosmetic deformity.
**From Aspiration:** Infection, bleeding, injury to nerves, tendons, or arteries (especially the radial artery). High rate of recurrence.

**From Surgery:** Standard surgical risks (infection, scar formation, bleeding), nerve injury (especially the sensory branch of the radial nerve), joint stiffness, ligamentous instability, recurrence.
sections.prognosis: Excellent. Ganglion cysts are benign and do not undergo malignant transformation. The primary morbidity is related to local symptoms (pain, nerve compression) and the high rate of recurrence with non-surgical treatment.

sections.overview: Spinal stenosis is the narrowing of the spinal canal, lateral recess, or neural foramen, leading to compression of the spinal cord, cauda equina, and/or nerve roots. This compression results in a clinical syndrome of pain, sensory loss, and weakness. It most commonly affects the lumbar and cervical spine. * **Central Stenosis:** Narrowing of the central spinal canal, potentially compressing the spinal cord (cervical/thoracic) or the cauda equina (lumbar). * **Foraminal (Lateral) Stenosis:** Narrowing of the intervertebral foramen where the nerve root exits, leading to radiculopathy. * **Lateral Recess Stenosis:** Narrowing of the area between the central canal and the foramen, compressing the traversing nerve root.
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** Very common, increases significantly with age. * **Age:** Primarily affects individuals **>60 years old**. * **Location:** Lumbar spine is the most common site, followed by the cervical spine. Thoracic stenosis is rare. * **Significance:** Most common reason for spine surgery in individuals over 65.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The classic presentation is an older adult with an insidious onset and slowly progressive course of back and leg pain. The patient's history is the most critical component for diagnosis. * **Lumbar Stenosis:** Patient complains of "neurogenic claudication." They report pain, numbness, or weakness in the legs that is worse with walking or prolonged standing. They often find relief by sitting or leaning forward, such as on a shopping cart (the **"Shopping Cart Sign"**). * **Cervical Stenosis:** Can present with neck pain, radicular arm symptoms (numbness/weakness in a dermatomal pattern), and/or **myelopathy** (spinal cord compression). Myelopathy symptoms include gait instability, loss of fine motor skills (e.g., buttoning a shirt, poor handwriting), and potential bowel/bladder changes.

diagnostics.notes: * **MRI:** **Gold standard / test of choice.** Directly visualizes neural element compression by soft tissues (disc, ligamentum flavum) and bone. * **X-Ray (AP/Lateral, Flexion/Extension):** Initial imaging. Can show degenerative changes like decreased disc height, osteophytes, and spondylolisthesis. Cannot visualize soft tissues or confirm stenosis. * **CT Myelogram:** Excellent for visualizing bony anatomy and canal dimensions. Used when MRI is contraindicated (e.g., incompatible pacemaker) or inconclusive. Involves injecting contrast into the thecal sac. * **Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI):** Can be used to rule out vascular claudication if the diagnosis is uncertain.

sections.prognosis: * Spinal stenosis is a chronic, progressive condition. * Many patients can be managed effectively with conservative treatment for years. * Surgical outcomes are generally favorable for relieving leg pain (neurogenic claudication) but are less predictable for relieving low back pain. * Symptoms can recur over time due to the ongoing degenerative nature of the disease.

sections.overview: Plantar fasciitis is the most common cause of heel pain in adults. It is an overuse injury characterized by inflammation and, more chronically, degenerative changes of the plantar fascia at its origin on the medial calcaneal tuberosity. It is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on a classic history and specific physical exam findings.
sections.etiology:
• **Eustachian tube dysfunction** is a primary predisposing factor, often secondary to an upper respiratory infection.
    ◦ Inflammation and edema of the Eustachian tube lining lead to obstruction.
    ◦ This obstruction causes negative pressure in the middle ear, leading to an accumulation of fluid and secretions.
• Subsequent **bacterial or viral infection** of the middle ear fluid.
    ◦ Common **bacterial pathogens**:
        ▪ **Streptococcus pneumoniae**
        ▪ **Haemophilus influenzae** (non-typeable)
        ▪ **Moraxella catarrhalis**
    ◦ Common **viral pathogens** that can precede or co-exist with bacterial infection:
        ▪ **Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)**
        ▪ **Rhinovirus**
        ▪ **Influenza virus**
• **Risk Factors**
    ◦ **Host Factors**:
        ▪ Age (peak incidence 6-18 months)
        ▪ Anatomic abnormalities (e.g., cleft palate)
        ▪ **Immunodeficiency**
        ▪ Genetic predisposition
    ◦ **Environmental Factors**:
        ▪ Daycare attendance
        ▪ **Secondhand smoke exposure**
        ▪ Pacifier use
        ▪ Lack of breastfeeding
sections.epidemiology: - **Prevalence**: Affects approximately 10% of the US population over their lifetime. - **Peak Incidence**: Ages 40-60. - **Populations**: Very common in runners and individuals in occupations requiring prolonged standing (e.g., teachers, factory workers, healthcare professionals).
riskFactors: **Pes Planus (flat feet)**: Causes increased tensile stress on the fascia.
**Pes Cavus (high arches)**: A rigid foot that is a poor shock absorber.
**Limited Ankle Dorsiflexion**: Often due to a tight Achilles tendon or gastrocnemius/soleus complex. This is a very strong and common association.
**Obesity / High BMI**: Increased axial load on the foot.
**Occupational**: Prolonged standing or walking on hard surfaces.
**Training Errors**: Sudden increase in running mileage, intensity, or change in running surface.
**Inappropriate Footwear**: Worn-out shoes, poor arch support, minimal cushioning.
sections.clinicalPresentation: - The classic presentation is a patient complaining of **insidious onset of heel pain**. - The pain is typically localized to the **plantar medial aspect of the heel**. - A hallmark feature is **post-static dyskinesia**: severe pain with the first few steps in the morning or after a period of inactivity (e.g., getting up after sitting for a long time). - The pain often improves slightly with initial activity as the fascia "warms up" but then worsens with prolonged weight-bearing or at the end of the day.
sections.physicalExam:
• **Otoscopic Examination** is the key to diagnosis.
    ◦ **Tympanic Membrane (TM)** findings:
        ▪ **Bulging** of the TM is the most specific sign.
        ▪ Marked **erythema** of the TM.
        ▪ **Opacification** of the TM (loss of translucency), often described as cloudy or yellow/amber.
        ▪ Loss of normal landmarks (e.g., short process of malleus, cone of light).
    ◦ **Tympanic Membrane Mobility**:
        ▪ Decreased or absent mobility on **pneumatic otoscopy**.
    ◦ **Middle Ear Effusion**:
        ▪ May be visualized as **air-fluid levels** or **bullae** on the tympanic membrane.
• Associated Findings:
    ◦ Possible fever.
    ◦ **Otalgia** (ear pain) may be elicited by asking the patient or observing ear pulling in infants.
    ◦ Conductive hearing loss on Weber/Rinne test (if performable).
    ◦ Examination of the external auditory canal is typically normal, without pain on manipulation of the pinna or tragus.

diagnostics.notes: - **Primarily a clinical diagnosis.** Imaging is not typically required for initial diagnosis. - **Imaging is indicated if:** - Diagnosis is uncertain. - Symptoms are atypical (e.g., night pain, neurologic symptoms). - Conservative treatment fails after several months. - **Radiographs (X-ray)**: - **Purpose**: To rule out other pathology (e.g., calcaneal stress fracture, bone cyst, arthritis). - **Finding**: May show a **calcaneal spur (heel spur)**. - **Clinical Pearl**: A heel spur is an **incidental finding** and is **NOT the cause of the pain**. It is a traction spur that forms in response to stress, and many asymptomatic individuals have them. - **Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (MSK US)**: - Can demonstrate fascial thickening (>4 mm), hypoechogenicity, and perifascial fluid. - Useful for guiding injections. - **MRI**: - Rarely needed. - Used for refractory cases to evaluate for fascial tears, stress fractures, tumors, or nerve entrapment.

sections.differentialDiagnosis:
• **Otitis Media with Effusion (OME)**
    ◦ Characterized by middle ear fluid **without** signs of acute inflammation (e.g., no bulging TM, no fever, no significant pain).
• **Otitis Externa**
    ◦ Inflammation of the external auditory canal.
    ◦ Key signs include **tragal tenderness**, pain with pinna manipulation, and visible canal edema or debris.
• **Bullous Myringitis**
    ◦ Presence of vesicles or bullae on the tympanic membrane; often considered a variant of acute otitis media.
• **Referred Otalgia**
    ◦ Ear pain originating from a non-otologic source, with a normal otoscopic exam.
        ▪ **Dental abscess** or caries
        ▪ **Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ) Dysfunction**
        ▪ Pharyngitis or tonsillitis
        ▪ **Eagle syndrome**
• **Mastoiditis**
    ◦ A complication of AOM, but can present with otalgia.
    ◦ Look for postauricular erythema, swelling, tenderness, and protrusion of the auricle.
treatment: Treatment is overwhelmingly conservative and stepwise. Patient education on the prolonged recovery course (6-12 months) is crucial.
**Phase 1: First-Line / Conservative (Mainstay of Treatment)**
**Stretching**:
**Plantar fascia-specific stretching**: Towel stretches, rolling the foot over a frozen water bottle or ball.
**Achilles tendon/Calf stretching**: Gastroc and soleus stretches. This is critical.
**Activity Modification**: Relative rest; decrease running mileage, avoid high-impact activities.
**Supportive Measures**:
**Footwear**: Well-cushioned shoes with good arch support. Avoid walking barefoot.
**Orthotics**: Over-the-counter or custom heel cups and arch supports.
**Pain/Inflammation Control**:
**Ice**: Apply to the heel for 15-20 minutes after activity.
**NSAIDs**: Oral or topical (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen) for short-term pain relief.
**Phase 2: If First-Line Fails (after 6-8 weeks)**
**Night Splints**: Worn during sleep to maintain the foot in a dorsiflexed position, preventing nocturnal fascial contracture.
**Formal Physical Therapy**: Supervised stretching, strengthening, and manual therapy.
**Corticosteroid Injections**: Can provide significant but often temporary pain relief.
**WARNING**: Carries a risk of **plantar fascia rupture** and **fat pad atrophy**. Use judiciously, often with ultrasound guidance.
**Phase 3: Refractory Cases (after 6-12 months of failed conservative therapy)**
**Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy (ESWT)**.
**Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) Injections**.
**Surgery (Last Resort)**: Partial **plantar fasciotomy** (release of the fascia).
management: **Patient Education**: Explain that this is a self-limiting condition, but recovery is slow. Compliance with the daily stretching regimen is the most important factor for success.
**Address Risk Factors**: Counsel on weight loss, appropriate footwear choices, and proper training techniques for athletes.
**Follow-up**: Re-evaluate in 4-6 weeks to assess response to initial therapy and advance treatment as needed.
complications: **Chronic Heel Pain**: Can lead to significant disability and limitation of daily and recreational activities.
**Altered Gait Mechanics**: Limping can lead to secondary pain in the knee, hip, or back.
**Plantar Fascia Rupture**:
Can occur spontaneously in chronic cases or iatrogenically after a corticosteroid injection.
Presents with an acute "pop" or tearing sensation, followed by ecchymosis and pain.
**Fat Pad Atrophy**: A known complication of repeated corticosteroid injections, leading to permanent loss of natural heel cushioning.
sections.prognosis: - **Excellent**. - Over 90% of patients experience resolution of symptoms within 12 months with diligent conservative, non-operative management. - Recurrence is possible if underlying risk factors are not addressed.
sections.preventionEducation:
• **Vaccinations**
    ◦ Routine administration of the **Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV)** series.
    ◦ Annual **influenza vaccination** for all eligible individuals.
• **Environmental and Lifestyle Modifications**
    ◦ Encourage exclusive **breastfeeding** for the first 6 months of life.
    ◦ Avoid **supine bottle feeding** (feeding while lying flat).
    ◦ Elimination of exposure to **tobacco smoke**.
    ◦ Consider smaller daycare settings to reduce exposure to upper respiratory infections.
    ◦ Promote frequent hand hygiene.
• **Patient and Parent Education**
    ◦ Educate on the signs and symptoms of AOM (e.g., fever, ear pulling, irritability).
    ◦ Discuss effective **pain management** with analgesics like acetaminophen or ibuprofen.
    ◦ Explain the principles of **antibiotic stewardship** and the rationale for watchful waiting in appropriate cases, emphasizing that many infections are viral and will resolve without antibiotics.
    ◦ Provide clear instructions on when to seek re-evaluation (e.g., worsening symptoms, no improvement in 48-72 hours).

sections.overview: Lumbar radiculopathy is a neurological condition characterized by pain, sensory changes, or weakness in a lower extremity, caused by the compression or irritation of a lumbar spinal nerve root. The most common cause is a herniated intervertebral disc, also known as a herniated nucleus pulposus (HNP). The term "sciatica" is often used to describe the radiating leg pain associated with this condition, typically affecting the L4, L5, or S1 nerve roots.
sections.epidemiology: - **Prevalence:** Very common; lifetime prevalence of low back pain is ~80%, with radiculopathy occurring in a significant subset. - **Peak Incidence:** 30 to 50 years of age. - **Gender:** Slightly more common in males.
riskFactors: **Occupational:** Repetitive lifting, twisting, operating vibrating machinery, prolonged sitting (e.g., truck drivers).
**Lifestyle:** Sedentary lifestyle, obesity, smoking (impairs disc nutrition).
sections.clinicalPresentation: The classic presentation is a patient (often 30-50 years old) with an acute onset of severe, radiating leg pain, often following a specific event like lifting or twisting. The pain typically overshadows any accompanying low back pain.

diagnostics.notes: - **Primarily a clinical diagnosis.** Imaging is not indicated in the first 4-6 weeks for patients with typical radicular symptoms and no "red flag" signs. - **MRI (Lumbar Spine, without contrast):** - **Test of Choice** for visualizing the disc, nerve roots, and soft tissues. - **Indications:** - **Red Flag Symptoms** (see below) - Progressive or severe neurologic deficit (e.g., significant foot drop) - Symptoms persisting >6 weeks despite conservative management - Pre-operative planning - **X-Ray (AP/Lateral):** - Limited utility for HNP itself. - Useful to rule out other pathologies like fracture, spondylolisthesis, or severe degenerative changes. - **CT Myelogram:** Alternative to MRI if contraindicated (e.g., pacemaker, certain implants). - **EMG/NCS:** Can confirm the presence and chronicity of radiculopathy and distinguish it from peripheral neuropathy. Not a first-line test.

management: **Acute Phase (0-6 weeks):**
Rule out red flags.
Initiate conservative care: Patient education, NSAIDs, referral to physical therapy.
Reassure the patient of the excellent natural history.
**Subacute Phase (>6 weeks):**
If symptoms are unimproved or worsening, obtain an **MRI**.
Consider referral to Pain Management (for ESI) or Spine Surgery.
complications: **Cauda Equina Syndrome:** Compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots. Symptoms include **saddle anesthesia**, bilateral leg weakness/sciatica, and **bowel/bladder dysfunction (urinary retention is most common)**. **This is a neurosurgical emergency.**
**Permanent Neurologic Deficit:** Persistent weakness (e.g., foot drop) or sensory loss.
**Chronic Pain Syndrome.**
sections.prognosis: - **Excellent.** Over 90% of patients improve significantly with conservative treatment within 3 months. - The size of the disc herniation on MRI does not always correlate with the severity of symptoms. Large extrusions may be more likely to be resorbed by the body's inflammatory response. - Recurrence rates are approximately 5-15%.

sections.overview: Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow, commonly known as **Cubital Tunnel Syndrome**, is the second most common compressive neuropathy of the upper extremity after carpal tunnel syndrome. It involves the compression or irritation of the ulnar nerve as it passes through the cubital tunnel, a narrow passageway on the medial side of the elbow. This compression leads to sensory and motor deficits in the ulnar nerve distribution of the forearm and hand.
sections.epidemiology: * **Incidence:** Approximately 25 per 100,000 person-years. * **Demographics:** More common in males than females. Can occur at any age but peaks in middle age.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient typically presents with a gradual onset of neurologic symptoms in the ulnar nerve distribution. They may complain of "falling asleep" of the 4th and 5th fingers, particularly at night or when holding the elbow in a flexed position for a prolonged period. As the condition progresses, they may report hand weakness, clumsiness, and difficulty with fine motor tasks like buttoning a shirt or opening a jar.

diagnostics.notes: * **Clinical Diagnosis:** Diagnosis is primarily based on history and physical exam findings. * **Electromyography (EMG) and Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS):** * **Gold standard** for confirming the diagnosis, localizing the site of compression, and determining severity (demyelination vs. axonal loss). * NCS will show **slowing of motor conduction velocity** across the elbow segment (>10 m/s decrease compared to the forearm segment is significant). * EMG can show signs of denervation (e.g., fibrillations, positive sharp waves) in ulnar-innervated muscles. * **Imaging:** * **X-rays:** Useful to rule out bony pathology such as osteophytes, arthritis, or old fractures. * **Ultrasound:** Can visualize the nerve directly to assess for swelling, compression, or subluxation. Can also identify space-occupying lesions like a ganglion cyst. * **MRI:** Rarely needed but can be useful for evaluating soft tissue masses or complex anatomy.

sections.prognosis: * **Excellent** for mild cases that respond well to conservative treatment. * **Good** for patients who undergo surgery before the onset of significant muscle atrophy. Most patients experience relief of sensory symptoms. * **Fair to Poor** if there is long-standing compression with severe muscle wasting and axonal loss on EMG. Motor recovery is often incomplete in these cases.

sections.overview: Spondylolysis is a unilateral or bilateral defect, most commonly a stress fracture, in the pars interarticularis of the vertebral arch. It is a common cause of activity-related low back pain in adolescents and young athletes. The pars interarticularis is the segment of bone connecting the superior and inferior articular processes. This condition can lead to spondylolisthesis if bilateral defects allow for anterior slippage of the vertebra.
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** Affects approximately 6% of the general population. * **Peak Incidence:** Adolescence (ages 10-15), coinciding with periods of rapid growth and high athletic participation. * **Sex:** More common in males than females (2:1 to 3:1 ratio). * **Athletic Population:** Significantly higher prevalence (up to 47%) in athletes participating in sports involving repetitive hyperextension.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The classic presentation is an adolescent athlete with an insidious onset of low back pain that is exacerbated by specific athletic activities and relieved by rest. There is typically no history of a single traumatic event.

diagnostics.notes: * **X-rays (First-Line Imaging):** * **Views:** Anteroposterior (AP), lateral, and bilateral obliques. * **Lateral View:** Best for assessing for associated spondylolisthesis. * **Oblique View:** The classic view for identifying the pars defect, which appears as a radiolucent line or "collar" on the **"Scotty dog."** * **Scotty Dog Anatomy:** Ear = Superior articular process; Eye = Pedicle; Nose = Transverse process; Neck = Pars interarticularis; Body = Lamina; Front Leg = Inferior articular process. * *Note: X-rays can be negative in early stress reactions.* * **MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging):** * **Indication:** High clinical suspicion with negative X-rays. * **Findings:** The most sensitive test for detecting early-stage "active" pars lesions (stress reactions), which appear as **bone marrow edema** (high signal on T2/STIR sequences). Also excellent for evaluating soft tissues, intervertebral discs, and nerve roots. * **CT (Computed Tomography):** * **Indication:** Gold standard for defining the bony anatomy of the pars defect. * **Findings:** Clearly demonstrates the fracture line and can differentiate between an acute fracture and chronic non-union (pseudoarthrosis). Involves higher radiation exposure. * **SPECT (Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography) / Bone Scan:** * **Indication:** To determine if the pars defect is metabolically "active" (acute/subacute) versus "chronic" (cold). * **Findings:** Increased radiotracer uptake ("hot spot") indicates an active lesion with healing potential. A "cold" scan suggests a chronic, stable non-union.

sections.prognosis: * **Excellent** for most patients treated conservatively. * The majority (>80%) of athletes can return to their previous level of sport after successful conservative management. * Prognosis for healing is better for acute, unilateral defects identified early. Chronic, bilateral defects are less likely to achieve bony union.

sections.overview: A vertebral compression fracture (VCF) is a pathologic fracture of a vertebral body, resulting in its collapse. This typically occurs in the anterior portion of the vertebra, leading to a "wedge-shaped" deformity on imaging. While they can occur from high-energy trauma in healthy individuals, they most commonly represent fragility fractures secondary to weakened bone, typically from osteoporosis. They are the most common type of fracture associated with osteoporosis. The thoracolumbar junction (T12-L1) is the most frequently affected region.
sections.epidemiology: * Extremely common, with an estimated 1.5 million occurring annually in the U.S. * Prevalence increases dramatically with age. * Affects ~25% of postmenopausal women in the U.S. * By age 80, approximately 40% of women will have sustained at least one VCF. * **Most Common Locations:** * **Thoracolumbar Junction (T12-L1):** Highest stress region where the rigid thoracic spine meets the more mobile lumbar spine. * Mid-thoracic spine (T7-T8).
sections.clinicalPresentation: The classic presentation is an **elderly patient** (often a postmenopausal female) with a history of osteoporosis who presents with **sudden, acute onset of severe, localized, midline back pain** after an inciting event of minimal trauma (e.g., lifting, bending, coughing). However, up to two-thirds of VCFs may be asymptomatic or present with gradual, chronic pain and are discovered incidentally on imaging.

diagnostics.notes: * **Initial Imaging: Plain Radiographs (AP and Lateral)** * **Findings:** * **Anterior wedging:** The anterior height of the vertebral body is less than the posterior height. * Loss of overall vertebral body height (>20% is significant). * Cortical disruption or endplate fracture. * **Advanced Imaging:** * **CT Scan:** * **Indication:** When X-ray is inconclusive, for better visualization of fracture detail, or to assess for suspected posterior wall involvement (retropulsion) and canal compromise. Essential for surgical planning. * **MRI:** * **Indication:** 1. **To determine acuity:** Bone marrow edema on a STIR sequence indicates an acute or subacute fracture. This is crucial when deciding on interventions like kyphoplasty. 2. **If neurologic deficits are present:** Best modality to visualize the spinal cord, nerve roots, and ligaments. 3. **To differentiate osteoporotic vs. malignant fracture:** Malignant fractures often involve the pedicles, have a convex posterior border, and may be associated with a soft tissue mass. * **Bone Density Scan (DEXA Scan):** * Essential for any patient with a suspected fragility VCF to diagnose and quantify the severity of osteoporosis. A T-score of -2.5 is diagnostic for osteoporosis. * **Laboratory Studies:** * Not required for a simple osteoporotic VCF. * Consider if malignancy or infection is suspected: CBC with diff, CMP (check calcium, alkaline phosphatase), ESR, CRP, SPEP/UPEP (for Multiple Myeloma).

sections.prognosis: * Pain from an acute VCF typically improves significantly within 4-6 weeks, although some residual pain may become chronic. * The presence of one VCF is a very strong predictor of future fractures. A patient with one VCF has a **5-fold increased risk** of a subsequent vertebral fracture and a **2-fold increased risk** of a hip fracture. * Overall prognosis is tied to the management of the underlying osteoporosis and prevention of future falls and fractures.

sections.overview: Cauda Equina Syndrome (CES) is a rare but severe neurosurgical emergency resulting from the compression of the cauda equina-the bundle of lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal nerve roots that descend from the conus medullaris (the terminal end of the spinal cord, typically at L1-L2). Acute compression leads to ischemia and neuronal damage, causing a constellation of debilitating symptoms. Prompt diagnosis and emergent surgical intervention are critical to prevent permanent paralysis, incontinence, and sensory loss.
sections.epidemiology: * **Incidence:** Rare, estimated at 1 in 33,000 to 1 in 100,000 people. * Accounts for approximately 1-2% of all lumbar disc herniation surgeries. * **Peak Age:** 30s-50s, aligning with the peak incidence of lumbar disc herniation. * **Sex:** No significant sex predilection.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation can be acute or insidious, but it is always considered an emergency. The patient typically presents with a combination of severe low back pain and neurological deficits. The classic presentation involves a "constellation of red flag symptoms." There are two main patterns: 1. **Acute Onset:** Rapid development of symptoms over hours with no prior history of sciatica. 2. **Chronic-to-Acute:** A patient with a history of chronic low back pain and sciatica who experiences a sudden, severe worsening of symptoms, including the onset of bladder/bowel dysfunction and saddle anesthesia.

diagnostics.notes: * **Imaging of Choice: STAT MRI of the Lumbar Spine** * This is the gold standard and must be performed emergently. * It directly visualizes the cauda equina, thecal sac, and the source of compression (e.g., disc herniation, tumor, hematoma). * Order **with and without contrast** if tumor, abscess, or inflammatory cause is suspected. * **CT Myelogram:** * Alternative if MRI is contraindicated (e.g., pacemaker, metallic implants) or unavailable. * Involves injecting contrast into the thecal sac followed by a CT scan. It is invasive but provides excellent visualization of the spinal canal and nerve roots. * **Labs:** * Generally not diagnostic for CES itself but crucial for pre-operative workup. * CBC, CMP, PT/INR, PTT. * If infection is suspected: ESR, CRP, Blood Cultures.

sections.prognosis: * The single most important prognostic factor is the **duration and severity of symptoms before surgical decompression**. * **Timing:** Surgery within 24-48 hours offers the best prognosis for recovery of motor, sensory, and visceral function. * **Pre-operative Deficits:** Patients with complete saddle anesthesia and established urinary retention at the time of surgery have a poorer prognosis for functional recovery compared to those with incomplete deficits. * Motor function recovery tends to be better and faster than the recovery of bladder and bowel function.

sections.overview: Scoliosis is a three-dimensional deformity of the spine characterized by a lateral curvature of **>10 degrees** combined with vertebral rotation. The curvature is defined by the **Cobb angle** measured on radiographs. While often associated with adolescence, it can occur at any age. The most common form is Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS).
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** Affects 2-3% of the adolescent population. * **Gender:** * Small curves (<10): Equal prevalence in males and females. * Clinically significant curves (>30): **Females are 10x more likely** to have curve progression requiring treatment. * **Age of Onset:** Most commonly diagnosed during the pre-pubertal growth spurt (ages 10-15).
sections.clinicalPresentation: * Most commonly discovered during a routine school screening, sports physical, or by a parent. * The patient is usually **asymptomatic**. * Chief complaint is often cosmetic (e.g., "my clothes don't fit right," "one shoulder is higher," "one hip sticks out"). * **Significant back pain is a red flag** in AIS and warrants investigation for other causes (e.g., tumor, infection, spondylolysis).

diagnostics.notes: * **Imaging:** * **Initial & Gold Standard:** Standing posteroanterior (PA) and lateral full-length spine radiographs (**scoliosis series**). "Standing" is critical to assess the curve under gravitational load. * **Cobb Angle Measurement:** * Used to quantify the magnitude of the curve. * **Scoliosis is defined as a Cobb angle > 10 degrees.** * Measured by drawing lines along the superior endplate of the most tilted upper vertebra and the inferior endplate of the most tilted lower vertebra. The angle between perpendicular lines drawn from these is the Cobb angle. * **Risser Sign:** Assesses skeletal maturity by evaluating the ossification of the iliac apophysis (graded 0-5). Risser 0-2 indicates significant growth remaining; Risser 4-5 indicates skeletal maturity. * **MRI of the Spine:** * **Not routinely indicated for AIS.** * **Indications (Red Flags):** * **Atypical curve patterns** (e.g., **left-sided thoracic curve**). * Significant pain. * Abnormal neurologic findings. * Rapid progression. * To rule out intraspinal pathology like a syrinx, tethered cord, or tumor.

sections.prognosis: * Excellent with early diagnosis and appropriate management. * The primary determinant of long-term outcome is the **magnitude of the curve at skeletal maturity**. * Curves **< 30** at maturity are unlikely to progress significantly in adulthood. * Thoracic curves **> 50** at maturity tend to progress at a rate of approximately 1 per year throughout life.

sections.overview: An Acromioclavicular (AC) joint separation, commonly known as a "shoulder separation," is an injury to the ligaments that stabilize the AC joint. It is distinct from a glenohumeral (shoulder) dislocation. The injury involves damage to the acromioclavicular (AC) and/or coracoclavicular (CC) ligaments, leading to a loss of congruity between the distal clavicle and the acromion. Severity is graded using the **Rockwood classification system**, which is based on the direction and degree of clavicular displacement.
sections.epidemiology: - **Prevalence:** Accounts for approximately 10% of all acute shoulder girdle injuries. - **Demographics:** Most common in young, physically active individuals, particularly in the second and third decades of life. - **Sex:** There is a significant male predominance (5:1 to 10:1), largely due to higher participation rates in contact sports.
riskFactors: Participation in contact sports (e.g., football, hockey, rugby, lacrosse).
High-impact activities (e.g., cycling, skiing, snowboarding, martial arts).
Occupations involving risk of falls or direct shoulder trauma.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient typically presents with a history of acute trauma (fall, direct blow) to the shoulder. They will often be guarding the injured arm, holding it in an adducted position and supported by the contralateral hand to relieve pressure on the AC joint. They can pinpoint the pain directly to the top of the shoulder.

diagnostics.notes: - **Imaging:** - **X-Rays:** The primary diagnostic modality. - **AP View:** Standard shoulder view. - **Zanca View:** An AP view with a 10-15 cephalic tilt. This is the **best view** to visualize the AC joint in isolation by removing overlapping bony structures (e.g., scapular spine). - **Axillary Lateral View:** Essential for evaluating horizontal (anterior-posterior) displacement and diagnosing a Type IV injury (posterior displacement). - **Stress Views (Weighted Views):** Historically used to differentiate between Type II and III injuries by having the patient hold a 10-15 lb weight. They have largely fallen out of favor due to patient discomfort and limited impact on management. Bilateral views can be used to compare the CC interspace of the injured vs. uninjured side. - **Rockwood Classification (High-Yield):** - **Type I:** Sprain of AC ligament. CC ligaments are intact. No deformity. Normal X-ray. - **Type II:** Tear of AC ligament, sprain of CC ligaments. Slight elevation of clavicle (<25% of clavicle height). CC distance is normal or minimally increased. - **Type III:** Complete tear of both AC and CC ligaments. Obvious superior displacement of the clavicle (25-100% increase in CC distance compared to contralateral side). The clavicle is elevated but remains below the superior border of the acromion on some views. - **Type IV:** AC and CC ligaments torn, with **posterior displacement** of the distal clavicle into the trapezius muscle. Best seen on axillary view. - **Type V:** Severe Type III. Complete tear of AC and CC ligaments plus disruption of the deltotrapezial fascia. Gross superior displacement of the clavicle (>100% increase in CC distance). - **Type VI:** Very rare. Inferior displacement of the distal clavicle below the coracoid or acromion.

treatment: **Type I & II:** Almost exclusively **non-operative**.
Sling for comfort (1-3 weeks).
Ice and NSAIDs for pain and inflammation.
Early, gentle range of motion exercises followed by physical therapy for strengthening.
**Type III:** **Controversial.**
**Non-operative:** Often the initial treatment of choice, especially for sedentary individuals. Outcomes are generally good.
**Operative:** Considered for high-demand overhead athletes, heavy laborers, or those who fail conservative management. Involves anatomic CC ligament reconstruction.
**Type IV, V, & VI:** Almost always require **operative** management to reduce and stabilize the clavicle.
management: **Non-Operative Protocol (Type I, II, most III):**
**Operative Protocol (Type IV, V, VI, selected III):**
Surgical fixation (e.g., CC ligament reconstruction with graft, suture button devices).
Post-operative immobilization in a sling for 4-6 weeks, followed by a structured physical therapy protocol similar to the non-operative plan but with a more delayed timeline.
complications: **Chronic Pain/Instability:** Most common complication, especially with under-rehabilitated or higher-grade injuries.
**Post-traumatic Osteoarthritis:** Degenerative changes in the AC joint can develop over time.
**Decreased Range of Motion:** Can result from prolonged immobilization (adhesive capsulitis) or residual deformity.
**Cosmetic Deformity:** A persistent "bump" is common in Type III+ injuries, even with good functional outcomes.
**Surgical Complications:** Hardware failure, infection, fracture, loss of reduction.
sections.prognosis: - **Type I & II:** Excellent. The vast majority of patients return to their pre-injury level of function with non-operative care. - **Type III:** Good to excellent, whether treated operatively or non-operatively. The decision is patient-specific. - **Type IV, V, VI:** Good with appropriate surgical intervention, but recovery is longer and more complex. Some residual deficits may persist.

sections.overview: A proximal humerus fracture is a break in the upper part of the humerus bone, which forms the "ball" of the shoulder's ball-and-socket joint (glenohumeral joint). These fractures involve one or more of four key segments: the articular surface (humeral head), the greater tuberosity, the lesser tuberosity, and the humeral shaft (at the level of the surgical neck). It is one of the most common fractures in the elderly population. The majority (~85%) are minimally displaced and can be managed non-operatively.
sections.epidemiology: * Third most common fracture type in the elderly (>65 years), after hip fractures and distal radius fractures. * Bimodal age distribution: 1. Young patients with high-energy trauma. 2. Elderly patients with low-energy falls (most common). * Strong female-to-male predominance (~3:1), especially in the elderly, correlating with the prevalence of osteoporosis. * Incidence increases significantly with age.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient, typically an elderly female, presents after a fall with acute, severe shoulder pain. They are often supporting the injured arm with their contralateral hand, holding it in an adducted and internally rotated position. There is a marked unwillingness to move the affected shoulder due to pain.

diagnostics.notes: * **Imaging of Choice:** Radiographs (X-rays). * **Standard Views (Trauma Series):** 1. **True AP (Grashey view):** Shows the glenohumeral joint in a true anteroposterior plane. 2. **Scapular "Y" View:** Assesses for displacement of the humeral head relative to the glenoid. 3. **Axillary View:** Crucial for identifying glenohumeral dislocations and displacement of the tuberosities. If the patient cannot abduct for a standard axillary view, a **Velpeau axillary view** can be obtained. * **CT Scan:** * **Indications:** * Evaluation of complex, comminuted, or intra-articular fractures. * Assessment of fracture-dislocations. * Preoperative planning for surgical fixation. * **MRI:** * Rarely used in the acute setting for the fracture itself. * May be used later to evaluate for associated soft tissue injuries, such as a rotator cuff tear.

sections.prognosis: * Prognosis is generally good for minimally displaced fractures treated non-operatively. * For complex, surgically treated fractures, outcomes are more variable. * Some degree of residual stiffness and weakness is common, particularly in the elderly. * The primary goal of treatment is often a painless, functional shoulder, not necessarily a return to pre-injury level of performance.

sections.overview: A clavicle fracture is a break in the collarbone, one of the most common fractures in the body. The clavicle is an S-shaped bone that acts as a strut connecting the sternum to the scapula, providing the only true bony articulation between the upper extremity and the axial skeleton. The vast majority of these fractures occur in the middle third of the bone and can be managed non-operatively with a high rate of union.
sections.epidemiology: - **Incidence:** Accounts for 2-5% of all fractures in adults and ~35% of all shoulder girdle injuries. - **Distribution:** Bimodal age distribution. - **First Peak:** Young, active males (< 30 years old) due to high-energy trauma (e.g., sports, motor vehicle collisions). - **Second Peak:** Elderly patients (> 70 years old), often women, due to low-energy falls associated with osteoporosis. - **Location of Fracture (Allman Classification):** - **Group I (Middle Third):** Most common (~80%). The bone is thinnest and has less muscular support here. - **Group II (Lateral/Distal Third):** Second most common (~15%). These are more unstable due to involvement of the coracoclavicular (CC) ligaments. - **Group III (Medial/Proximal Third):** Least common (~5%). Often requires a CT scan to fully evaluate due to overlying structures.
riskFactors: Participation in contact sports (football, hockey, rugby).
Activities with a high risk of falls (cycling, skiing, skateboarding, gymnastics).
Male gender in the younger population.
sections.clinicalPresentation: - The patient typically presents immediately following a traumatic event. - They will be guarding the injured arm, holding it adducted and close to the body to prevent painful motion. - The head is often tilted *toward* the affected side and the chin rotated *away* to relax the SCM muscle, reducing tension on the fracture site.

diagnostics.notes: - **Imaging:** - **X-rays:** The primary diagnostic modality. - **Standard Views:** Anteroposterior (AP) view of the clavicle. - **Zanca View (10-15 Cephalic Tilt):** Often ordered to better visualize the fracture pattern and degree of superior/inferior displacement without overlap from the ribs and thoracic cage. - **CT Scan:** Not routinely required. - **Indications:** Suspected intra-articular extension into the sternoclavicular (SC) or acromioclavicular (AC) joints, severe comminution, preoperative planning, or suspicion of associated injuries (e.g., scapular fracture).

treatment: **Non-Operative (Majority of Cases):**
**Indications:** Minimally displaced or non-displaced middle third fractures. Specifically, fractures with < 100% displacement and < 2 cm of shortening.
**Method:**
**Operative (Surgical Fixation - ORIF):**
**Absolute Indications:**
Open fracture
Associated neurovascular injury requiring repair
Severe skin tenting with impending skin perforation
**Relative Indications:**
> 100% displacement (fragments are not touching)
> 2 cm of shortening
Displaced distal third (Group II) fractures (high risk of nonunion)
"Floating shoulder" (ipsilateral fractures of the clavicle and scapular neck)
Polytrauma patient
Patient preference in active individuals desiring a faster return to function.
management: Most patients with isolated, closed fractures are discharged home from the ED with orthopedic follow-up within 1 week.
Patients with absolute indications for surgery require admission and orthopedic consultation.
Serial X-rays (e.g., at 1-2 weeks and 6 weeks) to monitor healing and ensure no significant displacement has occurred.
Clinical union (fracture site is non-tender) typically precedes radiographic union (callus visible on X-ray).
**Phase 1 (0-4 weeks):** Sling use, pendulum exercises.
**Phase 2 (4-8 weeks):** Discontinue sling, begin active-assisted and active ROM exercises as healing progresses.
**Phase 3 (8-12+ weeks):** Begin strengthening exercises. Return to contact sports is typically not allowed until radiographic evidence of complete union, usually around 3-4 months.
complications: **Acute:**
**Pneumothorax/Hemothorax:** Rare, but can occur with a sharp medial fragment piercing the pleura.
**Brachial Plexus Injury:** Can occur from the initial trauma or fracture fragments.
**Subclavian Artery/Vein Injury:** A vascular emergency.
**Delayed:**
**Nonunion:** Failure of the fracture to heal. Highest risk is in displaced distal third fractures and significantly displaced mid-shaft fractures, especially in smokers.
**Malunion:** Healing in a shortened or angulated position. Can lead to cosmetic deformity, pain, and shoulder dysfunction.
**Post-traumatic Arthritis:** If the fracture extends into the AC or SC joint.
**Hardware Irritation:** The plate and screws used in ORIF can be prominent under the skin and may require a second surgery for removal after healing.
sections.prognosis: - **Excellent.** Most mid-shaft clavicle fractures treated non-operatively heal without significant long-term issues (>95% union rate). - Operative fixation also has a very high union rate but carries the inherent risks of surgery (infection, nerve damage, anesthesia risk, hardware problems). - Functional outcomes are generally very good, with most patients returning to their previous level of activity.

sections.overview: Anterior shoulder dislocation is the most common type of shoulder dislocation, accounting for over 95% of all glenohumeral dislocations. It occurs when the head of the humerus is forcibly displaced from its normal articulation with the glenoid fossa, moving to an anterior and typically inferior position. This is a common and often painful orthopedic emergency that requires prompt reduction. The glenohumeral joint's high degree of mobility makes it inherently less stable and thus susceptible to dislocation.
sections.epidemiology: - The most commonly dislocated major joint in the body. - Incidence is approximately 24 per 100,000 person-years. - **Bimodal Distribution:** - **Primary Peak:** Young, athletic males (ages 15-29) due to high-energy trauma in sports. - **Secondary Peak:** Elderly females (ages 60-80) due to low-energy falls. - Recurrence is extremely common, especially in younger patients. The recurrence rate can be >90% in patients under 20 years old.
riskFactors: **Age:** Patients < 20 years old have the highest risk of recurrence.
**Sports Participation:** Contact and collision sports (e.g., football, hockey, rugby, lacrosse).
**Previous Dislocation:** The single greatest risk factor for a subsequent dislocation.
**Ligamentous Laxity:** Congenital conditions like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
**Glenoid or Humeral Bony Defects:** Glenoid dysplasia or a large Hill-Sachs lesion.
sections.clinicalPresentation: - Patients typically present in the emergency department with a history of an acute traumatic event. - The patient is in significant distress, holding the affected arm close to their body with the contralateral hand for support. - The arm is held in a characteristic position of slight **abduction and external rotation**. The patient will resist any attempt to adduct or internally rotate the arm.

diagnostics.notes: - **Imaging of Choice:** Plain Radiographs (X-rays). - **Standard Views:** - **Anteroposterior (AP):** Shows the humeral head displaced inferiorly and medially relative to the glenoid. - **Scapular "Y" View:** Crucial for determining the direction of dislocation. The humeral head appears anterior to the "Y" (formed by the acromion, coracoid, and body of the scapula). - **Axillary View:** The most reliable view to assess the glenohumeral relationship and diagnose subtle subluxations. It clearly shows the anterior displacement but can be difficult to obtain due to patient pain. - **MRI / MR Arthrogram:** - Not indicated for acute diagnosis. - Used in the outpatient setting to evaluate for soft-tissue injuries (Bankart lesions, rotator cuff tears) and plan for potential surgery.

treatment: **Immediate goal is closed reduction.**
**Analgesia/Sedation:** Procedural sedation (e.g., ketamine, propofol) or intra-articular lidocaine injection is usually required to overcome pain and muscle spasm.
**Reduction Techniques:**
**Stimson Technique:** Patient is prone with the affected arm hanging off the table with weights attached to the wrist.
**Traction-Countertraction:** Longitudinal traction is applied to the arm while an assistant provides counter-traction with a sheet across the patient's chest.
**Scapular Manipulation:** With the patient prone, the provider rotates the inferior tip of the scapula medially.
**Milch Technique:** The arm is gently abducted and externally rotated, followed by direct pressure on the humeral head.
**Post-Reduction Protocol:**
management: **Immobilization:** A sling is used for comfort and to protect the joint, typically for 1-3 weeks. Shorter duration is favored in older patients to prevent adhesive capsulitis.
**Physical Therapy:** Essential for recovery. Begins with passive range of motion, progressing to active ROM and finally strengthening exercises focusing on the rotator cuff and scapular stabilizers.
**Orthopedic Follow-up:** All patients should follow up with an orthopedic specialist.
**Surgical Intervention (Arthroscopic Bankart Repair):**
**Indications:** Young, high-demand athletes after a first-time traumatic dislocation; recurrent instability; irreducible dislocation; significant associated fractures.
complications: **Recurrent Instability:** Most common complication, especially in patients < 20.
**Neurologic Injury:** Axillary nerve neuropraxia is the most common (5-10% of cases). Usually transient and resolves within 3-6 months.
**Bony Injury:**
**Hill-Sachs Lesion** (up to 80% of cases).
**Bony Bankart Lesion** (fracture of the anterior glenoid rim).
**Associated Fractures:** Greater tuberosity of the humerus is most common.
**Rotator Cuff Tears:** Increasingly common in patients > 40 years old.
**Vascular Injury:** Axillary artery or vein injury (rare, <1%).
**Adhesive Capsulitis ("Frozen Shoulder"):** Increased risk with prolonged immobilization.
sections.prognosis: - Prognosis is generally good for returning to normal function. - The primary factor influencing long-term outcome is the risk of recurrence, which is inversely proportional to the patient's age at the time of the first dislocation. - Surgical stabilization can significantly reduce the rate of recurrence in high-risk populations.

sections.overview: A supracondylar humerus fracture is a complete or incomplete fracture of the distal humerus, located in the metaphyseal bone just proximal to the elbow joint's condyles and physis (growth plate). It is the most common elbow fracture in children and is considered a true orthopedic emergency due to the high risk of associated neurovascular injury. The vast majority are extension-type injuries resulting from a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH).
sections.epidemiology: * **Age:** Most common in children aged **5-7 years**. * **Prevalence:** Accounts for approximately 60% of all pediatric elbow fractures and 3% of all pediatric fractures. * **Sex:** Slight male predominance. * **Limb:** More common in the non-dominant arm.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A child typically presents to the emergency department with a history of a fall, usually from a height (e.g., bed, playground equipment), followed by immediate and severe elbow pain. The child will be guarding the injured limb, holding it in a flexed position against their body and refusing to move it.

diagnostics.notes: * **Imaging:** X-ray is the primary diagnostic tool. * **Views:** AP and a true Lateral of the elbow are essential. * **Key Radiographic Lines/Signs:** * **Anterior Humeral Line:** On a true lateral view, a line drawn along the anterior cortex of the humerus should pass through the **middle third of the capitellum**. In an extension-type fracture, the capitellum is displaced posteriorly, and this line passes through the anterior third or completely misses it. * **Fat Pad Sign:** The presence of a **posterior fat pad** is *always abnormal* and indicates an intra-articular effusion (hemarthrosis), suggesting an occult fracture even if no fracture line is visible. An elevated anterior fat pad ("sail sign") is also abnormal. * **Gartland Classification (for Extension-Type Fractures):** Used to guide treatment. * **Type I:** Non-displaced or minimally displaced (<2 mm). * **Type II:** Displaced with the posterior cortex still intact (hinged). * **Type III:** Completely displaced with no cortical contact. High risk of neurovascular injury.

sections.prognosis: The prognosis is **excellent** for appropriately and promptly treated fractures. Most children regain near-full to full range of motion and function. The prognosis worsens with delayed treatment, severe initial displacement, or the development of complications like compartment syndrome.

sections.overview: A posterior shoulder dislocation is an orthopedic injury where the humeral head displaces posteriorly relative to the glenoid fossa of the scapula. It is significantly less common than anterior shoulder dislocation, accounting for only 2-5% of all shoulder dislocations. Due to its subtle clinical and radiographic findings, it is frequently missed on initial presentation, with some series reporting up to 50-80% of cases being missed in the emergency department. Prompt and accurate diagnosis is crucial to prevent long-term complications such as chronic instability, pain, and avascular necrosis. ***
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** Accounts for 2-5% of all glenohumeral dislocations. * **Demographics:** Most commonly affects young, active males (20-40 years old) due to trauma. A second peak is seen in patients with seizure disorders. * **Bilateral dislocations:** While rare, they are almost pathognomonic for a seizure or electrical shock event. ***
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation is often much more subtle than an anterior dislocation. Patients typically present holding the affected arm in a characteristic position: **adducted and internally rotated**. They will be in significant pain and unwilling to move the arm, particularly into external rotation. Unlike an anterior dislocation where a prominent humeral head creates an anterior bulge ("squared-off shoulder"), the anterior shoulder may appear flattened with a prominent coracoid process. ***
sections.prognosis: The prognosis is generally good if the dislocation is diagnosed and reduced acutely. Outcomes are significantly worse for missed or chronic dislocations, often requiring complex open surgery and resulting in some degree of permanent stiffness and pain. The size of the reverse Hill-Sachs lesion is a major prognostic factor for future instability. ***

sections.overview: A **Galeazzi fracture** is an unstable fracture of the **distal third of the radial shaft** with an associated **dislocation or instability of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ)**. It is considered a fracture-dislocation of the forearm. Due to its inherent instability, it is often called a **"fracture of necessity,"** as it almost always requires surgical intervention in adults for a good functional outcome.
sections.epidemiology: * Relatively uncommon, accounting for 3-7% of all forearm fractures. * Most frequently occurs in young to middle-aged adults, with a male predominance. * Bimodal age distribution: * Younger patients: High-energy trauma (e.g., motor vehicle accidents, contact sports). * Older patients: Low-energy falls (less common).
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient typically presents with a history of acute trauma to the forearm or wrist, holding the injured arm protectively against their body. There is often an obvious deformity of the forearm and wrist.

diagnostics.notes: * **Imaging:** * **X-rays:** The primary diagnostic tool. * **Required Views:** AP and Lateral views of the **entire forearm**, including dedicated views of the **wrist and elbow joints.** Failure to include the entire forearm can lead to a missed DRUJ dislocation. * **Radiographic Findings:** 1. **Radial Fracture:** Transverse or oblique fracture at the junction of the middle and distal thirds of the radius. 2. **DRUJ Dislocation:** * **Widening of the DRUJ space** on the AP view. * **Dorsal or volar displacement of the ulna** relative to the radius on the lateral view. * **Radial shortening** of >5mm relative to the ulna. * Associated **ulnar styloid fracture** (present in ~60% of cases, highly suggestive of TFCC injury and DRUJ instability). * **CT Scan:** Rarely needed but can be useful for surgical planning in complex fracture patterns or to better evaluate the DRUJ.

sections.prognosis: * Excellent with prompt and accurate diagnosis followed by anatomic ORIF of the radius and stabilization of the DRUJ. * Poor outcomes are strongly associated with a missed DRUJ injury, inadequate radial reduction, or persistent DRUJ instability. The status of the DRUJ is the primary determinant of long-term function.

sections.overview: A **Smith fracture** is a fracture of the distal radius characterized by **volar (palmar) angulation or displacement** of the distal fracture fragment. It is often referred to as a **"reverse Colles' fracture"** because the mechanism of injury and resulting deformity are the opposite of the more common Colles' fracture.
sections.epidemiology: - Less common than Colles' fractures. - Exhibits a bimodal age distribution: - **Younger patients (primarily males):** Resulting from high-energy trauma (e.g., motor vehicle accidents, falls from height, contact sports). - **Older patients (primarily females):** Resulting from low-energy trauma (e.g., a simple ground-level fall), often secondary to osteoporosis.
riskFactors: **Osteoporosis:** The most significant risk factor in the elderly population, leading to fractures from low-energy mechanisms.
**Advanced age:** Associated with decreased bone mineral density and increased risk of falls.
**High-impact activities/sports:** Increases risk in younger individuals (e.g., snowboarding, football).
**Poor balance or neuromuscular disorders:** Increases the risk of falling.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient typically presents with a history of a recent fall onto a flexed wrist or a direct blow to the back of the wrist. They will complain of immediate, severe pain, swelling, and an obvious deformity of the affected wrist. The patient will often be cradling the injured arm with their other hand.

diagnostics.notes: - **Primary Modality: X-ray** - **Required Views:** Anteroposterior (AP) and **Lateral**. - **Key Finding:** The **lateral view is essential** for diagnosis. It will clearly demonstrate the characteristic **volar angulation and displacement** of the distal radial fragment. - **Other Findings:** The AP view helps assess for intra-articular extension, fracture comminution, radial shortening, and associated ulnar styloid fracture (present in ~50% of cases). - **Secondary Modality: CT Scan** - **Indications:** Not routinely needed. Indicated for complex, comminuted, or intra-articular fractures to better define the fracture pattern and assist with pre-operative planning.

treatment: **Non-Operative:**
**Indications:** Stable, extra-articular, and minimally displaced/angulated fractures that are amenable to closed reduction.
**Procedure:**
**Initial:** **Sugar tong splint** is applied to allow for swelling while immobilizing the wrist and preventing pronation/supination.
**Definitive:** Converted to a **short arm cast** after 7-10 days once initial swelling has subsided. Total immobilization is typically for 4-6 weeks.
**Operative:**
**Indications:** Unstable fractures, significant displacement (>20 angulation, >2mm articular step-off), comminution, intra-articular involvement, open fractures, or failed closed reduction.

**Procedure:** **Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF)** is the most common approach, typically using a **volar locking plate and screws**. This provides stable fixation, allowing for early range of motion.
management: **Emergency Department:**
Perform a thorough neurovascular exam before and after any intervention.
Provide adequate analgesia.
Perform closed reduction and apply a sugar tong splint.
Obtain post-reduction films to confirm acceptable alignment.
Discharge with strict instructions for elevation, ice, and pain control.
**Outpatient Follow-up:**
Mandatory orthopedic follow-up within one week.
Serial x-rays are obtained to ensure the reduction is maintained.
After cast removal, initiate **Physical/Occupational Therapy** to regain strength, flexibility, and function.
complications: **Acute:**

**Median Nerve Injury / Acute Carpal Tunnel Syndrome:** The most common neurological complication due to direct compression or swelling within the carpal tunnel. May require urgent carpal tunnel release if neurovascularly compromised.
**Compartment Syndrome:** A surgical emergency characterized by pain out of proportion, pallor, paresthesias, pulselessness, and paralysis.
**Associated Injuries:** Ulnar styloid fracture, Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex (TFCC) tear, scapholunate ligament injury.
**Delayed/Chronic:**
**Malunion:** The most common overall complication. The fracture heals in an unacceptable (volarly angulated) position, leading to the "garden spade deformity," pain, and limited supination.
**Post-traumatic Osteoarthritis:** High risk with intra-articular fractures.
**Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS):** A chronic pain condition characterized by severe pain, swelling, and autonomic dysfunction.
**Tendon Rupture:** Delayed rupture of the **Extensor Pollicis Longus (EPL)** tendon can occur due to irritation over the fracture site.
**Nonunion:** Rare.
sections.prognosis: The prognosis is generally good for fractures that are anatomically reduced and properly managed. Outcomes are worse for patients with significant intra-articular displacement, severe comminution, advanced age, or associated nerve injury. Early mobilization after stable fixation (ORIF) can lead to excellent functional recovery.

sections.overview: A **Monteggia fracture** is a specific injury pattern defined by a **fracture of the proximal third of the ulna** combined with a **dislocation of the radial head**. The ulnar fracture is typically obvious on imaging, but the radial head dislocation can be subtle and is a commonly missed diagnosis. Proper identification is critical, as mismanagement leads to significant long-term disability. The injury is classified using the **Bado classification system**, which is based on the direction of the radial head dislocation.
sections.epidemiology: * Relatively uncommon, accounting for <5% of all forearm fractures. * **Bimodal age distribution:** * **Peak 1:** Children aged 4-10 years. * **Peak 2:** Young adults. * **Bado Type I** is the most common type in both children (>75%) and adults (>60%).
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient typically presents to the emergency department after a fall or direct blow to the arm, complaining of severe pain and inability to move the elbow or forearm. The ulnar fracture deformity may be apparent, but the elbow dislocation can be masked by swelling. **Crucial Clinical Point:** Always maintain a high index of suspicion for a radial head dislocation in any patient with a proximal ulna fracture. The mantra is to **image the joint above and below** any long bone fracture.

diagnostics.notes: * **X-rays:** * **Required Views:** AP and lateral views of the **entire forearm**, ensuring both the elbow and wrist joints are included. * **Key Finding (The Diagnostic Line):** The **Radiocapitellar Line**. A line drawn through the center of the radial shaft and neck should **always intersect the capitellum** on *every* radiographic view. * If this line does not point to the capitellum, the radial head is dislocated, and a Monteggia fracture is diagnosed. * The ulnar fracture is usually easily visualized on the proximal third of the bone. * **Bado Classification (based on direction of radial head dislocation):** * **Type I (60-75%):** **Anterior** dislocation of the radial head. Associated with an anteriorly-angulated (apex posterior) ulnar fracture. * **Type II (15%):** **Posterior** dislocation of the radial head. Associated with a posteriorly-angulated (apex anterior) ulnar fracture. * **Type III (5-20%):** **Lateral** or anterolateral dislocation of the radial head. Associated with a fracture of the ulnar metaphysis. * **Type IV (<5%):** **Anterior** dislocation of the radial head with an associated fracture of **both the radius and ulna**.

sections.prognosis: * **Children:** Excellent prognosis with prompt diagnosis and treatment. Most regain full function with minimal complications. * **Adults:** Good prognosis, but the risk of complications is higher. Stiffness (loss of motion) is the most frequent long-term issue. Outcomes are directly related to the quality of the ulnar reduction and the stability of the radiocapitellar joint.

sections.overview: A radial head fracture is a break in the proximal part of the radius, one of the two forearm bones that form the elbow joint. It is one of the most common elbow fractures in adults. These injuries typically result from a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH) and can range from a simple, non-displaced crack to a severely comminuted fracture with associated elbow dislocation and ligamentous injury. Diagnosis is confirmed with radiography, and treatment is guided by the fracture pattern and displacement, most commonly using the **Mason Classification**.
sections.epidemiology: * Accounts for approximately **33% of all elbow fractures** and about 2-5% of all fractures in adults. * Most common in adults between **30-60 years of age**. * More common in **females** than males (ratio of approx. 2:1). * Frequently associated with other injuries, such as elbow dislocation, coronoid process fractures, and ligamentous tears (e.g., lateral collateral ligament complex).
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient typically presents to the emergency department or an urgent care clinic after a fall, cradling the injured arm close to their body. They will report an acute onset of severe elbow pain and will be hesitant to move the arm, particularly in rotation.
sections.prognosis: * **Excellent** for Mason Type I fractures, with most patients returning to full function. * **Good to fair** for Mason Type II and III fractures treated operatively. Some residual stiffness is common, but functional outcomes are generally positive. * **Guarded** for complex injuries like the "Terrible Triad" (elbow dislocation, radial head fracture, and coronoid fracture), which have a high rate of stiffness and instability.

sections.overview: A scaphoid fracture is a break in the scaphoid bone, one of the eight small carpal bones in the wrist. It is the most commonly fractured carpal bone.
