**Nail Dystrophy:** Pitting and ridging from chronic inflammation near the nail matrix.
**Psychosocial Impact:** Significant effect on quality of life due to severe itching, pain, and cosmetic appearance.
sections.prognosis: - The condition follows a **chronic, relapsing-remitting course**. - Individual flares typically resolve within 3-4 weeks, but recurrence is the rule. - Many patients experience spontaneous improvement with age. - The prognosis is significantly better if an avoidable trigger (like a contact allergen) can be identified.

sections.overview: Contact dermatitis is an inflammatory eczematous skin reaction resulting from direct contact with an external substance. It is broadly divided into two main categories: * **Irritant Contact Dermatitis (ICD):** The more common type (~80%). A non-immunologic inflammatory reaction caused by direct cytotoxic damage to the skin barrier from an offending chemical or physical agent. * **Allergic Contact Dermatitis (ACD):** A less common type (~20%). A delayed, Type IV hypersensitivity reaction (T-cell mediated) that occurs after sensitization to a specific allergen.
sections.epidemiology: * One of the most common occupational skin diseases. * ICD accounts for approximately 80% of all contact dermatitis cases. * ACD accounts for the remaining 20%. * Affects all ages and ethnicities. * High prevalence in certain occupations: healthcare workers, food handlers, hairdressers, mechanics, cleaners.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A thorough history is critical to identify the causative agent. Key questions should focus on occupation, hobbies, new products, topical medications, and potential plant exposures. | Feature | Irritant Contact Dermatitis (ICD) | Allergic Contact Dermatitis (ACD) | | - | - | -- | | **Onset** | Hours after exposure (strong irritant) or gradual (weak irritant) | Delayed: 12-72 hours after re-exposure | | **Prior Exposure** | Not required | Sensitization (prior exposure) is required | | **Distribution** | Sharply demarcated, confined strictly to site of contact | May spread beyond the site of contact; borders can be less distinct | | **Classic Example** | "Dishpan hands" from detergents; diaper dermatitis. | Linear vesicles from poison ivy; rash under a watch buckle (nickel). |

diagnostics.notes: * **Clinical Diagnosis:** Diagnosis is primarily based on a detailed history and a physical exam that reveals a characteristic morphology and distribution. * **Patch Testing:** * **Gold standard for identifying the causative allergen in ACD.** * Standardized allergens are applied to the patient's back on adhesive patches. Patches are removed at 48 hours, and the skin is evaluated for reactions at 48 and 72-96 hours. * A positive test shows erythema, papules, or vesicles at the allergen site. * **Not used for ICD.** * **KOH Preparation:** Can be performed on skin scrapings to rule out tinea (fungal infection), which can mimic chronic contact dermatitis of the hands or feet.

sections.prognosis: * **Excellent** if the causative agent is identified and strictly avoided. * May become chronic, relapsing, and difficult to control if the agent cannot be identified or if exposure is unavoidable (e.g., in an occupational setting).

sections.overview: Seborrheic dermatitis is a common, chronic, or relapsing inflammatory skin condition that primarily affects seborrhea-prone (oily) regions of the body. It is not contagious. In its mildest form, it is known as dandruff (pityriasis capitis). In infants, it is commonly called "cradle cap."
sections.epidemiology: - **Prevalence:** Affects approximately 3-10% of the general population. Dandruff, the mildest form, affects up to 50%. - **Age:** Bimodal age distribution: - **Infancy:** First 3 months of life ("cradle cap"). - **Adulthood:** Post-puberty, with a peak incidence between 30-60 years. - **Sex:** Slightly more common in males.
riskFactors: **HIV/AIDS:** Very common and often severe. Severity can correlate with CD4 count decline.
sections.clinicalPresentation: - **Infants:** Presents as "cradle cap" - thick, yellow, greasy, adherent plaques on the scalp vertex. It is typically non-pruritic and self-limited. Can also affect the face and diaper area. - **Adults:** Presents with a chronic, relapsing course of "dandruff" or erythematous patches with greasy scales in characteristic locations. Flares are common, often triggered by stress or seasonal changes.

diagnostics.notes: - **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic morphology and distribution of the rash. - **KOH Preparation:** Can be performed to rule out tinea (dermatophytosis), especially on the scalp (tinea capitis) or body (tinea corporis). KOH prep will be **negative for hyphae** in seborrheic dermatitis. - **Skin Biopsy:** Rarely necessary. Performed only if the diagnosis is uncertain or there's a poor response to treatment. Histology shows parakeratosis, acanthosis, spongiosis, and a superficial perivascular inflammatory infiltrate.

treatment: **Scalp (Dandruff/Adult Seborrheic Dermatitis):**
**First-line:** Medicated shampoos used 2-3 times weekly. Rotate agents to prevent tachyphylaxis.
**Antifungals:** **Ketoconazole 2%** (Rx) or 1% (OTC), **selenium sulfide**, ciclopirox.
**Keratolytics:** Salicylic acid, coal tar.
**Anti-inflammatory:** Zinc pyrithione.
**Second-line:** Topical corticosteroids (e.g., fluocinolone solution, clobetasol foam) for short-term use during flares to control inflammation and pruritus.
**Face and Body:**
**First-line:**
Topical antifungals: **Ketoconazole 2% cream**.
Low-potency topical corticosteroids: **Hydrocortisone 1%** or **desonide 0.05% cream** for flares (use for <2 weeks to avoid side effects).
**Second-line (Steroid-sparing):**
Topical calcineurin inhibitors: **Pimecrolimus cream** or **tacrolimus ointment**. Excellent for facial use to avoid steroid-induced atrophy.
**Infants (Cradle Cap):**
**Conservative:** Reassurance. Apply emollients (baby oil, petroleum jelly) to soften crusts, followed by gentle removal with a soft brush and washing with a mild baby shampoo.
**Medical:** If persistent, can use low-potency hydrocortisone cream or ketoconazole 2% shampoo/cream sparingly.
**Severe or Refractory Disease:**
Consider oral antifungals (itraconazole or fluconazole).
Oral isotretinoin may be used in rare, severe cases.
management: **Patient Education:** Emphasize the chronic, relapsing nature of the condition. Explain that the goal is control, not cure.
**Maintenance Therapy:** Once a flare is controlled, regular use of medicated shampoos (1-2 times/week) or creams can help prevent recurrence.
**Trigger Avoidance:** Counsel patients on managing stress and avoiding harsh soaps or known irritants.
complications: **Secondary bacterial infection (impetiginization):** Due to scratching and skin barrier breakdown.
**Side effects of treatment:** Skin atrophy, telangiectasias, and hypopigmentation from long-term, potent topical steroid use, especially on the face or in skin folds.
**Psychosocial impact:** Can affect self-esteem due to the visible nature of the condition.
**Erythroderma:** Rare complication where the rash becomes generalized, affecting >90% of body surface area.
sections.prognosis: - **Infantile form:** Excellent. Usually self-resolves by 6-12 months of age. - **Adult form:** Considered a chronic condition. While symptoms can be effectively controlled with treatment, it tends to follow a relapsing and remitting course throughout life.

sections.overview: Nummular Dermatitis, also known as discoid eczema or nummular eczema, is a chronic, inflammatory skin condition characterized by well-demarcated, coin-shaped (nummular) or oval plaques of eczematous skin. It is intensely pruritic and follows a relapsing-remitting course. The etiology is not fully understood, but skin barrier dysfunction (xerosis) is a key contributing factor.
sections.epidemiology: * **Bimodal Age Distribution:** * First peak: Young adult women (ages 15-25). * Second peak: Older men (ages 50-65). * **Prevalence:** More common in winter months due to lower humidity and increased xerosis. * **Association:** Can occur in patients with or without a history of atopic dermatitis.
sections.clinicalPresentation: * **History:** Patients typically report the sudden onset of intensely itchy, round spots, often on the arms or legs. The spots may have started as small bumps or blisters that merged together. The pruritus is often severe and may interfere with sleep. There is often a personal or family history of atopic conditions, though not always. Patients frequently report dry skin, especially during the winter.

diagnostics.notes: Nummular dermatitis is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on history and the characteristic appearance of the lesions. * **Clinical Diagnosis:** Based on the presence of pruritic, coin-shaped eczematous plaques on a background of xerotic skin. * **Potassium Hydroxide (KOH) Prep:** **Essential to perform.** A skin scraping is examined under a microscope to rule out tinea corporis (ringworm), the main differential diagnosis. A negative KOH prep (no hyphae or spores) supports the diagnosis of nummular dermatitis. * **Bacterial Culture & Sensitivity:** Indicated if secondary bacterial infection is suspected (e.g., significant crusting, pustules, purulence, or failure to respond to initial therapy). *S. aureus* is the most common pathogen. * **Patch Testing:** Consider in persistent or recalcitrant cases to rule out an underlying allergic contact dermatitis. * **Skin Biopsy:** Rarely necessary. Performed only if the diagnosis is uncertain or if there is suspicion for another condition like cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

sections.prognosis: * Nummular dermatitis is a chronic condition with a high rate of recurrence. * Lesions often recur in the same locations. * While complete cure is uncommon, the condition can be well-managed and controlled with consistent skin care and appropriate treatment during flares.

sections.overview: Perioral dermatitis is a common inflammatory facial skin eruption characterized by clusters of erythematous papules, papulopustules, and sometimes vesicles. Despite its name, it is considered a variant of rosacea rather than a true eczematous dermatitis. The eruption classically occurs around the mouth, nose, and eyes. A key diagnostic feature is the sparing of the skin directly adjacent to the vermilion border of the lips.
sections.epidemiology: * **Primary Demographic:** Most commonly affects **young women**, typically between the ages of 16 and 45. * **Prevalence:** Accounts for approximately 90% of cases in women. * **Other Populations:** Can occur in men and children, but it is far less common.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient, typically a young woman, presents with a persistent rash around her mouth that has been present for weeks to months. She may report a history of using over-the-counter or prescribed hydrocortisone cream on the area, which initially helped but now seems to make the rash worse or cause a significant flare when she stops using it. The main complaint is often cosmetic.

diagnostics.notes: * **Clinical Diagnosis:** Diagnosis is almost always made based on the characteristic history and classic physical exam findings (papules/pustules with vermilion border sparing). * **Biopsy:** Rarely necessary. If performed, histopathology shows a perifollicular and perivascular lymphohistiocytic inflammatory infiltrate. * **Culture:** A bacterial culture of a pustule can be performed to rule out staphylococcal folliculitis if the diagnosis is uncertain, but it is not routinely required.

sections.prognosis: * **Excellent:** With proper treatment and trigger avoidance, the prognosis is excellent and most cases resolve completely. * **Recurrence:** Recurrence is common if triggers, particularly topical corticosteroids, are reintroduced.

sections.overview: Diaper dermatitis, commonly known as diaper rash, is a general term for an acute inflammatory skin reaction in the region covered by a diaper. It is most commonly a form of irritant contact dermatitis. While typically benign, it causes significant discomfort for the infant and concern for caregivers.
sections.epidemiology: * One of the most frequent dermatologic conditions in infancy. * Peak incidence occurs between **9 and 12 months** of age. * Affects approximately 25-35% of diaper-wearing infants at any given time. * Slightly higher incidence in formula-fed infants compared to breastfed infants (due to higher stool pH).
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation depends on the underlying etiology. Parents typically report a new-onset rash in the diaper area, often associated with infant fussiness or crying, especially during diaper changes. The history should focus on diapering habits, diet, recent illnesses (especially diarrhea), and medication use.

diagnostics.notes: * Diagnosis is almost always **clinical**, based on history and physical exam findings. * **KOH Preparation:** Can be performed on scrapings from a satellite lesion to confirm *Candida*. Will reveal budding yeast and pseudohyphae. This is rarely necessary in practice due to the classic clinical appearance. * **Culture:** A bacterial culture can be done if a secondary bacterial infection (impetigo) is suspected (e.g., honey-colored crusting). * **Skin Biopsy:** Reserved for severe, atypical, or treatment-refractory cases to rule out less common diagnoses (e.g., Langerhans cell histiocytosis).

sections.prognosis: The prognosis is **excellent**. Most cases of uncomplicated diaper dermatitis resolve within 3-7 days with appropriate management. Recurrence is common if preventive measures are not consistently followed.

sections.overview: Prurigo Nodularis (PN) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by intensely pruritic (itchy), firm, hyperkeratotic, and often excoriated nodules. The condition is driven by a self-perpetuating **itch-scratch cycle**, where intense pruritus leads to chronic scratching, which in turn causes the development of the characteristic skin lesions. These lesions themselves are pruritic, thus continuing the cycle. It significantly impacts quality of life due to the severity of the itch and the disfiguring nature of the lesions.
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** Uncommon, but likely underdiagnosed. * **Age of Onset:** Typically affects middle-aged to older adults (50-65 years). * **Race/Ethnicity:** Higher prevalence and disease severity are noted in **African Americans**.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The hallmark of PN is the patient history of an **intense, debilitating, and chronic itch** that has been present for months to years, often preceding the visible lesions. Patients report that the itch is deep and unrelenting, leading to uncontrollable scratching. This has a profound negative impact on sleep, work, and social functioning.

diagnostics.notes: * **Clinical Diagnosis:** Diagnosis is primarily made based on the characteristic history of severe chronic pruritus and the presence of typical nodules on physical exam. * **Skin Biopsy (Punch or Excisional):** * **Indication:** Performed to confirm the diagnosis, especially in atypical cases, or to rule out malignancy (e.g., Squamous Cell Carcinoma, Keratoacanthoma, Cutaneous Lymphoma). * **Histopathology Findings (High-Yield):** * Massive epidermal thickening (**acanthosis**) and hyperkeratosis. * Thickened papillary dermis with vertically oriented collagen bundles. * **Thickened and increased number of nerve fibers (neural hypertrophy)** - a pathognomonic feature. * Mixed inflammatory infiltrate, often with prominent eosinophils. * **Laboratory Workup:** Ordered to investigate for underlying systemic causes. * CBC with differential (to check for anemia, eosinophilia, polycythemia) * Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) (to assess renal and hepatic function) * TSH (thyroid function) * HIV and Hepatitis C serologies * Fasting glucose/HbA1c

sections.prognosis: PN is a chronic disease with a relapsing-remitting course. It is often difficult to achieve complete, long-term remission. The prognosis is significantly improved when an underlying cause is identified and treated. The advent of highly effective targeted biologics like dupilumab has dramatically improved the outlook for patients with moderate-to-severe, refractory disease.

sections.overview: Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS), also known as acne inversa, is a chronic, recurrent, inflammatory skin disease of the hair follicle. It is not a primary infection nor a disease of the sweat glands. HS characteristically affects intertriginous skin areas (areas where skin rubs together) and is defined by painful, deep-seated inflammatory nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts, and progressive scarring.
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** Affects approximately 1% of the population. * **Gender:** More common in females (Female:Male ratio 3:1). * **Age of Onset:** Typically occurs after puberty, most commonly in the 2nd and 3rd decades of life (ages 20-29). Disease activity often decreases after menopause.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient, typically a young adult female who smokes, presents with a history of recurrent, painful "boils" in the armpits or groin. The lesions are chronic, lasting for weeks, and often drain purulent, foul-smelling fluid before healing with significant scarring. The patient reports a significant negative impact on quality of life due to pain and embarrassment.

diagnostics.notes: HS is a **clinical diagnosis** based on three key criteria: 1. **Typical Lesions:** Nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts. 2. **Typical Location:** Axillae, groin, anogenital, inframammary regions. 3. **Chronicity & Recurrence:** The lesions are long-lasting and recurrent. * **Lab Studies:** Generally not required for diagnosis. May show non-specific signs of inflammation (elevated CRP, ESR, leukocytosis). * **Bacteriology:** Swabs of draining lesions are often polymicrobial and reflect colonization, not causation. Swabs are primarily useful to rule out a primary staphylococcal abscess or identify secondary infection (e.g., MRSA) guiding acute antibiotic choice. * **Biopsy:** Rarely needed. May be performed in atypical cases or to rule out Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) in a chronic, non-healing lesion.

sections.prognosis: * HS is a chronic, lifelong disease with a relapsing and remitting course. * There is no cure, but treatment can manage symptoms, reduce flare frequency, and prevent progression. * Early and aggressive management is key to preventing the development of irreversible tissue damage (Stage III disease). * The disease has a profound negative impact on quality of life, comparable to conditions like psoriasis, heart failure, or COPD.

sections.overview: Urticaria (hives) is a common skin condition characterized by the development of wheals (transient, circumscribed, edematous, and erythematous plaques), angioedema (swelling of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissues), or both. It is classified based on duration: * **Acute Urticaria:** Lasts **< 6 weeks**. Often due to an identifiable trigger like an infection, food, or medication. * **Chronic Urticaria:** Lasts **> 6 weeks**. The cause is often idiopathic or autoimmune. It is further subdivided into Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria (CSU) and Chronic Inducible Urticaria (CIndU).
sections.epidemiology: * **Lifetime Prevalence:** Approximately 20% of the population will experience urticaria at some point. * **Acute Urticaria:** Very common, especially in children, often associated with viral infections. * **Chronic Urticaria:** Affects about 0.5-1% of the population. * **Peak Incidence:** 20-40 years of age. * **Sex Predilection:** More common in females (2:1 ratio).
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient typically presents with a sudden onset of skin lesions accompanied by intense itching. The history should focus on identifying a potential trigger (new food, medication, recent illness, physical exposure). It is crucial to inquire about symptoms of anaphylaxis (shortness of breath, wheezing, throat tightness, dizziness, hypotension). The hallmark of urticaria is the **transient nature of individual lesions**. Each wheal appears and resolves completely **within 24 hours** without leaving any residual marking (e.g., bruising, scaling). New lesions may appear as old ones fade, giving the impression of a continuous rash.

diagnostics.notes: * **Acute Urticaria:** Usually a **clinical diagnosis**. No laboratory workup is necessary if the cause is clear and it is not associated with anaphylaxis. * **Chronic Urticaria (>6 weeks):** Workup aims to rule out underlying conditions and identify triggers. * **First-Line Labs:** * CBC with differential (to screen for eosinophilia or systemic inflammation). * ESR and/or CRP (inflammatory markers). * **Second-Line Labs (based on H&P):** * **TSH and anti-TPO antibodies:** To screen for autoimmune thyroid disease, a common comorbidity. * Hepatitis panel, stool O&P if infectious etiology is suspected. * **Provocation Testing (for CIndU):** * **Ice Cube Test:** Place an ice cube on the forearm for 5-10 minutes. Wheal formation upon rewarming is diagnostic for cold urticaria. * **Stroking the skin** with a tongue depressor to elicit dermatographism. * **Skin Biopsy:** Indicated if lesions are atypical: * Last > 24-48 hours. * Are painful rather than pruritic. * Leave behind purpura or bruising (petechiae/ecchymosis). * *Findings:* A biopsy can differentiate simple urticaria (perivascular infiltrate without vessel wall destruction) from **urticarial vasculitis** (leukocytoclasis, fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls).

sections.prognosis: * **Acute Urticaria:** Excellent. The vast majority of cases resolve spontaneously within days to a few weeks. * **Chronic Urticaria:** Variable and unpredictable. * Approximately 50% of patients with CSU experience remission within 1 year. * However, symptoms can persist for 5-10 years or longer in a significant minority. * Chronic inducible urticarias often have a longer course than CSU.

sections.overview: Angioedema is a localized, well-demarcated, non-pitting edema affecting the deep dermal, subcutaneous, or submucosal tissues. It most commonly involves the face, lips, tongue, larynx, extremities, and gastrointestinal tract. The primary danger is laryngeal edema, which can lead to rapid airway compromise and asphyxiation. The pathophysiology is broadly divided into two main categories, which dictates the clinical presentation and treatment: 1. **Mast Cell (Histaminergic) Mediated:** The most common type. Associated with urticaria and pruritus. Responds to standard allergy treatments. 2. **Bradykinin-Mediated:** Less common but critical to identify. **Not** associated with urticaria or pruritus. Does **not** respond to epinephrine, antihistamines, or steroids.
sections.epidemiology: * **General:** Affects up to 25% of the population at some point. * **Mast Cell-Mediated:** The most common form overall. * **ACE Inhibitor-Induced:** Occurs in 0.1-0.7% of patients on ACE inhibitors. More common in African Americans, women, and smokers. * **Hereditary Angioedema (HAE):** Rare, with a prevalence of approximately 1 in 50,000.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient presents with acute onset of asymmetric, non-pitting swelling. The history is critical for determining the underlying cause. Key questions revolve around new medications (especially ACE inhibitors), allergic triggers, personal or family history of similar episodes, and associated symptoms (itching, hives, abdominal pain). The most urgent consideration is airway involvement.

diagnostics.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical. Labs are used to confirm suspected bradykinin-mediated angioedema, not for acute management. * **Initial Assessment:** ABCs take priority. Laryngoscopy (flexible fiberoptic) is the gold standard to directly visualize laryngeal edema if airway compromise is suspected. * **Laboratory Studies (for suspected HAE/AAE):** * **Screening Test:** **C4 complement level.** * C4 is consumed in the pathway leading to bradykinin production. * A **low C4 level** during or between attacks is highly suggestive of HAE or AAE. * A normal C4 makes HAE Type I/II very unlikely. * **Confirmatory Tests:** * **C1-INH quantitative (antigenic) level:** Low in HAE Type I. * **C1-INH functional assay:** Low in both HAE Type I and II. * **C1q level:** Used to differentiate HAE from AAE. C1q is **normal in HAE** but **low in AAE**. * **Allergy Testing:** May be useful later to identify triggers for IgE-mediated angioedema.

sections.prognosis: * Excellent if the airway is managed appropriately and the correct diagnosis is made. * Mortality is almost exclusively due to airway obstruction. * For HAE, prognosis has dramatically improved with the availability of specific on-demand and prophylactic therapies.

sections.overview: Erythema Multiforme (EM) is an acute, self-limiting, immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction characterized by distinctive target-like lesions on the skin. It may also involve one or more mucous membranes. The condition exists on a spectrum, classically divided into EM minor and EM major. It is crucial to distinguish EM from Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN), which are now considered separate, more severe entities.
sections.epidemiology: * **Age:** Most common in young adults, typically between 20-40 years old. Can occur at any age. * **Sex:** Slight male predominance. * **Incidence:** Relatively common, though exact figures are difficult to obtain due to its self-limiting nature. * **Seasonality:** May show a slight peak in spring and autumn, possibly mirroring the incidence of HSV outbreaks.
sections.clinicalPresentation: * **Onset:** Acute, developing over several days. * **Prodrome:** May be preceded by 1-7 days of low-grade fever, malaise, myalgias, headache, or sore throat. * **Evolution of Rash:** Lesions appear abruptly and symmetrically. They often begin on the extensor surfaces of the extremities (dorsal hands, feet, elbows, knees) and spread centripetally (towards the trunk). Palms and soles are commonly involved. * **Course:** The condition is self-limiting, typically resolving within 2-4 weeks without scarring, although post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation may occur.

diagnostics.notes: * **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on history and the presence of typical target lesions. * **Skin Biopsy:** Not always necessary but performed in atypical cases to rule out other conditions (e.g., SJS, bullous pemphigoid). * **Findings:** Perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, dermal edema, and focal keratinocyte necrosis. * **Laboratory Studies:** Generally not required for diagnosis but useful for identifying the underlying trigger. * **HSV PCR or culture** from a preceding herpetic lesion. * ***Mycoplasma* serology (IgM)** or PCR from a throat swab. * CBC, CMP, ESR/CRP are non-specific but may show inflammation.

sections.prognosis: * **Excellent.** * **EM Minor:** Resolves completely in 2-4 weeks without scarring. * **EM Major:** Takes longer to resolve (3-6 weeks) and has a higher risk of complications (especially ocular), but mortality is very rare. * Recurrence is common, particularly in HSV-triggered cases, if prophylactic antivirals are not used.

sections.overview: Erythema Nodosum (EN) is an acute, nodular, erythematous inflammatory condition of the subcutaneous fat. It is a form of **panniculitis**-specifically, a **septal panniculitis without vasculitis**. EN is considered a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to a variety of underlying stimuli and is often a cutaneous marker for an underlying systemic disease, infection, or drug reaction. The lesions are self-limited and resolve without scarring.
sections.epidemiology: * **Age:** Most common in young adults, typically 20-40 years old. * **Sex:** Strong female predilection (Female:Male ratio of 3-6:1).
sections.clinicalPresentation: A typical patient is a young woman who presents with the acute onset of tender, red nodules on the shins, often accompanied by systemic symptoms like fever, malaise, and joint pain. She may report a recent sore throat, diarrheal illness, or starting a new medication (like OCPs).

diagnostics.notes: The diagnosis is often clinical. The workup is aimed at identifying the underlying cause. * **Initial Workup (Essential):** * **Chest X-ray (CXR):** Crucial to evaluate for **bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy** (suggesting sarcoidosis/Lfgren's Syndrome) or evidence of TB or fungal infection. * **CBC with differential:** May show leukocytosis. * **Inflammatory Markers:** ESR and CRP are almost always elevated. * **Workup Based on Suspicion:** * **ASO Titer or Throat Culture:** To rule out recent streptococcal infection. * **PPD Skin Test or IGRA:** To screen for Tuberculosis. * **Stool Cultures:** If GI symptoms are present (for *Yersinia*, *Salmonella*, etc.). * **Pregnancy Test (hCG).** * **Biopsy:** * **Indication:** Rarely needed; reserved for atypical cases where the diagnosis is uncertain. * **Procedure:** A deep incisional biopsy is required to obtain an adequate sample of subcutaneous fat. A punch biopsy is often insufficient. * **Histology:** Confirms **septal panniculitis without vasculitis**.

sections.prognosis: * The prognosis for the skin lesions is **excellent**, with spontaneous resolution within weeks to months. * The overall prognosis is entirely dependent on the successful identification and management of the underlying etiology.

sections.overview: A simple exanthematous drug eruption, also known as a morbilliform or maculopapular drug eruption, is the most common type of cutaneous adverse drug reaction. It is a T-cell mediated (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction characterized by a widespread, symmetric, erythematous maculopapular rash that appears 7-14 days after starting a new medication. It is considered "simple" due to the absence of systemic symptoms, mucosal involvement, or organ damage, distinguishing it from severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs).
sections.epidemiology: - Accounts for ~90% of all cutaneous drug eruptions. - Incidence is approximately 1-5% for users of high-risk medications. - Can occur at any age, in any race, and affects both sexes, with a slight predilection for females.
riskFactors: **Specific Medications:** Certain drugs (see Etiology) have a higher incidence.

**Viral Infections:** Concurrent viral infections can increase risk. The classic example is the high incidence (~90%) of a morbilliform rash when **amoxicillin is given to a patient with Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) mononucleosis**.
**Immunocompromised States:** Patients with **HIV** have a significantly higher risk (up to 50-60%) of drug eruptions, especially to sulfonamides.
**Genetic Predisposition:** Certain HLA alleles are associated with increased risk for specific drugs (though this is more strongly linked to SCARs).
**History of Prior Drug Eruption:** A previous reaction increases the likelihood of future reactions.
sections.clinicalPresentation: - **History is key:** The patient will report starting a new medication **7-14 days prior** to rash onset. If it's a re-exposure, the onset may be within 24-72 hours. - The rash typically begins on the **trunk and upper extremities** and then becomes more widespread and confluent over several days, spreading centrifugally (outward) to the distal extremities. - Patients may report mild malaise or a low-grade fever, but are otherwise systemically well.

diagnostics.notes: - **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on morphology of the rash and a thorough medication history (including OTCs and supplements). - **Labs (generally not necessary for simple cases):** - If the diagnosis is uncertain or there is concern for a severe reaction, labs may be ordered. - **CBC with differential:** Typically normal. Mild eosinophilia may be present but significant eosinophilia (>1500/L) is a red flag for DRESS. - **CMP:** Liver function tests (AST/ALT) and creatinine are normal. Abnormalities suggest organ involvement (DRESS). - **Skin Biopsy:** Rarely needed. If performed, shows a nonspecific perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, sometimes with eosinophils. It is primarily used to rule out other conditions.

treatment: **Topical Corticosteroids:** Medium-to-high potency (e.g., triamcinolone 0.1% cream) applied BID to affected areas can reduce inflammation and pruritus.
**Oral Antihistamines:** Second-generation (cetirizine, loratadine) for daytime use and first-generation (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) for nighttime use due to sedative effects.
Generally **not required or recommended** for simple eruptions.
May be considered for very severe or persistent cases after SCARs have been definitively ruled out.
management: **Patient Education:**
Inform the patient of the offending drug. The drug should be listed as an allergy in their medical record.
Educate them to avoid the specific drug and structurally related medications in the future.

Provide strict "return to clinic" or "go to ED" instructions if they develop any signs of a severe reaction (high fever, blisters, mouth sores, facial swelling, difficulty breathing, severe skin pain).
**Follow-Up:**
The rash should begin to improve within a few days of stopping the drug and typically resolves over **1-2 weeks**.
The rash may temporarily worsen for 24-48 hours after drug cessation, which is normal.
Resolution is often followed by a fine **desquamation** (peeling) and possible post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
complications: Complications are rare in a truly simple exanthematous eruption.
**Misdiagnosis:** The most significant risk is failing to recognize a developing severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SCAR).
**Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation:** Can occur after the rash resolves, especially in individuals with darker skin tones.
**Excoriations and secondary bacterial infection:** From intense scratching.
sections.prognosis: - **Excellent.** - The condition is self-limiting upon withdrawal of the offending agent. - Full recovery without long-term sequelae is the expected outcome.

sections.overview: Acute Generalized Exanthematous Pustulosis (AGEP) is a rare, severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SCAR) characterized by the acute onset of numerous, small, sterile, non-follicular pustules on a background of widespread edematous erythema. It is most commonly triggered by medications and is typically accompanied by high fever and neutrophilia. Despite its dramatic presentation, AGEP is usually self-limiting with an excellent prognosis upon withdrawal of the offending agent.
sections.epidemiology: * **Incidence:** Rare, estimated at 1-5 cases per million people per year. * **Age:** Can occur at any age, but most common in adults. * **Sex:** Slight female predominance.
sections.clinicalPresentation: * **Latency Period:** **Rapid onset**, usually within **48 hours** of drug exposure, but can be up to 2 weeks. * **Prodrome:** Often begins with a high fever (>38C) and malaise. * **Eruption:** 1. Starts as a burning or pruritic, edematous erythema, often beginning on the **face or in intertriginous areas** (axillae, groin). 2. The rash rapidly generalizes within hours to a few days. 3. **Hundreds to thousands of small (<5 mm), non-follicular, pinhead-sized pustules** erupt on the erythematous base. * **Resolution:** After drug cessation, pustules resolve spontaneously over 1-2 weeks, followed by a characteristic superficial, "collarette-like" desquamation.

diagnostics.notes: * **Diagnosis is primarily clinical**, based on history (drug timeline) and physical exam. * **Laboratory Studies:** * **CBC:** **Marked neutrophilic leukocytosis** is characteristic. Eosinophilia may be present in about 30% of cases but is less pronounced than in DRESS. * **CMP:** May show transient, mild elevation of liver transaminases (AST/ALT) or mild renal insufficiency (elevated BUN/Cr). * **Inflammatory Markers:** Elevated CRP and ESR. * **Skin Biopsy (Confirmatory):** * **Classic finding:** **Spongiform subcorneal and/or intraepidermal pustules**. * Prominent edema of the papillary dermis. * Perivascular inflammatory infiltrate with abundant neutrophils and some eosinophils. * **Patch Testing:** Can be performed 4-6 weeks after resolution to help identify the causative drug.

sections.prognosis: * **Excellent.** * Most cases are self-limiting, with resolution of fever and pustules within 1-2 weeks of drug withdrawal. * Mortality rate is low (<5%), typically occurring in elderly patients with significant comorbidities.

sections.overview: An urticarial drug eruption is a common, acute cutaneous adverse drug reaction characterized by the development of wheals (hives), angioedema, or both. It is typically a Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction to a medication. The eruption is defined by intensely pruritic, transient, erythematous, and edematous plaques. The cornerstone of management is the identification and discontinuation of the offending drug.
sections.epidemiology: * Urticarial drug eruptions are one of the most common types of cutaneous adverse drug reactions. * They account for a significant portion of all drug-induced skin reactions. * Can occur at any age, in any race, and affects both sexes, though some studies suggest a slight female predominance. * Occurs in ~2-5% of hospitalized patients receiving medications.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The clinical history is paramount. A thorough medication history, including timing of administration, is critical. * **Timing:** The reaction typically occurs within minutes to hours after drug administration in a previously sensitized individual. In a first-time exposure, it may take **7-14 days** for sensitization to occur, with the rash appearing late in the treatment course or even after it has finished. * The patient presents with an acute onset of an intensely itchy rash. They may report associated swelling of the lips, tongue, or around the eyes (angioedema). * In severe cases, the patient may report symptoms of anaphylaxis: difficulty breathing, wheezing, throat tightness, dizziness, or syncope.

diagnostics.notes: * **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on a characteristic history and physical exam. * **Laboratory studies are not routinely necessary** for uncomplicated urticaria. * **CBC with differential:** May show eosinophilia, but this is non-specific. * **ESR/CRP:** May be elevated but are also non-specific. * **Skin Biopsy:** Rarely performed. If done (e.g., to rule out urticarial vasculitis), it shows dermal edema with a sparse perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, often containing eosinophils. * **Allergy Testing (Skin Prick, Intradermal):** Can be performed by an allergist to confirm the causative agent *after* the acute reaction has completely resolved. It carries a risk of inducing another reaction.

sections.prognosis: * **Excellent** for most cases once the offending drug is identified and withdrawn. * Symptoms typically begin to improve within 24-48 hours of drug cessation and fully resolve within days to a week. * The prognosis depends on the severity of the reaction; anaphylaxis can be fatal if not treated promptly.

sections.overview: A Lichenoid Drug Eruption is a cell-mediated (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction to a systemic medication that clinically and/or histologically mimics idiopathic Lichen Planus (LP). It is characterized by the appearance of pruritic, violaceous, flat-topped papules and plaques. The key to diagnosis and management is identifying and discontinuing the causative drug. The latency period between starting a drug and the rash appearing can be highly variable, ranging from weeks to over a year.
sections.epidemiology: * **Incidence:** Less common than other drug eruptions like morbilliform exanthems. * **Age:** More common in middle-aged and older adults, likely due to increased medication use (polypharmacy). * **Sex/Race:** No significant predilection, but incidence is tied to the prescription patterns of causative drugs. * **Latency Period:** Highly variable and a key clinical feature. Can develop from **2-3 weeks to over a year** after drug initiation, making the historical connection challenging.
sections.clinicalPresentation: * **Onset:** Typically subacute to chronic. * **Distribution:** Often begins on the trunk and extremities. Can be more widespread and symmetric compared to idiopathic LP. A **photodistribution** (sun-exposed areas like face, neck, dorsal hands/arms) is a strong clue for a drug-induced cause. * **Morphology:** * Lesions are papules and plaques. * **Color:** Violaceous (purple-hued), erythematous, or dusky-brown. * **Shape:** Polygonal or irregularly shaped; can be less well-defined than classic LP. * **Surface:** Flat-topped ("lichenoid") with a fine scale. May appear more eczematous or psoriasiform than classic LP.

diagnostics.notes: * **1. Thorough Medication History:** This is the most crucial diagnostic step. Obtain a detailed list of all current and recently started medications, including prescription, over-the-counter (OTC), and herbal supplements. Note the start date for each. * **2. Skin Biopsy (Punch Biopsy):** * Confirms the "lichenoid" pattern of inflammation. * **Histology Findings:** * **Lichenoid Interface Dermatitis:** A dense, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermal-epidermal (D-E) junction that obscures the border. * Vacuolar degeneration of the basal keratinocyte layer. * Apoptotic keratinocytes (Civatte or colloid bodies) in the lower epidermis or upper dermis. * **Key Histologic Clue:** The presence of **eosinophils** in the infiltrate is more suggestive of a drug-induced etiology than idiopathic LP. Parakeratosis may also be present. * **3. Labs:** Generally not required for diagnosis but may be used to rule out other conditions (e.g., ANA for lupus, LFTs for hepatitis). A CBC may show peripheral eosinophilia.

sections.prognosis: * **Excellent** once the causative drug is identified and discontinued. * Resolution is slow but steady over a period of **weeks to months (sometimes up to a year)**. * Relapse will occur if the patient is re-challenged with the same medication.

sections.overview: Henoch-Schnlein Purpura (HSP), now preferentially called **IgA Vasculitis (IgAV)**, is the most common systemic small-vessel vasculitis in children. It is characterized by the deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes in the walls of small blood vessels, primarily affecting the skin, joints, gastrointestinal (GI) tract, and kidneys. The hallmark of the disease is its cutaneous manifestation: **palpable purpura**, typically distributed on the lower extremities and buttocks.
sections.epidemiology: * **Age:** Primarily a disease of childhood, with 90% of cases occurring in patients <10 years old. The peak incidence is between ages 4 and 6. * **Sex:** Slight male predominance (Male:Female ratio 1.5:1). * **Seasonality:** Higher incidence in the fall, winter, and spring, correlating with the prevalence of URIs. * **Prevalence:** Most common systemic vasculitis in the pediatric population.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The classic presentation is a child who recently recovered from a sore throat or cold and now develops a characteristic rash on their legs, along with potential joint pain, abdominal cramping, and/or blood in the urine. The full **classic tetrad** includes: 1. **Palpable Purpura** (present in 95-100% of cases) 2. **Arthritis/Arthralgia** (~75%) 3. **Abdominal Pain** (~50%) 4. **Renal Disease** (~20-50%) The cutaneous findings are almost always the presenting feature.

diagnostics.notes: IgAV is a **clinical diagnosis** based on the EULAR/PRINTO/PRES criteria: **Palpable purpura** (mandatory criterion) plus at least one of the following: 1. Diffuse abdominal pain 2. Arthritis or arthralgia 3. Renal involvement (hematuria and/or proteinuria) 4. Biopsy showing predominant IgA deposition * **Laboratory Studies (to support diagnosis and rule out differentials):** * **CBC:** Platelet count is **normal or elevated (thrombocytosis)**. This is essential to differentiate from thrombocytopenic purpuras (e.g., ITP, TTP, leukemia). * **Coagulation Studies (PT, PTT, INR):** **Normal**. * **Urinalysis (UA) with Microscopy:** **CRITICAL** for assessing renal involvement. Look for hematuria and/or proteinuria. * **Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP):** Assess BUN and creatinine for renal function. * **ASO Titer / Throat Culture:** May be positive for recent GABHS infection. * **Serum IgA:** Elevated in ~50% of patients, but has low sensitivity and specificity. Not required for diagnosis. * **Biopsy:** * **Skin Biopsy:** The **gold standard** for confirming vasculitis if the diagnosis is uncertain. * **Light Microscopy (H&E stain):** Shows **leukocytoclastic vasculitis** in post-capillary venules (neutrophilic infiltrate, nuclear debris, fibrinoid necrosis). * **Direct Immunofluorescence (DIF):** **Pathognomonic finding** is granular **IgA deposition** in the vessel walls. * **Renal Biopsy:** Indicated for severe or progressive nephritis. Shows **mesangial IgA deposition**, identical to IgA nephropathy (Berger disease).

sections.prognosis: * **Generally excellent.** IgAV is typically a self-limiting disease, with most cases resolving completely within 4-6 weeks. * **Recurrence:** Occurs in up to one-third of patients, usually within the first year. Recurrent episodes are typically milder. * **Long-term prognosis is determined entirely by the degree of renal involvement.**

sections.overview: Erythroderma, also known as exfoliative dermatitis, is a severe, generalized inflammation of the skin characterized by **diffuse erythema and scaling involving greater than 90% of the body surface area (BSA)**. It is not a specific disease but rather a cutaneous reaction pattern to a variety of underlying conditions. Erythroderma is considered a **dermatologic emergency** due to its potential for profound metabolic and systemic decompensation.
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** A rare condition. * **Age:** Predominantly affects adults, with a mean age of onset > 50 years. * **Sex:** More common in males (M:F ratio of 2:1 to 4:1).
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient typically presents with a rapidly progressing, generalized, fiery-red rash associated with systemic illness. The history is critical and should focus on: * Timeline of rash onset and progression. * Personal or family history of skin disease (psoriasis, eczema). * Recent medication changes (new prescriptions, dose changes). * Constitutional "B" symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) to screen for malignancy.
sections.prognosis: * Prognosis is highly dependent on the underlying etiology. * **Good:** Drug-induced erythroderma typically resolves with withdrawal of the offending agent. * **Variable/Chronic:** Caused by psoriasis or atopic dermatitis, often follows a relapsing-remitting course. * **Poor:** Associated with malignancy (CTCL) or in elderly, debilitated patients where complications are more likely.

sections.overview: Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) is a rare, life-threatening, and severe mucocutaneous adverse drug reaction characterized by extensive necrosis and detachment of the epidermis. It represents the most severe end of a spectrum of diseases that includes Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS). The distinction is based on the percentage of Body Surface Area (BSA) with epidermal detachment: * **Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS):** <10% BSA detachment * **SJS/TEN Overlap:** 10-30% BSA detachment * **Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN):** >30% BSA detachment TEN is considered a medical emergency requiring immediate hospitalization, typically in a burn unit or intensive care unit (ICU).
sections.epidemiology: * **Incidence:** Rare, affecting approximately 1-2 persons per million per year. * **Mortality:** High, ranging from 25-35%. * **Demographics:** Can affect any age but is more common in adults. Slightly higher incidence in females. * **Increased Risk:** Patients with HIV have a ~1000-fold increased risk, particularly with sulfa drugs.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation follows a distinct timeline: 1. **Prodrome (1-3 days prior to rash):** * Flu-like symptoms: fever (>39C or 102.2F), malaise, myalgias, arthralgias. * Sore throat, cough, headache. * Ocular symptoms: burning, itching, photophobia. 2. **Cutaneous Eruption:** * Initial rash is often ill-defined, erythematous macules with purpuric centers ("atypical targets"). * Begins on the face and trunk, spreading symmetrically and rapidly. * Lesions are associated with significant pain and a burning sensation. * Over 1-4 days, the macules coalesce, and the epidermis begins to wrinkle and detach, forming large, flaccid bullae that slough off in sheets.

diagnostics.notes: * **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on history (new medication), characteristic rash progression, positive Nikolsky sign, and extensive mucosal involvement. * **Skin Biopsy (Gold Standard for Confirmation):** * A frozen section can provide rapid results. * **Histopathology:** Shows **full-thickness epidermal necrosis** with subepidermal cleavage (separation at the dermo-epidermal junction). The dermal infiltrate is characteristically sparse ("pauci-inflammatory"). * **Laboratory Studies (for management and prognosis, not diagnosis):** * **CBC:** Anemia, lymphopenia (poor prognostic sign). * **CMP:** Electrolyte abnormalities (from fluid loss), hypoalbuminemia, elevated LFTs. * **BUN/Creatinine:** To assess for acute kidney injury. * **Blood cultures:** To rule out sepsis. * **Serum Bicarbonate & Glucose:** Part of the SCORTEN score.

sections.prognosis: * Prognosis is poor, with mortality rates of 25-35%. * The **SCORTEN score** is a validated tool used on day 1 and day 3 to predict mortality. One point is given for each of the 7 criteria: 1. **A**ge > 40 years 2. **M**alignancy (presence of) 3. **H**eart Rate > 120 bpm 4. **E**pidermal detachment on admission > 10% BSA 5. **R**enal: BUN > 28 mg/dL (or Urea > 10 mmol/L) 6. **S**erum Glucose > 252 mg/dL (> 14 mmol/L) 7. **B**icarbonate < 20 mEq/L * **SCORTEN Score & Mortality:** 0-1 (~3%), 2 (~12%), 3 (~35%), 4 (~58%), 5 (>90%).

sections.overview: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) is a severe, life-threatening, immune-mediated mucocutaneous reaction characterized by extensive necrosis and detachment of the epidermis. It is considered a dermatologic emergency. SJS is part of a spectrum of disease with Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN), differentiated by the percentage of body surface area (BSA) with skin detachment. * **SJS:** <10% BSA detachment * **SJS/TEN Overlap:** 10-30% BSA detachment * **TEN:** >30% BSA detachment
sections.epidemiology: * **Incidence:** Rare, affecting approximately 1-2 people per million per year. * **Mortality:** SJS has a mortality rate of ~10%. The rate increases significantly with progression to TEN (>30%). * **Demographics:** Can occur at any age, in any race, and in both sexes. Incidence is higher in patients with HIV and active cancer.
sections.clinicalPresentation: * **Prodrome:** Begins 1-3 days before the rash with non-specific, flu-like symptoms: * Fever (>39C / 102.2F) * Malaise, myalgias, arthralgias * Headache * Pharyngitis * **Cutaneous Eruption:** * Starts with ill-defined, erythematous macules, often with purpuric centers. * Lesions typically begin on the face and trunk and spread symmetrically. * Progresses to **atypical target lesions** (2 zones of color, dusky center, indistinct border). * Lesions coalesce, forming flaccid bullae that slough off with minimal pressure, leaving behind raw, denuded dermis. * **Mucosal Involvement:** A hallmark of SJS. Occurs in >90% of cases and **at least two mucosal surfaces** are typically involved.

diagnostics.notes: * **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on history (drug exposure) and physical exam findings (characteristic rash, positive Nikolsky sign, mucosal involvement). * **Skin Biopsy (Gold Standard for confirmation):** * Shows **full-thickness epidermal necrosis** and a subepidermal split. * Dermal inflammatory infiltrate is characteristically sparse. * Immunofluorescence is negative, helping to rule out autoimmune blistering diseases. * **Laboratory Studies (for management and prognosis, not diagnosis):** * CBC: Anemia, lymphopenia. Neutropenia is a poor prognostic sign. * CMP: Assess for electrolyte abnormalities, renal dysfunction (prerenal azotemia), and low albumin. * Blood cultures: To rule out sepsis. * CRP/ESR: Markedly elevated.

sections.prognosis: * Prognosis is determined using the **SCORTEN** scale on day 1 and 3 of admission. It predicts mortality based on 7 independent risk factors. * **SCORTEN Variables (1 point each):** 1. **A**ge > 40 years 2. **M**alignancy present 3. **H**eart rate > 120 bpm 4. **I**nitial BSA detachment > 10% 5. **B**UN > 28 mg/dL 6. **B**icarbonate < 20 mEq/L 7. **G**lucose > 252 mg/dL * Mortality increases exponentially with a higher SCORTEN score.

sections.overview: Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS), also known as Drug-Induced Hypersensitivity Syndrome (DIHS), is a severe, idiosyncratic, delayed-type (Type IVb) hypersensitivity reaction. It is characterized by a classic triad of **widespread rash**, **eosinophilia** (or atypical lymphocytosis), and **internal organ involvement**. The defining feature is a long latency period of **2-8 weeks** between drug initiation and symptom onset. It carries a significant mortality rate (~10%), primarily due to fulminant hepatitis.
sections.epidemiology: - **Incidence**: Rare, estimated at 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 10,000 drug exposures. - **Demographics**: Affects all ages, races, and sexes, but certain genetic predispositions increase risk in specific populations.
riskFactors: **Genetic Predisposition (High-Yield)**: Strong associations exist between specific HLA alleles and drug-induced DRESS.
**HLA-B\*5801**: Increased risk with **Allopurinol**, particularly in Han Chinese and Thai populations.
**HLA-A\*3101**: Increased risk with **Carbamazepine** in Northern European populations.
**HLA-B\*1502**: Strongly associated with Carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN, but also a risk factor for DRESS in some Asian populations.
**Viral Co-infection**: Latent or active HHV-6, EBV, or CMV.
**Drug-Related**: Rapid dose escalation (e.g., lamotrigine), high daily dosage.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation is marked by a **long latency period of 2-8 weeks** following the initiation of the culprit drug. The illness typically begins with a non-specific prodrome before the characteristic rash appears.

diagnostics.notes: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by lab findings and ruling out other causes. The **RegiSCAR criteria** are often used for definitive diagnosis. - **Laboratory Studies**: - **CBC with Differential**: - **Eosinophilia**: Hallmark finding. Count often **>1,500 cells/L**. May be delayed. - **Atypical Lymphocytosis**: Also a very common and characteristic finding. - Anemia, thrombocytopenia may also be present. - **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**: - **Elevated Liver Transaminases (ALT/AST)**: The most common sign of organ involvement. Can range from mild elevation to fulminant hepatic necrosis. - **Elevated BUN and Creatinine**: Indicates acute interstitial nephritis (AIN). - **Inflammatory Markers**: Elevated CRP and ESR. - **Viral Serology/PCR**: Can test for **HHV-6 reactivation** to support the diagnosis. - **Skin Biopsy**: Not always necessary but can be useful to exclude other conditions. Findings include a dense, perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, often with eosinophils. - **Imaging**: - **Chest X-ray or CT**: To evaluate for interstitial pneumonitis.

treatment: **First-Line**: **Systemic Corticosteroids**.
Dose: **Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day** (or equivalent).
**Crucial Point**: Requires a **very slow taper over 8-12 weeks** or longer. Rapid tapering can cause a severe relapse of the disease.
**Topical Therapy**: High-potency topical corticosteroids for skin symptoms.
**Second-Line (for severe/steroid-refractory cases)**:
Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG)
Cyclosporine
Mycophenolate Mofetil
management: **Inpatient Monitoring**: Daily monitoring of CBC (for eosinophils), CMP (for liver/renal function), and clinical status is essential.
**Outpatient Follow-up**: Continue to monitor labs weekly to monthly during the steroid taper.
**Patient Education**:
Counsel the patient to **strictly avoid the culprit drug for life**.
Inform them of potential cross-reactivity with structurally similar medications (e.g., other aromatic anticonvulsants).
Provide a medical alert bracelet or wallet card.
complications: **Acute**:
**Fulminant Hepatic Failure** (most common cause of death).
Acute Interstitial Nephritis leading to renal failure.
Myocarditis, pericarditis.
Pneumonitis, ARDS.
Encephalitis, thyroiditis, colitis.
**Long-Term**:
Increased risk of developing **autoimmune diseases**, such as Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), Type 1 Diabetes, and Autoimmune Thyroiditis (Grave's or Hashimoto's).
sections.prognosis: - **Mortality**: Approximately **10%**. - **Cause of Death**: Most commonly due to **fulminant hepatitis**, followed by myocarditis. - **Recovery**: The course is often prolonged, lasting weeks to months. Relapses are common if steroids are tapered too quickly.

sections.overview: Impetigo is a highly contagious, superficial bacterial skin infection affecting the epidermis. It is one of the most common skin infections in children. It primarily manifests in two forms: non-bullous (crusted) and bullous (blistering). A deeper, ulcerative form is known as ecthyma.
sections.epidemiology: * Most common bacterial skin infection in children, with a peak incidence in ages 2-5. * More prevalent in warm, humid climates and during summer months. * Spreads easily in crowded environments like daycares and schools through direct contact.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient, typically a young child, presents with non-painful skin lesions that started as small red spots, often around the nose or mouth. The parent reports that the initial spots quickly turned into small blisters that popped and formed a distinctive yellowish-brown crust. The lesions may be itchy, and scratching has caused new spots to appear nearby. Systemic symptoms like fever are generally absent.

diagnostics.notes: * **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic appearance of the lesions. * **Gram Stain and Bacterial Culture**: Recommended in cases of treatment failure, atypical presentation, or suspicion of MRSA. * Sample is obtained from the moisture beneath a crust or fluid from an intact pustule/bulla. * Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters (_S. aureus_) or chains (_S. pyogenes_). * Culture confirms the organism and provides antibiotic sensitivities. * **Biopsy**: Rarely necessary.

sections.prognosis: * Excellent. With appropriate treatment, lesions typically resolve within 7-10 days. * Post-inflammatory pigmentary changes may occur but usually fade over time. * Recurrence is possible, especially if underlying risk factors (e.g., nasal carriage of _S. aureus_, atopic dermatitis) are not addressed.

sections.overview: Erysipelas is a specific type of superficial cellulitis, an acute infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics. It is clinically characterized by a raised, intensely erythematous plaque with a sharply demarcated border that distinguishes it from surrounding normal skin.
sections.epidemiology: * **Age:** Primarily affects young children and older adults (>60 years). * **Location:** * **Adults:** Most commonly affects the **lower extremities** (~85% of cases). * **Children:** The **face** (malar or "butterfly" distribution) is a more common location. * No significant gender or racial predilection.
sections.clinicalPresentation: * **Onset:** Typically abrupt and acute. * **Prodrome:** Often preceded by systemic symptoms for 4-48 hours before the rash appears. * Fever, chills, malaise, headache. * **Skin Lesion:** A small erythematous patch rapidly progresses to a fiery-red, indurated, tense, and shiny plaque. The area is exquisitely tender and warm to the touch.

diagnostics.notes: * **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on the characteristic physical exam findings. * **Laboratory Studies (often not required for mild cases):** * **CBC:** Leukocytosis with a neutrophilic predominance ("left shift") is common. * **Inflammatory Markers:** Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR). * **Blood Cultures:** Low yield (<5% positive) but should be obtained in systemically ill or immunocompromised patients to rule out bacteremia. * **Imaging:** * Generally not indicated. * **Ultrasound or MRI** may be used if there is suspicion of a deeper infection, such as an abscess or necrotizing fasciitis.

sections.prognosis: * Excellent with prompt and appropriate antibiotic therapy. * Fever typically resolves within 24-72 hours of starting antibiotics. Skin changes resolve more slowly over 1-2 weeks. * Recurrence is common (~30% of patients), especially if underlying risk factors are not managed.

sections.overview: Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection of the skin, specifically involving the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue. It manifests as a spreading area of erythema, warmth, swelling, and tenderness. Unlike erysipelas, which is more superficial and has sharply demarcated borders, cellulitis has ill-defined, non-palpable borders. It typically occurs after a breach in the skin barrier, allowing bacteria to invade.
sections.epidemiology: * One of the most common infectious disease-related reasons for hospitalization in the U.S. * Incidence increases with age, most common in middle-aged and older adults. * The lower extremities are the most frequently affected site (>80% of cases). * No significant difference in incidence between sexes.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient typically presents with the acute onset of a localized area of skin that is red, swollen, warm, and painful. The symptoms often develop over 1-2 days and progressively worsen. The patient may also experience systemic symptoms such as fever, chills, and malaise, especially with rapidly spreading or severe infection. A history of a preceding minor skin injury may or may not be present.

diagnostics.notes: Cellulitis is **primarily a clinical diagnosis**. Ancillary testing is reserved for patients with systemic toxicity, extensive disease, underlying comorbidities, or failure of initial therapy. * **Laboratory Studies:** * **CBC with differential:** May show leukocytosis with a neutrophilic predominance ("left shift"). * **Inflammatory Markers:** Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) are common but non-specific. Can be useful to track response to therapy. * **Blood Cultures:** Low yield (~5%) in uncomplicated cellulitis. Indicated for patients with SIRS/sepsis criteria, extensive disease, or severe immunosuppression. * **Creatine Kinase (CK):** Order if concern for necrotizing fasciitis (will be markedly elevated). * **Imaging:** * **Ultrasound:** Highly useful at the bedside to differentiate uncomplicated cellulitis from a drainable abscess (appears as a hypoechoic or anechoic fluid collection) or to rule out DVT. * **X-ray:** Can show soft tissue swelling. Primarily used to rule out osteomyelitis or subcutaneous gas (a sign of necrotizing fasciitis). * **CT / MRI:** Not routinely needed. Reserved for cases where necrotizing fasciitis or deep space infection is suspected and clinical diagnosis is uncertain. MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality for these conditions. * **Microbiology:** * **Wound/Pus Culture:** Indicated for purulent cellulitis (after I&D), open wounds, or animal bites. * **Needle Aspiration/Biopsy:** Low yield in non-purulent cellulitis. Considered for immunocompromised patients or in cases of treatment failure.

sections.prognosis: * The prognosis is excellent for uncomplicated cellulitis treated promptly with appropriate antibiotics. * Recurrence is common (~30%), especially if underlying risk factors (lymphedema, venous insufficiency) are not managed. * Mortality is low but increases significantly with complications like sepsis or necrotizing fasciitis, or in patients with severe comorbidities.

sections.overview: Folliculitis is the inflammation of one or more hair follicles. It can be superficial or deep and can occur anywhere on the skin where hair is present. The condition is characterized by erythematous papules or pustules centered around a hair follicle. It can be infectious (bacterial, fungal, viral) or non-infectious (mechanical, inflammatory).
sections.epidemiology: * Folliculitis is a very common condition affecting individuals of all ages, sexes, and races. * *P. aeruginosa* folliculitis often occurs in outbreaks related to contaminated recreational water sources. * *Malassezia* folliculitis is more common in young adults living in warm, humid climates. * Pseudofolliculitis barbae is most prevalent in individuals with tightly curled hair who shave closely.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The patient typically presents with an eruption of small, tender, or pruritic bumps, which may or may not contain pus, in hair-bearing areas. The onset can be acute.

diagnostics.notes: * **Primarily a clinical diagnosis** based on history and physical exam. * **Gram Stain and Bacterial Culture:** Indicated for recurrent, treatment-refractory, or severe cases. A sample is obtained by unroofing a pustule with a sterile needle and swabbing the purulent material. Helps identify the organism (e.g., *S. aureus*) and determine antibiotic sensitivities (crucial for MRSA). * **KOH Preparation:** Used if a fungal etiology is suspected. Skin scrapings or pustule contents are examined under a microscope. * *Malassezia*: Shows "spaghetti and meatballs" pattern of budding yeasts and hyphae. * Dermatophyte: Shows septate hyphae. * **Skin Biopsy:** Rarely necessary. Performed for persistent, atypical, or non-infectious cases (e.g., eosinophilic folliculitis). Histology will show a perifollicular inflammatory infiltrate. * **Viral Culture or Tzanck Smear:** If herpetic folliculitis is suspected.

sections.prognosis: * **Excellent** for most cases of superficial folliculitis, which often resolve with conservative care and topical therapy. * Deep folliculitis (furuncles/carbuncles) has a good prognosis with appropriate antibiotic therapy and/or I&D but may lead to scarring. * Recurrence is common if underlying risk factors are not addressed.

sections.overview: An abscess is a localized collection of pus (purulent material) that accumulates in a tissue, organ, or confined space. It is the result of the body's inflammatory response to an infection, typically bacterial. The defining feature is a central core of necrotic leukocytes (neutrophils) and tissue debris, often encapsulated by a fibrous wall (pyogenic membrane) that isolates the infection from surrounding tissue.
sections.epidemiology: * Abscesses are extremely common and occur in all age groups. * Cutaneous abscesses are one ofthe most frequent skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) seen in emergency departments. * The incidence of CA-MRSA as the primary cause of cutaneous abscesses has significantly increased over the past two decades.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The presentation varies based on location (cutaneous vs. deep/internal). * **Cutaneous Abscess:** Patients typically present with a new or enlarging painful, localized mass on the skin. The area is red, swollen, and warm. It may or may not be spontaneously draining pus. * **Deep Abscess (e.g., intra-abdominal, psoas, hepatic):** Presentation can be insidious. Patients often present with non-specific systemic symptoms like fever, chills, malaise, and anorexia, along with localized pain (e.g., abdominal pain, flank pain). A palpable mass is rare.
sections.prognosis: * **Excellent** for simple cutaneous abscesses treated promptly with I&D. * **Guarded** for deep, large, or multi-loculated abscesses, especially in immunocompromised or critically ill patients. Mortality is associated with the development of sepsis.

sections.overview: Necrotizing fasciitis (NF) is a rare, life-threatening, and rapidly progressive infection of the deep soft tissues. It spreads quickly along the fascial planes, causing widespread necrosis of the subcutaneous tissue and fascia. The overlying skin may initially appear unaffected, masking the severity of the underlying destruction. NF is a **true surgical emergency** requiring immediate diagnosis and aggressive intervention to prevent limb loss, systemic toxicity, and death. It is often referred to by the layman's term "flesh-eating bacteria."
sections.epidemiology: * **Incidence:** Rare, estimated at 0.4 to 1.0 cases per 100,000 people per year in the US. * **Mortality:** High, ranging from 20% to 30% even with aggressive treatment. * **Location:** Can occur anywhere on the body, but most common on the extremities, perineum (**Fournier's gangrene**), and trunk.
sections.clinicalPresentation: The classic presentation is a patient with a rapidly progressing soft tissue infection whose systemic signs of toxicity and severe pain are **wildly out of proportion** to the initial cutaneous findings. What may look like simple cellulitis can be a devastating underlying infection.

diagnostics.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, but labs and imaging can support suspicion. **Definitive diagnosis is made in the operating room.** * **Surgical Exploration (Gold Standard):** Direct visualization of necrotic fascia. Fascia appears gray and dull, does not bleed when cut, and separates easily from underlying tissue ("finger test" - blunt dissection with a finger meets no resistance). Tissue is sent for Gram stain and culture. * **Laboratory Findings:** * **LRINEC Score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis):** A scoring system to stratify risk. A score of **6 is suspicious**, and **8 is highly predictive**. *This tool should never delay surgical consultation.* * Components: CRP (>150), WBC (>15), Hemoglobin (<13.5), Sodium (<135), Creatinine (>1.6), Glucose (>180). * **Leukocytosis** with a profound left shift. * **Hyponatremia** (common and significant). * Elevated **Creatine Kinase (CK)** indicating muscle involvement. * Elevated **Lactate**, indicating tissue hypoperfusion. * Signs of AKI (elevated BUN/Cr) and DIC (thrombocytopenia, elevated INR). * **Imaging:** **Should NOT delay surgery.** Used for equivocal cases or to assess the extent of disease. * **CT Scan:** Best initial imaging test. Findings include **subcutaneous gas**, fascial thickening (>3 mm), fluid collections, and fat stranding. * **Plain X-ray:** May show subcutaneous gas but is very insensitive.

sections.prognosis: * Mortality remains high (20-30%). * Poor prognostic factors include: * Delay in diagnosis and surgical debridement (>24 hours) * Age > 60 * Presence of comorbidities (especially Diabetes and PVD) * Truncal or perineal involvement * Development of septic shock

sections.overview: Tinea corporis, commonly known as "ringworm," is a superficial dermatophyte infection of the glabrous skin (skin of the trunk, extremities, and face). It is characterized by the classic presentation of an annular (ring-shaped), erythematous, scaling plaque with central clearing. It is one of the most common fungal infections worldwide.
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** Worldwide distribution. More common in warm, humid climates. * **Age:** Affects all ages, but is particularly common in children and young adults. * **Setting:** Outbreaks can occur in settings with close physical contact, such as schools, daycare centers, and among athletes (especially wrestlers, known as tinea gladiatorum).
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient typically presents with a complaint of an "itchy, ring-shaped rash" that has been slowly enlarging over several days to weeks. The history may include exposure to an infected person or animal, or participation in high-risk activities. Lesions can be single or multiple and may appear on any part of the body, most commonly the trunk and limbs.

diagnostics.notes: * **Clinical Diagnosis:** Often made based on the classic history and physical exam findings. * **KOH Preparation (Potassium Hydroxide Microscopy):** * **Procedure:** Vigorously scrape scales from the active, advancing border of the lesion onto a glass slide. Add a drop of 10-20% KOH solution and a coverslip. Gently heat the slide to dissolve keratinocytes. * **Finding:** Visualization of **segmented (septate) hyphae** confirms the diagnosis of a dermatophyte infection. This is the most cost-effective and rapid confirmatory test. * **Fungal Culture (Sabouraud's Agar):** * Gold standard for identifying the specific species. * Indicated for atypical presentations, treatment failure, or when KOH is negative but suspicion remains high. * Results take 2-4 weeks. * **Wood's Lamp Examination:** * Most tinea corporis caused by *T. rubrum* does **not** fluoresce. * Some *Microsporum* species (*M. canis*, *M. audouinii*) may show a blue-green fluorescence. Primarily useful for tinea capitis. * **Skin Biopsy with PAS Stain:** * Rarely needed. * Reserved for cases where the diagnosis is uncertain and other diagnoses (e.g., granuloma annulare, psoriasis) are being considered. * Histology shows hyphae in the stratum corneum.

sections.prognosis: * Excellent with appropriate treatment. * Lesions typically resolve completely, although post-inflammatory pigment changes may take months to fade. * Recurrence is common if underlying risk factors are not addressed or if treatment is not completed.

sections.overview: Tinea capitis is a dermatophyte fungal infection of the hair follicles and scalp skin. It is the most common dermatophytosis of childhood. The infection invades the hair shaft and follicle, leading to scaling, inflammation, and alopecia (hair loss). Prompt diagnosis and treatment with systemic antifungals are crucial to prevent permanent hair loss and transmission.
sections.epidemiology: - **Primary Population**: Prepubertal children, typically ages 3-7. - **Gender**: Slightly more common in males. - **Geography**: More prevalent in urban, overcrowded environments. - **Race**: Higher incidence in African American children, potentially due to hair care practices and hair structure.
riskFactors: Contact with infected individuals or asymptomatic carriers
Contact with infected pets (kittens and puppies are common vectors for *M. canis*)
sections.clinicalPresentation: A parent typically brings in a child due to one or more patches of hair loss on the scalp that may be scaly or itchy. The presentation is highly variable and can be inflammatory or non-inflammatory.

diagnostics.notes: - **Clinical Diagnosis**: Often made based on classic presentation (scaling alopecia + occipital lymphadenopathy in a child). Confirmation is recommended. - **Wood's Lamp Examination**: - Shining a black light on the scalp. - **Positive (bright blue-green fluorescence)**: Suggests *Microsporum* species (*M. canis*, *M. audouinii*). - **Negative (no fluorescence)**: Characteristic of ***T. tonsurans***, the most common cause. **A negative exam does not rule out tinea capitis.** - **KOH Prep (Potassium Hydroxide)**: - **Best initial test.** - Scalp scrapings and plucked hairs are placed on a slide with KOH. - Microscopy reveals hyphae and spores. - Can differentiate endothrix vs. ectothrix patterns. - **Fungal Culture**: - **Gold standard for diagnosis.** - Identifies the exact species, which can be useful for epidemiology and treatment failures. - Takes 2-4 weeks for results.

treatment: **First-Line Agents**:
Classic treatment of choice, especially for *Microsporum*.
Dose: 20-25 mg/kg/day of microsize formulation for 6-8 weeks.
**Administration**: Must be taken with a **fatty meal** (e.g., milk, ice cream) to enhance absorption.
Monitoring: LFTs at baseline and periodically for long courses.
Highly effective for *T. tonsurans* and often preferred due to shorter course (4-6 weeks).
Less effective for *Microsporum*.
Dosing is weight-based.
**Adjunctive Therapy**:
**Antifungal Shampoo** (Ketoconazole 2% or Selenium Sulfide 2.5%):
Use 2-3 times per week.
**Does not cure the infection** but decreases spore shedding and reduces transmissibility.
Should be used by the patient and household contacts.
**Treatment of Kerion**:

In addition to systemic antifungals, a short course of **oral corticosteroids** (e.g., Prednisone 1-2 mg/kg/day for 1-2 weeks) is recommended to reduce inflammation and decrease the risk of permanent scarring alopecia.
management: **Patient Education**: Emphasize the importance of medication adherence for the full course and taking griseofulvin with a fatty meal.
**Fomite Control**: Wash all combs, brushes, hats, pillowcases, and bedding in hot water to prevent reinfection and spread.
**Screen Household Contacts**: Examine close family members for signs of infection or asymptomatic carriage. Treat carriers with antifungal shampoo.
**Return to School**: Children may return to school once systemic therapy has been initiated.
**Follow-up**: Re-evaluate in 4-8 weeks to assess for clinical improvement. Treatment should continue until clinical and mycological cure is achieved.
complications: **Cicatricial (Scarring) Alopecia**: Permanent hair loss, the most significant complication. Highest risk with kerion and favus.
**Id (Dermatophytid) Reaction**: An allergic, sterile vesicular rash that can appear on the face, trunk, or hands in response to the fungal antigens.
**Secondary Bacterial Infection (Impetiginization)**: Superimposed bacterial infection, especially with kerion.
**Psychosocial Distress**: Significant impact on self-esteem due to hair loss.
sections.prognosis: - **Excellent** with early diagnosis and appropriate, full-course systemic therapy. - Hair regrowth typically begins within 4-6 weeks of starting treatment and can take 6-12 months to be complete. - Prognosis is guarded if significant scarring has already occurred.

sections.overview: Tinea cruris, commonly known as "jock itch," is a superficial dermatophyte (fungal) infection of the inguinal folds, proximal inner thighs, and buttocks. It is a form of dermatophytosis that specifically affects the groin region. The infection is characterized by a pruritic, erythematous, and scaling rash, typically with a raised, advancing border and central clearing.
sections.epidemiology: * **Prevalence:** A very common dermatologic condition. * **Demographics:** * Significantly more common in males (male-to-female ratio ~3:1). * Most frequently affects adolescents and young adult men. * **Geography:** More common in hot, humid climates and during summer months.
sections.clinicalPresentation: A patient typically presents with a complaint of a persistent, intensely itchy rash in the groin that has been slowly expanding over several weeks. They may report that it worsens with sweating or physical activity. They often have a history of recent athletic activity or live in a warm environment.

diagnostics.notes: * **Clinical Diagnosis:** Diagnosis is most often made based on the characteristic history and physical exam findings. * **KOH Preparation (Potassium Hydroxide):** * **Indication:** To confirm the diagnosis, especially in atypical cases or if unresponsive to initial therapy. * **Procedure:** Scrape scales from the most active area (the advancing border) onto a glass slide.
